sessions.title: From Schedule of Activities to Define.xml: Automating the Pathway from Design to Submission
sessions.abstract:
CDISC’s Unified Study Definitions Model (USDM) captures the complete study design, from textual elements to objectives, endpoints, and eligibility criteria, through to the schedule of activities, including its underlying logic and detailed structure. Driven by ICH M11 protocol adoption and the increasing use of AI to enable automated structuring and content libraries, USDM is becoming one of the most important enablers of digital data flow. For CDISC 360i, USDM, in combination with CDISC Biomedical Concepts (BCs), provides the starting point for a fully digitised pathway from study design to submission.
Through hands-on experience, this workshop will give you direct insight into how the schedule of activities can be stored in the USDM timeline structure. From there, we move on to the actual assessments linked to the Schedule of Activities, and see how we can structure them as biomedical concepts, link them to the corresponding SDTM specializations, and then use these specializations to inform define.xml creation. We will conclude with an introduction to the new CDISC handbooks, which explain the requirements and technical implementation details of this digital data flow process.

sessions.title: Agentic AI in Clinical Programming: Separating Hype from Production-Ready Practice with R/Python
sessions.abstract:
AI-assisted coding has moved from demonstration to deployment — but what works in practical, regulated environments? This workshop cuts through the noise to show what is ready for use today. We explore the questions teams are actively asking: how to achieve consistent, traceable outputs from AI tools, how to keep programmers in the loop, and which governance patterns are emerging across the industry.
This workshop demonstrates implementation patterns through hands-on exercises. Participants will work with Positron (Posit’s polyglot IDE with native AI capabilities), Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, and open-source tools (ellmer, ragnar, shinychat) to build LLM-assisted ADaM spec-to-code workflows with human-in-the-loop validation. Participants will leave with practical approaches, reusable patterns, and ideas they can take back to their teams.
Key Takeaways:
– Technical trade-offs: Evaluating deterministic versus probabilistic code generation for CDISC programming and trial integrity
– Compliance-friendly workflows: Building AI pipelines that support audit readiness, access controls, and traceability within enterprise SCEs
– Hands-on automation: Developing governed AI agents that convert complex study specifications into standards-aligned R code
Statistical programmers and data scientists will gain hands-on experience with practical AI tooling workflows, structured prompt engineering, and Positron’s native IDE features. Biometrics leads and IT architects will learn operational strategies for human-in-the-loop oversight and secure pathways for progressing AI deployments from pilot to production workloads.

sessions.title: QC Workflow in the AI-enabled Open World
sessions.abstract:
As AI, open-source programming, automation, and global delivery models reshape clinical development, traditional Quality Control (QC) approaches are under increasing pressure. How can organisations move beyond blanket double programming while remaining compliant, inspection-ready, and confident in their results?
This interactive workshop invites participants to tackle some of the most pressing QC challenges facing the industry today. Working in small, multidisciplinary groups, attendees will explore realistic scenarios covering topics such as risk-based QC, AI-assisted review, validation of open-source environments, reusable code, and inspection-ready evidence. Together, participants will design practical QC approaches, discuss trade-offs and evolving guardrails, and compare solutions across organisations and roles.
Whether you are a statistical programmer, statistician, QA professional, regulator, software vendor, or biometrics leader, this workshop offers an opportunity to share experiences, learn from peers, and help shape emerging best practice. The outcomes will directly contribute to the PHUSE QC Workflow Optimisation white paper, ensuring that attendees play an active role in defining the future of QC in an AI-enabled world.

Leadership Under Pressure, Resilience Through Setbacks, and the Ability To Inspire Teams When It Matters Most Are Challenges That Define High-Performing Organisations
sessions.abstract:
Gary McAllister is a Scottish football legend whose career exemplifies what it means to lead with vision, adapt across decades, and deliver results at the highest level. As a central midfielder who captained clubs to championship glory and earned 57 caps for Scotland, McAllister is recognised not only for his technical brilliance on the pitch but for his capacity to galvanise teams, read complex situations, and perform when the stakes are highest.
McAllister's professional journey began at Motherwell FC in 1981, where his skill and composure quickly attracted attention from English football. His move to Leicester City in 1985 established him as a player of remarkable consistency and vision, qualities that led Leeds United to secure his signature in 1990. At Leeds, McAllister captained the team to the English First Division title in the 1991-92 season, a triumph built on tactical intelligence and unwavering determination. Perhaps his most memorable chapter came at Liverpool, where, at the age of 35, he played a pivotal role in the club's treble-winning season in 2000–01, securing the FA Cup, League Cup, and UEFA Cup. His stunning free kick in the FA Cup final replay remains one of football's iconic moments. Beyond his playing career, McAllister transitioned seamlessly into coaching and management, leading clubs including Coventry City, Leeds United, and Aston Villa, and serving as assistant manager at Rangers and Liverpool. Awarded an MBE in 2001 for his services to football and inducted into the Scottish Football Hall of Fame in 2016, his credentials reflect a lifetime of contribution to the sport.
McAllister brings audiences practical insights into leadership, teamwork, and mental resilience drawn from real experience at the top of professional sport. He speaks with authenticity about overcoming adversity, maintaining focus under scrutiny, and building cultures where individuals thrive collectively. Whether addressing corporate teams, sporting organisations, or leadership forums, McAllister connects the lessons of elite competition to the everyday challenges faced by audiences. His presentations are engaging, grounded, and motivational, offering actionable strategies that help teams perform with confidence, adapt to change, and sustain success over time. Audiences leave with a renewed perspective on what it takes to lead effectively and a clear understanding of how resilience and vision translate into lasting impact.

sessions.title: Shiny App Validation for GxP: Practical Challenges, Operational Patterns, and Next-Generation Tooling
sessions.abstract: The migration of clinical workflows from SAS to R has matured: SCEs are being qualified, package risk-assessment frameworks are established, and Shiny apps increasingly support clinical and biostatistical work. The next challenge has surfaced: validating Shiny apps for GxP use, where R-validation guidance offers limited practical direction.This talk outlines the challenges and methodologies for validating Shiny apps in regulated deliverables. We focus on operational patterns for collaboration between app teams and QA, including risk-based artifacts aligned with GAMP 5 and anchoring to existing SOPs through lightweight working practices.We then introduce `shiny.val.tools`, an open-source R package that automates validation document generation through static analysis of Shiny code. The package emits a closed reactive subgraph for each user-facing output, scoping evidence to features QA reviewers recognize, alongside a package and function inventory with risk-classification stubs. Artifacts regenerate on code change and slot directly into a validation package.Attendees will leave with a working mental model of Shiny app validation and a concrete tooling pattern to apply.

sessions.title: Trust, Not Templates: Rethinking Partnerships Through a Professional Development Lens
sessions.abstract:
What actually makes a partnership work, when timelines don't align, priorities compete and organisational cultures are worlds apart? The answer isn't process, it's people. Trust, relationship-building skills and the ability to adapt across boundaries are what turn a working relationship into a genuinely productive one, yet these are the skills we talk about least.
This interactive session brings together practitioners with experience working across regulatory, HTA and industry boundaries, including representatives from NICE. The first half is a panel discussion, with candid, personal stories of what it takes to build effective working relationships across boundaries: the moments that built trust, lessons learned the hard way, and the interpersonal skills that made the difference. The second half is hands-on, with attendees working through real scenarios to sharpen their own approach to boundary-spanning relationships.

sessions.title: Decompose, Group, or Route? Strategies to Optimize LLM-Based Extraction in Literature Reviews
sessions.stream: Machine Learning, AI & Large Language Models
sessions.abstract: Data extraction from medical publications is a foundational step in systematic and targeted literature reviews but extracting hundreds of variables across hundreds of publications makes manual extraction a major bottleneck in evidence generation. We investigated the use of Large Language Models (LLMs) to automate this. An initial LLM-based extraction pipeline, configured by subject-matter experts (SMEs) around semantically grouped variables, performed well for simple variables in well-structured documents, but showed reduced accuracy on complex cases including subgroup-level data or data distributed across text, tables, and figures. We developed, evaluated and compared three strategies: grouped multivariate extraction, automated decomposition into single-variable extractions, and a hybrid routing approach that decomposes only on complex variables or documents. Strategies were assessed across GPT model variants and benchmarked against gold-standard human extractions, reporting accuracy alongside token cost and latency. We discuss the trade-offs, estimated SME-hours saved per literature review and next steps for literature review automation.

sessions.title: CDISC 360i Phase 2: Learning by Doing in Digital Standards Innovation
sessions.abstract: CDISC 360i was established as an iterative program to explore how clinical research standards can evolve through rapid development, hands‑on testing, and structured learning. Rather than assuming a fixed end state, CDISC 360i Phases 1, 2, and beyond are designed to exercise emerging standards in realistic scenarios to understand what works, where gaps remain, and what requires refinement.This presentation focuses on the intent, project approach, and key learnings from CDISC 360i Phase 2, informed by outcomes shared at the CDISC US Interchange. Phase 2 concentrates on operationalizing concepts previously established in Phase 1 by exercising four core capabilities: a machine‑readable digital protocol with automated impact analysis, automated generation of eCRFs, Define.xml and datasets, a digital data transfer agreement model, and a standardized, configurable analysis concept model. The session will highlight the most important insights gained, where assumptions were challenged, and how these learnings are shaping subsequent phases of CDISC 360i.

sessions.title: Beyond Standard Summaries: Evaluating and Visualizing the Impact of Information Loss in Clinical Trial Adverse Event Reporting
sessions.abstract: Standard adverse event reporting relies on frequency thresholds and severity aggregation, which are conventions that systematically reduce data dimensionality and may hide clinically relevant safety signals.This study quantifies that information loss and evaluates visualization-based alternatives. Using entropy, coverage, and structural divergence metrics, information loss is shown to increase non-linearly with threshold stringency, with the sharpest losses at commonly used cut-offs.Alternative safety visualizations were assessed in an expert study using the ICE-T (Insight, Confidence, Efficiency, Trust) framework. A striking finding emerged: the most information-rich representation, a Correspondence Analysis biplot, achieved the highest task accuracy (69%) yet received the lowest subjective ratings for confidence and trust, revealing a tension between objective information retention and perceived interpretability.These results challenge assumptions about what makes a safety summary "good" and offer a reproducible framework for evaluating reporting trade-offs, with direct implications for regulatory safety reporting and visualization design in clinical trials.

sessions.title: Pinned, Approved, Audit-Ready: A Governance Framework for R and Python Package Management in GxP Statistical Programming
sessions.abstract: The industry's move to open source statistical computing has outpaced its governance frameworks. Controlling a SAS installation is well understood. Controlling R and Python in a GxP environment at scale is not. Package versions must be pinned. New tools need evaluation and approval. Study teams running concurrent programs often need different versions simultaneously. The policies governing all of this are still being written.Most organizations are resolving this through manual process and informal workarounds. That approach creates reproducibility risk that is difficult to detect until a submission is under regulatory scrutiny, at which point the audit trail for environment decisions is what an inspector wants to see and what manual processes fail to reliably produce.This presentation examines what robust package governance actually requires in a multilingual GxP environment: controlled repository architecture, version pinning strategies, update management during live studies, and the documentation trail regulators expect. The goal is a framework practitioners can take back and apply, not a product recommendation.

sessions.title: Clinical Data as a Product: Beyond SDTM and ADaM, Towards an AI-Ready Data Foundation
sessions.abstract: The industry has spent decades standardising outputs - SDTM, ADaM, define.xml. The rise of AI-driven analytics exposes a structural gap: the data pipelines were designed to satisfy regulators, not to serve systems.Data as a Product reframes the question. Instead of pipelines that produce standards, we build pipelines that produce value - robust, reusable, observable data products that any downstream consumer - analyst, model, agent - can build on.This talk introduces an agentic ETL architecture for clinical data: an orchestrated pipeline layer that ingests, transforms, and curates with embedded lineage, quality contracts, and semantic consistency. SDTM and ADaM become outputs of the system, one of many, not its purpose.Based on implementation experience across multiple trials, we explore what it looks like to treat clinical data as a product and why this shift unlocks the analytics and AI capabilities the industry has been trying to build on unstable foundations.

sessions.title: From SAS Code to CDISC Lineage: Building Transparent and Auditable Workflows
sessions.abstract:
Understanding and documenting complex SAS workflows can often feel like untangling spaghetti code: time-consuming, error-prone, and difficult to communicate. In this hands-on workshop, we transform that challenge into clarity by building a modern web application that automatically converts SAS programs into intuitive lineage diagrams.
Participants will learn how to reverse-engineer SAS workflows into structured, traceable representations aligned with CDISC standards. By translating code into end-to-end lineage graphs, the application generates a ‘visual DNA’ of SAS pipelines, making dependencies, transformations, and data flows transparent and auditable.
The session will demonstrate how to bridge the gap between raw SAS code and CDISC traceability maps, enabling improved collaboration, regulatory readiness, and faster validation cycles. Attendees will work through practical examples and build their own lineage visualisation pipeline from scratch.
In addition, the workshop is designed as an interactive exchange: we will actively gather participant feedback on requirements, expectations, and best practices for lineage in real-world statistical programming environments, helping to shape future development and industry approaches.
This workshop is designed for statistical programmers who want to enhance transparency, traceability, and productivity in their SAS environments. Participants are expected to bring their own laptops to engage fully in the hands-on exercises.

sessions.title: From Confusion to Compliance: Lessons From Establishing In-House GxP-Compliant Imaging Analysis Workflows
sessions.abstract: Imaging analyses in clinical trials are frequently outsourced to specialised vendors, which can limit internal ownership of analysis workflows and image quality assurance, and pose challenges for the future secondary use of data. However, imaging analyses tend to be complex and may involve non-standard analytic tools and human interactions with the data, such as creation of image annotations or assessing image quality. Together, these factors introduce additional challenges in the context of GxP validation. This presentation describes our recent efforts in establishing in-house GxP-compliant imaging analysis workflows for clinical trials. The presentation will outline a risk-based GxP validation approach established through close collaboration between data scientists, imaging experts, IT teams and quality representatives, ultimately resulting in CDISC/SDTM formatted data ready for regulatory submission. The presentation will also share practical lessons for organisations exploring in-house advanced imaging analyses for regulatory submissions.

sessions.title: Who Checks the AI? Making AI Generated Analyses Auditable
sessions.stream: Machine Learning, AI & Large Language Models
sessions.abstract: The integration of AI into statistical programming promises a significant reduction of submission timelines. However, unlike traditional programming, AI-generated code can be deceptive: failures may be structurally plausible yet analytically incorrect, which may slip through standard double-programming checks and are difficult to audit. Regulatory expectations for data integrity and reproducibility remain high, despite automatic code generation. We introduce provenance-by-design as a replacement for output-level review. We outline an architecture in which every analytical decision, transformation, and result remains traceable to its origin across the full analysis lifecycle.We present a graph-based traceability framework connecting source data, analysis specifications, code, and outputs as a queryable structure. Using oncology examples, we show how this surfaces hidden dependencies that manual reviews miss. This approach gives regulators the ability to interrogate the entire analytical chain, ensuring the human stays in the loop.Attendees will receive a strategic framework and actionable insights for managing AI-assisted biometrics with the required rigor.

sessions.title: Analysis Concepts: Towards a Executable Statistical Analysis Plan - Approach, Theory and Design
sessions.abstract: The Statistical Analysis Plan remains one of the last unstructured documents in the clinical trial lifecycle. Written in natural language, it is ambiguous, difficult to automate, and disconnected from the protocol it is meant to execute. This presentation introduces the electronic Statistical Analysis Plan (eSAP) - a structured, machine-readable framework built on CDISC standards including the Unified Study Definition Model (USDM) and the emerging Analysis Concepts (AC) Model. We describe the theoretical foundations of Analysis Concepts: how they capture the precise definition of a statistical analysis in a language-agnostic, reusable form, and how they model the inputs analyses depend on. We examine how the eSAP connects protocol intent to analysis specification, and make the case for why this shift - from narrative to executable - is both technically achievable and strategically necessary for the industry.This presentation is part of a broader CDISC 360i phase 2 theme together with the abstract from Peter Van Reusel and Kirstin Langendorf.

sessions.title: Making Virtual Controls Visible: Visual Analytics for Fit-for-Purpose VCG Review in Toxicology
sessions.abstract: Virtual Control Groups (VCGs) offer a promising way to reuse historical control data in nonclinical toxicology, but establishing whether a candidate VCG is fit for purpose requires more than static listings and summary tables. This presentation explores a focused set of visualisation strategies for examining VCG quality, suitability, and internal behaviour using Standard for Exchange of Nonclinical Data (SEND)-structured study data. Key views include coverage heatmaps to assess variable availability, metadata completeness scorecards to identify critical gaps, temporal drift plots to highlight instability, and domain-level dashboards to compare endpoint behaviour across studies. By comparing these views, the work aims to identify which visual approaches are most effective for revealing hidden heterogeneity, source-study imbalance, and fit-for-purpose limitations. The selected methods are then brought together in an interactive R Shiny tool to support exploratory analysis, comparative assessment, and fit-for-purpose evaluation of candidate VCGs for toxicologists, statisticians, and pathologists.

sessions.title: Enable Biometrics to utilise R/Open-Source as a tool for both exploratory and regulatory activities for drug projects
sessions.abstract:
Biometrics analysis and reporting team has long relied on SAS, but demand for open-source makes R a natural choice. The challenge is operating R in a GxP context: maintaining an approved package stack, managing dependency risk, and producing auditable, reproducible evidence.
We describe AstraZeneca’s end-to-end, risk-based pipeline for scaling R on Analysis & Reporting platforms. A Master Validation Plan defines roles and required artifacts. Package onboarding captures business rationale via a request portal, then combines automated objective risk signals (maintenance activity, releases, issues, documentation/tests, dependency footprint) with an SME review of intended use and regulatory impact. Evidence and release traceability support a curated, deployed package library.
We show regulated use cases enabled by this foundation, including containerised R/Shiny apps with governed access to study data, automation of SDTM datasets and TFL outputs, and converting RTF tables into PowerPoint. We conclude with lessons on dependencies, platform constraints, and keeping evidence current.

sessions.title: LIBNAME Is Great — But What About the {REST}?
sessions.abstract: In Novo Nordisk, we are currently transitioning our automated data flow to a next gen multi-system Statistical Compute Environment (SCE) that spans across SAS Viya, Databricks, PostgreSQL and OneLake. Our connectivity story is not a “one platform, one way”-kind of tale. While LIBNAME (powered by a variety of SAS/ACCESS engines) works great for many of our use-cases, we have also had to explore a range of REST APIs to efficiently bridge the various systems within and across SCEs. The result is a practical, hybrid reality: multiple authentication models, different system identities, and several integration methods running side by side to enable the data flow required for automation.In this presentation, we will share how we handle that complexity without losing control. We focus on what we learned about choosing between API and LIBNAME based on operational needs, maintaining consistent access, and ensuring the data flow from source extraction through to analysis and submission-ready data. We will also cover some of the key challenges — endpoints, permissions, and reliability — and the governance patterns we are using to keep our data flow stable while the system landscape evolves.

sessions.title: Reengineering Standard Programs and Study Setup to Support the Adoption of a New GxP Compliant Statistical Computing Environment
sessions.abstract:
Modernising statistical computing as required to meet evolving regulatory expectations, requires a fundamental rethink of how standard programs and study setup are designed, governed, and maintained. A simple lift-and-shift from legacy platforms is not always feasible, as many standard programs must be reengineered to operate effectively within a modern environment. Standard programs were assessed and either retired, transferred, or redesigned in accordance with GxP. A phased, risk-based approach guided the transfer and redesign of standard programs from the legacy platform. Changes in architecture and operating processes required a comprehensive redesign of the controlled-document landscape, covering the transfer, development, release, Git, and Azure DevOps-based practices for standard code within the new Statistical Computing Environment.
This paper offers practical guidance for organisations modernising their Statistical Computing Environment with a standards-first mindset that supports sustainability and long-term operational resilience.

sessions.title: A Skeptic's Guide to Using AI for Programming - Updated
sessions.stream: Machine Learning, AI & Large Language Models
sessions.abstract: Like it or not, “AI” is everywhere – on your phone, in your fridge, and even government systems. But is it a buzzword, a costly gimmick, or a genuine productivity tool? The truth is: it can be all of the above. Chances are your organization is already using AI or is planning to soon. So let this skeptic walk you through safely using AI for programming without compromising your skills, productivity, clinical data integrity, or sanity. This presentation willbuild on the PHUSE US Best in Connect paper and take a pragmatic look at the current AI capabilities with an emphasis on limitations, pitfalls, and practical applications in creating clinical outputs. Let’s face it, we don’t have to be enthusiastic about AI, but we do need to understand how to work with it.

sessions.title: Analysis Concepts: From Specification to Output - Building and Executing an eSAP in Practice
sessions.abstract: Theory becomes compelling when it works. This presentation moves from concept to practice, demonstrating the end-to-end construction of an electronic Statistical Analysis Plan using a reference implementation tool. Starting from a study protocol, we show how Analysis Concepts are selected from a structured library and assembled into an executable eSAP linked directly to USDM study metadata. We then demonstrate how that specification drives the automated generation of analysis datasets and analysis results - without manual re-specification in code. Key topics include the practical experience of authoring an eSAP, the mapping of Analysis Concepts to ADaM derivations, and the traceability chain from protocol through specification to output. Attendees will leave with a concrete understanding of what metadata-driven automation looks like in practice and what it would take to adopt this approach within their own organizations.This presentation is part of a broader CDISC 360i phase 2 theme together with the abstract from Peter Van Reusel and Edwin van Stein.

sessions.title: Accelerating Study Insights: Agile Data Visualisation Using R-Shiny
sessions.abstract: Interactive, real-time data visualization is transforming how study teams assess efficacy and safety. This project leverages R Shiny to convert raw datasets into actionable insights with agility and precision.The application converts raw efficacy data into structured analysis datasets and interactive visualizations, enabling study teams to explore efficacy trends rapidly and intuitively. Visualizations include Waterfall plots, Spider plots, Swimmer plots, Kaplan-Meier analyses, and Overall Response Rate tables, with listings also in spreadsheet format.For safety, a dedicated Adverse Event (AE) module derives TEAE TFLs from raw datasets, enabling interactive exploration of safety profiles. Integrating safety with efficacy provides a holistic view of outcomes and balanced evaluation.By using this tool, study teams reduce reliance on static reporting and streamline transformation. An agile approach allows iterative refinement without waiting for SDTM/ADaM processing. This initiative positions statistical programmers as innovators in agile analytics, improves efficiency, and enables timely, data-driven decision-making

sessions.title: R Ready, Open-Source Ready, AI Ready: Building a Validated Foundation for Agentic Analytics
sessions.abstract: Open-source languages such as R and Python are now widely used in clinical trial submission work, while large language models are increasingly capable “expert users” of these languages. IQVIA has established a validated, controlled, reproducible, and flexible framework for using R that enables clients to benefit from the open-source pharma community while strengthening IQVIA’s AI readiness.This presentation describes IQVIA’s R framework, currently used for submission work with several clients. It includes governed validation of open-source packages, a curated validated package collection, and a protected execution environment that restricts unvalidated packages. The process is language-agnostic by design, supporting future validation of other tools, including Python packages from COSA and analytics packages such as pandas and NumPy.The same foundation has direct relevance to AI-enabled and agentic workflows by constraining AI coding assistants to validated environments with controlled dependencies and reproducible behavior. This presentation argues that AI readiness is not simply the adoption of new tooling, but the result of being R-ready and open-source-ready first.

sessions.title: Floating in Time: Explore the Data Pooling Time Machine
sessions.abstract: As time is a central aspect when maintaining clinical data pools we build iPool, a SAS macros system which fully supports the transparent handling of all changes to a pool over time.From starting with the first definition of the pool structure (metadata and codelist) over adding the first studies, updating pool structure, define data modifications and changes in controlled terminology (on single values up to the whole pool) and loading more studies, again and again, up to the final existing pool: You can go back to every stage in between.We will show how these aspects are maintained over time and how it is possible to reconstruct a specific pool for a given point in time. This is possible because data is stored only once and changes on the data are defined but not applied. It is achieved by organizing timestamps and identifiers in a consistent and efficient way for all aspects of the definition tables in the pool.

sessions.title: Advancing Global Regulatory Submissions through Next Generation Submission (NGS): A Collaborative Implementation Case Study
sessions.abstract: The adoption of Next Generation Submission (NGS) levers is transforming our preparation of global regulatory submissions and enabling accelerated timelines through standardized, automation-driven, more efficient processes. This paper presents a collaborative submission acceleration implementation between a CRO and a global sponsor, focusing on pre-DBL planning, Dress Rehearsal approach, and post-DBL strategies. Key NGS levers include alignment with CDISC standards for multi-regional submissions, shadow team for early restricted unblinded PK/ADA data access and analysis readiness, CSR acceleration plan and checklist, and automation-enhanced process for in-text tables and safety narratives. Challenges like cross-functional coordination, Intercurrent Event (ICE) handling, prompt third-party vendor (TPV) data transfer and issue handling, and regional regulatory variability were addressed through structured governance and iterative approaches. This case study provides practical insights and best practices for accelerated, scalable, future-ready global submissions leveraging NGS principles. Results demonstrate improved submission process, consistent quality, reduced timelines, and enhanced regulatory compliance.

sessions.title: Practical AI in Clinical Trial Biometrics: Why Metadata and Standards Matter
sessions.abstract: Introducing AI into clinical trial biometrics raises a practical question: how do you make tools built on probabilistic Large Language Models (LLMs) reliable enough for regulated work? Without proper grounding, access to authoritative standards, and controlled metadata flows, LLMs are just guessing. People see opportunities for AI to free up time, but don’t yet trust it. And for good reason. This paper presents practical approaches for grounding AI in regulated environments. The unifying principle is garbage-in-garbage-out - the quality of context provided to an LLM dominates the quality of its output. Metadata and authoritative standards (CDISC and internal conventions) form a critical part of that context, providing a contract the LLM can be asked to satisfy. Deterministic logic should be applied first, with probabilistic inference as a fallback for novel cases. Other forms of guiding content, such as conventions files like agents.md, extend the same idea beyond data standards into project-level context. Emerging CDISC semantic standards - USDM, Biomedical Concepts, and Dataset Specialisations - are discussed as a foundation for more reliable, context-grounded AI.

sessions.title: From Programmer to Associate Director: What Changed, What Worked, and Why It Matters
sessions.abstract: Stepping into management is a shift from delivering work to delivering outcomes through people and the stakes rise quickly when you become accountable for others’ progression and a team’s direction. However, this move doesn’t have to be terrifying. It is a fantastic opportunity that allows you to help guide another person throughout their career journey and allows you to develop a greater level of empathy and become a better contributor to your department. You’re able to learn a lot about yourself and how you communicate with others and become a better advocate not only for your line reports but for yourself.

sessions.title: Gen AI in Statistical Programming: EU Connect 2026 Edition
sessions.stream: Machine Learning, AI & Large Language Models
sessions.abstract: An interactive session exploring the evolving role of Generative AI in statistical programming. Through live polling and audience discussion, we will gather real-time insights into adoption, use cases, challenges, governance, and the future direction of the industry.

sessions.title: Associated Persons in an ADaM Library
sessions.abstract: In SDTM, we have a specific implementation guide for Associated Persons. However, Associated Persons in ADaM remains a much less discussed area and we need to build from the SDTM-AP and ADaM-IG standards only. With a growing number of neonatology studies, we have added associated persons specific variables and domains to our standard ADAM library. In this presentation I will discuss the decisions made and the challenges faced.

sessions.title: Automatic Generation of Dashboards
sessions.abstract: This talk presents a streamlined process leveraging SAS Viya REST APIs to create a reusable, repeatable method for leveraging existing SAS Visual Analytics reports and applying them to new data sources. To enhance accessibility for users unfamiliar with APIs, we encapsulated the code within a user-friendly Custom Step interface. This Custom Step can be seamlessly integrated into existing Flows to automate data processing and update SAS Visual Analytics reports, or used independently. Additionally, the code can be adapted as a macro, offering flexible implementation options to meet diverse user needs and workflows.

sessions.title: Automating Teal App Development in Clinical Trials: What Works in Practice
sessions.abstract: Open-source frameworks such as teal have made clinical trial analytics more standardized and reusable, enabling clinical scientists to build tailored applications with less reliance on specialized app developers. The emergence of LLMs and tools such as the Teal MCP Server further expands what can be automated across development and maintenance workflows.This talk presents an empirical guide derived from migration and maintenance work on dozens of teal modules and apps after adopting a new data-extraction package. Specifically, we classify activities into three groups. First, we show tasks that are highly automatable, such as cross-branch comparisons of module outputs using screenshots, reproducible code, and run logs. Second, we identify activities that still require human oversight, especially design decisions that depend on framework context and intended usage. Third, we describe the controls needed for reliability in regulated settings, for example constraints in package usage and controlled test additions.The result is a practical automation model that enables faster delivery without compromising traceability, quality, or team learning.

sessions.title: Engineering Metadata-Driven Blinding in Clinical Data Pipelines: The Novo Nordisk Approach to Scalable, Automated Data Protection
sessions.abstract: Blinding is critical to trial integrity, yet traditional implementations are often manual, inconsistent, and difficult to integrate in modern data architectures. As clinical data ecosystems evolve, there is a growing need for automated, standardised blinding embedded directly in the data lifecycle.We have introduced a metadata-driven and policy-based approach to blinding. Built on integrated EDC, CDMS, and CDR components, the blinding approach replaces fragmented, study-specific configurations with centralised governance, rule-based execution and automated testing. Blinding is applied consistently across studies, incl. subject-level masking and topic-based nulling, with support for both blinded and unblinded data products. Automated validation checkpoints, audit trail generation, and fail-fast controls ensure traceability and prevent downstream propaga-tion of incorrectly processed data. This presentation will share the technical design, integration patterns, and implementation learn-ings from our blinding setup, demonstrating how engineering-driven blinding improves data in-tegrity, scalability, and compliance in increasingly complex clinical data environments.

sessions.title: The Metadata Mystery: Solving the Case From Protocol to Submission
sessions.abstract:
A study visit disappears. A codelist doesn't match. Validation passes, but something still isn't right.
Every submission leaves clues.
In this interactive 90-minute workshop, you'll become part of the investigation team for a fictional clinical study. Working in small groups, you'll examine realistic study documents, uncover new evidence, and solve a series of metadata mysteries that unfold throughout the study lifecycle. Each investigation challenges you to determine what happened, where the problem first surfaced, where it actually began, and, most importantly, how it could have been prevented.
As new evidence emerges, you'll compare your team's conclusions with other investigators, explore the downstream impact of each decision, and discover how seemingly small metadata changes can affect study quality, collaboration, and submission readiness.
Participants will learn how to:
• Distinguish symptoms from root causes when investigating study issues.
• Recognize common sources of metadata drift across the study lifecycle.
• Assess the downstream impact of protocol changes and other study updates.
• Apply practical strategies to improve traceability, collaboration, and submission readiness.
• Think more critically about how connected metadata supports a modern digital study.
Every clue tells part of the story. Join our Pinnacle 21 team to test your investigative skills, compare theories with your peers, and discover whether your team can solve the metadata mystery before the submission deadline.
Attendees will be treated to a 'Taste o' Scotland' with some extra special sweet treats & refreshments along with some fascinating history on these delicacies.

sessions.title: Bridging CDISC Standards and HIV-1 Regulatory Expectations: Practical Virology Data Implementation
sessions.abstract: CDISC standards provide a common framework for clinical data submission; however, therapeutic area or regulatory specific guidance can introduce additional expectations. In HIV‑1 studies, FDA technical specifications describe reviewer‐focused expectations that extend beyond industry standard data structures, particularly for virology and efficacy endpoints. For HIV‑1 regulatory submissions, sponsors are typically asked to submit an Analysis Efficacy Outcomes dataset (ADEFFOUT) summarizing subject level virologic outcomes. This dataset includes snapshot based viral load suppression flags and categories at key time points, along with relevant baseline and treatment information. Additionally, a dedicated Virology Analysis dataset (ADVR) is often used to store all HIV‑1 RNA endpoint data and associated resistance results. This specialized dataset complements general ADaM datasets by capturing detailed virologic measurements and outcomes for each subject. This paper will highlight practical approaches to maintaining CDISC compliance while addressing regulatory review needs, with an emphasis on traceability, consistency, and clear documentation.

sessions.title: The Metadata Trap: Why Current Automation Approaches Are Failing Statistical Programming Teams
sessions.abstract: Statistical programming teams have invested heavily in automation, yet late-stage data issues and protracted responses to regulatory reviewer queries remain common. The reason is simpler than it appears. Most automation tools treat Define.XML, SDTM and ADaM specifications and TLF shells as ground truth, yet they are rarely verified for internal consistency. These submission documents, however, are human-authored and version-prone. Double programming is not designed to catch shared misinterpretation or inconsistencies between submission documents. And it routinely doesn’t! A team that followed every established QC standard, current specifications, verified programs, double programming sign-off, can still receive an FDA reviewer query they cannot answer quickly. Regulatory response windows rarely allow more than a few days. The bottleneck is never the answer itself, it is the “traceability-debt”, time spent reconstructing a derivation chain that should have been structured from the start. Attendees leave with a practical checklist for identifying inconsistencies in their own submission packages, and a framework for evaluating where end-to-end-traceability closes the gap.

sessions.title: Training the Future Workforce: Adapting Learning Strategies for Gen Z and Emerging Professionals
sessions.abstract: Traditional training models in clinical research and statistical programming have long relied on extensive manuals, SOP-driven learning, and passive onboarding approaches. However, the expectations and learning preferences of Gen Z and emerging professionals are reshaping workforce development. Today’s learners often value interactive engagement, rapid feedback, digital accessibility, collaboration, and clear opportunities for growth.This presentation explores how training strategies can evolve to better support modern learners while maintaining industry and regulatory standards. Topics include micro-learning, mentorship, scenario-based learning, digital learning tools, and the role of psychological safety in building confidence and encouraging independent thinking.By adapting learning approaches to the future workforce, organizations can improve engagement, knowledge retention, trainee development, and long-term talent retention.

sessions.title: Visualizing ICE Strategies in ADaM: Making Estimands Accessible
sessions.abstract: Intercurrent events (ICEs) are central to the ICH E9(R1) estimand framework, yet their implementation in ADaM datasets often remains abstract and difficult to communicate. This presentation takes a programming-first perspective, demonstrating how ICE strategies can be systematically mapped into ADaM structures while following CDISC standards. We showcase reusable code templates, metadata-driven workflows, and visualization techniques that transform ICE handling from a theoretical exercise into a transparent, reproducible process. With technical rigor, we highlight how programmers can make estimands accessible to statisticians, clinicians, and regulators alike.

sessions.title: Flex It: Using R Flexdashboard to Deliver an Interactive, Dynamic Dashboard Displaying TLFs for Stakeholders
sessions.abstract: Traditionally, tables, listings, and figures (TLFs) are delivered to clinical and statistical stakeholders as static Word or PDF reports. While this format is familiar, it can be limiting when teams need to rapidly explore data, compare results across studies, or support real-time decision-making. Flexdashboard in RStudio can be used to transform static TLF outputs into interactive HTML dashboards integrating TLFs from multiple studies within a single project dashboard and enabling users to navigate between outputs with intuitive menus and tabs. This paper describes the basic Flexdashboard workflow, from initial setup and layout design to the incorporation of TLFs and deployment of the final HTML output. It demonstrates how adopting Flexdashboard can enhance stakeholder engagement and modernize the communication of statistical analyses.

sessions.title: A Framework for Large-Scale Automated Harmonisation
sessions.abstract: For several years, Roche has prioritised the secondary use of clinical trial data by developing large-scale, diverse data assets known as Data Marts. A foundational step in this process is harmonising source SDTM datasets for data pooling, yet traditional mapping is labour-intensive, error-prone, and unsustainable given the explosive demand for analysis-ready data. To solve this scalability challenge, we have built a highly automated, R-based solution, moving beyond repetitive manual coding to industrialise the process.This presentation details how the pipeline executes standard curation steps through automated code generation, harnessing an extensive mapping database, a flexible ruleset, and contextual metadata. Attendees will see how the framework programmatically handles harmonisation challenges, such as recategorising data, performing mathematical unit conversions, and recalculating key reference dates. This framework has significantly reduced manual intervention and code maintenance while ensuring semantic consistency across datasets. It has transformed our clinical data repositories from static, end-of-trial archives into a scalable, active engine for scientific discovery.

sessions.title: Integrated Safety Data Platforms: Building and Governing a Direct‑to‑ADaM Pooled Clinical Database for Real‑Time Safety Surveillance
sessions.abstract: Modern drug development spans multiple indications, phases, and study designs, creating fragmented safety landscape.Sponsors increasingly need a governed, project‑level repository that delivers standardized, traceable, and near‑real‑time safety analytics to support DSUR,ISS deliverables and regulatory interactions. This outlines a pragmatic framework and implementation playbook for a pooled clinical safety database that curates direct‑to‑ADaM analysis datasets, enforces terminology governance, preserves lineage, and supports routine and ad‑hoc safety reporting with inspection‑ready traceability. Practical implementation demonstrated measurable improvements across three dimensions: regulatory responsiveness (faster, higher‑quality responses to HAQs with full traceability), operational efficiency (2.5 FTE savings per major aggregate report request), data quality (early detection of unit normalization issues, dictionary version drift and derivation inconsistencies through automated profiling). A blinding governance protocol further enabled simultaneous unblinded study team access and blinded safety team surveillance across a complex platform trial program without ompromising integrity

sessions.title: Conflict & Convergence for Accelerated Disclosure of Clinical Documents
sessions.abstract: Clinical trial disclosure is highly regulated, yet sponsors continue to struggle due to how data privacy is operationalized. Under the current public disclosure guidelines, inefficiencies persist: late-stage anonymization, repeated redaction cycles, and submissions requiring extensive rework.Drawing on real-world submission and regulatory experience, this session challenges the assumption that late-stage anonymization alone will protect sensitive data. In practice, this mindset leads to disagreements between regulators, sponsors, and the public.Transparency and disclosure teams act as the corrective force by embedding disclosure considerations into authoring practices, data standards, and cross-functional frameworks. They reduce rework, enable consistent, defensible anonymization strategies and support the justification of commercially confidential information in line with regulatory expectations.Through cross-agency case studies, we demonstrate how this approach improves alignment with regulators, reduces iterative review cycles, and strengthens submission quality. Transparency is not just a compliance requirement; it is a system designed to build trust in healthcare.

sessions.title: Open Source & AI Readiness in Clinical Biometrics: A Pulse Check on Pharma
sessions.abstract: The pharmaceutical industry is shifting how clinical data is managed, analyzed, and submitted. Open source languages are gaining ground, pharmaverse packages are maturing, and AI-assisted workflows are moving from pilot to production.This paper presents findings from structured 1-on-1 interviews with biometrics leaders across pharma companies of varying sizes, mapping the current state of open source adoption, AI readiness, and statistical computing modernization across five dimensions: system integration maturity, SAS-to-OS transition progress, package validation approaches, AI and automation priorities, and standards management practices. The goal is a practitioner-driven snapshot of where biometrics organizations actually are today.Interviews with Heads of Statistical Programming, Biostatistics, and Data Management at pharma and biotech organizations globally. Thematic analysis identifies patterns and recurring challenges, complemented by real-world SCE deployment experience.Three outputs for the PHUSE community: a benchmarking snapshot; a practical maturity framework identifying common blockers and high-leverage interventions; and actionable recommendations.

sessions.title: Will AI Make Clinical Programming a Less Attractive Career? Rethinking How We Adopt AI to Retain and Attract Talent
sessions.abstract: Innovation, quality, and progress in clinical trial programming depend on one resource above all others: talented people. Talented programmers are drawn to our industry because the work is important, intellectually demanding, creative, and collaborative. We derive complex datasets, solve non-obvious problems, mentor and learn from colleagues, and ultimately contribute to bringing new therapies to patients. These are the very qualities that attract sharp minds into clinical programming and that keep them here.As AI tools begin to penetrate every layer of our daily work, we must ask an uncomfortable question: what happens to the aspects of our work that make it worth doing? If AI absorbs the challenging, creative, and learning-rich portions of the job, leaving programmers as reviewers of machine output, do we risk hollowing out the very roles we need to fill?This talk explores the potential knock-on effects of AI adoption on talent attraction and retention in clinical programming. We discuss practical approaches to AI implementation, that preserve the intellectual substance of our roles and continue to attract the talent our industry depends on.

sessions.title: Agentic AI for SDTM Mapping, Promise vs. Reality
sessions.stream: Machine Learning, AI & Large Language Models
sessions.abstract: Agentic AI systems, capable of multi-step reasoning and goal-directed execution, are accelerating SDTM mapping, one of the most time-intensive, expertise-dependent processes in clinical trials. Vendors increasingly claim end-to-end automation: from raw source data to CDISC-compliant datasets, with derivation logic, controlled terminology resolution and define.xml readiness. This paper presents a candid, experience-based evaluation drawing on a real-world AI-assisted SDTM automation workflow, examining performance across standard domains, supplemental qualifiers, and complex derivations. We find that human expert oversight remains indispensable, particularly for study-specific logic, edge cases and GxP compliance. Industry data confirms that 80–95% of pharma AI pilots fail to reach production, mostly due to governance and validation gaps rather than technical shortcomings. We provide a practical evaluation framework for sponsors, CROs and technology teams assessing agentic SDTM mapping tools, keeping in mind the governance, validation and human-in-the-loop design principles required to move from promising pilots to scalable, inspection-ready adoption

sessions.title: smartARS: Turning the CDISC Analysis Results Standard into a Daily Tool for Output Generation
sessions.abstract: Imagine a world where every number in a clinical report carries its full recipe, every output dataset shares the same structure, and define.xml can be auto-populated. CDISC's Analysis Results Standard (ARS) can be utilized in this endeavor - turning analyses into machine-readable metadata, enabling reuse of filters, groupings and methods across outputs, and producing harmonised Analysis Results Datasets (ARDs) ready for cross-study meta-analysis. We present smartARS, an open-source R package ecosystem that enables this vision. Clinical data scientists work through simple functions, while behind the scenes, smartARS populates the ARS specification, generates tables and figures, and emits fully unfolded, standalone R code suitable for regulatory submission and direct define.xml feed. The modular design separates ARS classes, storage-agnostic backends, a scripting interface, a statistical-methods repository, and dedicated visualisation packages. Collectively, these packages create publication-ready output, complete metadata, and submittable code - hereby turning ARS from a written specification into a daily tool for output generation.

sessions.title: Validating R Shiny Applications for Data Driven Decision Making: A DaVinci Case Study
sessions.abstract: R Shiny applications are becoming increasingly important as they enable rapid and interactive visualization of complex data. To support efficient and consistent development of such applications, the Shiny framework DaVinci was designed to facilitate the creation of standardized and reusable applications.To enable the use of results generated by Shiny applications beyond exploratory purposes and to support well informed decision making, validation is required. This is particularly relevant in regulated environments such as the pharmaceutical industry. This presentation presents an approach developed at Boehringer Ingelheim for the validation of R Shiny applications. The validation process enables the reliable and transparent use of Shiny applications and thereby supports data driven decision making on a solid foundation.

sessions.title: From Summary Tables to Patient‑Level Analytics: A Standardized R and SAS Framework
sessions.abstract: This paper introduces standardized R functions and SAS macros that extend traditional statistical analyses beyond conventional table generation. Regardless of table type or layout, these tools consistently produce two outputs: the standard table and a corresponding subject‑level dataset, enabling clear traceability to individual patients. In clinical trial reporting, statistical programming has long focused on aggregated summaries, such as counts of TE adverse events or study discontinuations. While these outputs meet regulatory needs, they offer limited visibility into the patients behind the results, making it difficult to identify which subjects drive observed patterns or whether specific subgroups are disproportionately affected. By systematically linking aggregate outputs with subject‑level data, this approach enables deeper exploration of patient‑level patterns, variability, and subgroup effects. This enriched dataset creates a strong foundation for further data science including clustering, predictive modeling, signal detection, and identification of individual risk factors, enhancing interpretation of key endpoints and enabling more patient‑centric analyses.

sessions.title: Faster, Semi-Automatic Data Transfer Validation Through Machine-Readable DTAs
sessions.abstract: Within SGS, we have enhanced the traditional Word-based DTA by transforming it into a machine readable Excel-based format. This transformation enables automatization and standardization of the DTA structure, as well as seamless integration with data transfers received from third parties. It is supported by a robust DTA validation rule package designed to ensure structural integrity and compliance. When trial-specific DTA is loaded, automated validation rules detect inconsistencies against the established DTA library structure. Similarly, upon receiving a data transfer, the system validates the structure and content compliance with the corresponding DTA, highlighting any discrepancies. These inconsistencies are compiled into a report for communication with third parties, ensuring transparency and accuracy. By automating these processes, we have significantly reduced manual intervention, achieving up to 60% time savings in the transfer validation process, while enhancing quality and reliability. This innovation not only optimizes workflows, but also strengthens compliance, delivering measurable efficiency gains.

sessions.title: Beyond the CRT Package Preparing Clinical Programmers for True Submission Readiness
sessions.abstract: In many clinical programming environments, regulatory submission readiness is often reduced to timely delivery of the Case Report Tabulations (CRT) package. While SDTM and ADaM datasets, define.xml, and annotated CRFs are essential, focusing solely on these deliverables creates a false sense of readiness. Regulatory success also depends on how effectively programming teams support health authority interactions, respond to regulatory questions, and enable clear, traceable decision-making throughout the review lifecycle.This presentation provides an end-to-end overview of the regulatory submission process from a programmer’s perspective, redefining submission readiness as a cross-functional, lifecycle-driven discipline. Topics include CRT package assembly; reviewer guides (SDRG/ADRG); submission modules, HAQs and IRs; briefing documents; pooling strategies; programming support for regulatory meetings; and structuring robust responses that minimise dataset revisions; eCTD submissions, including structure, validation & publishing.Regional regulatory expectations (FDA, NMPA, PMDA) and emerging AI-enabled workflows for validation and submission review are discussed.

sessions.title: Trust the Agent? Building Confidence in Agentic AI for Regulated Clinical Programming
sessions.abstract: Agentic Artificial Intelligence (AI) is reshaping how statistical programming teams tackle complex tasks, yet practical accounts of its deployment within regulated environments remain limited. This paper presents how a professional statistical analyst programming team adopted multi-agent AI orchestration to accelerate the migration of a validated SAS codebase into R, offering an early blueprint for responsible agentic adoption.Agent roles were designed for SAS logic interpretation, R code generation, and automated test creation, operating inside security boundaries that governed model access, data exposure, and auditability from the start. Open-source orchestration frameworks were adapted to meet clinical requirements, enabling the team to progress from isolated experimentation to coordinated, reproducible multi-agent pipelines.Because trust is the primary barrier to adoption, we implemented automated validation loops, human-in-the-loop checkpoints, and clear accountability boundaries that position agents as measurable team contributors rather than automation. The paper provides practical guidance for statistical programming teams seeking to integrate agentic AI.

sessions.title: Am I the Imposter?
sessions.abstract: Imposter syndrome is a persistent and hidden challenge, even among experienced professionals with proven expertise. This talk will navigate imposter syndrome through a combination of established research and candid personal reflection, showing how self‑doubt can coexist with long and successful careers. Drawing on over 20 years in clinical programming across multiple CRO environments, the session highlights how imposter syndrome often surfaces during periods of change, increased visibility, or professional growth. We will examine what imposter syndrome is, who experiences it, and why it occurs, particularly among high achievers and those adapting to new roles, environments, or technologies. Personal real‑world examples from transitioning from SAS to R, speaking at international conferences and to performing live music demonstrate how the fear of being “found out” can persist despite clear evidence of competence. By normalising self‑doubt, the talk will reinforce a key message: confidence grows through action, courage, and reflection, and you are where you are because you have earned it!

sessions.title: Who Authorised That? Enforcing Governance in Multi-Agent AI Pipelines
sessions.stream: Machine Learning, AI & Large Language Models
sessions.abstract: As pharmaceutical organisations deploy orchestrated AI systems - where one agent prepares data for consumption by another - a critical governance gap emerges: pipeline rules are written into system prompts, but nothing enforces or records that those rules were followed at execution. This presentation examines what governance infrastructure multi-agent clinical reporting pipelines actually require.Drawing on pharmaceutical implementations of two-agent architectures in clinical reporting workflows, we analyse where conventional approaches fail: agent-level constraints exist as natural language instructions rather than enforceable policies, outputs cross agent boundaries without a verifiable record, and compliance cannot be independently confirmed.We present a governance framework that moves beyond written instructions — locking each agent's behaviour at execution and generating a tamper-evident record of what actually happened. The result is a pipeline where compliance can be demonstrated, not just asserted. Implications for GAMP 5 validation and FDA-EMA Good AI Practice guidance are drawn.

sessions.title: Rethinking QC: Utilising ARS for ARD-based validation
sessions.abstract: The CDISC Analysis Results Standard (ARS), part of the broader CDISC 360 framework, introduces a structured way to describe clinical trial analysis results through metadata. A key output of this approach is the Analysis Results Dataset (ARD) — a flat, machine-readable dataset containing all results required for a given TFL, with full traceability to the underlying metadata.While ARDs are often discussed in the context of TFL automation, they also hold significant value for validation. This presentation explores how ARDs generated by the open-source R package "siera" can serve as an independent, standards-based reference point in the TFL validation process — enabling reliable comparison against traditionally programmed outputs.By using ARS-driven ARDs as the basis for validation, teams gain consistency, traceability, and a clearer audit trail. The session will demonstrate this workflow and discuss its governance implications within an ARS- and CDISC 360-aligned environment.

sessions.title: R-Evolutionising Medical Data Review in Neuroscience Through {teal}
sessions.abstract: Medical Data Review (MDR) traditionally relies on expensive, proprietary platforms like Spotfire, whose 'black box' architecture lacks transparency and restricts customisation. As a cross-functional team of statistical programmers, in-house software developers, and visual analytics managers, we developed a modular MDR app using the open-source {teal} R package for a Huntington’s Disease study, shaping the development of the in-house MDR package {teal.modules.mdr} built on {teal}. By regularly integrating clinical and safety stakeholder feedback, we built actionable, fit-for-purpose MDR modules encompassing adverse events, vital signs, laboratory results, and neuroscience-specific questionnaires, including features like subject-level indicator dashboards, audit trail visualisation, raised query annotations, and decision logging, amongst others. This pilot drives broader adoption of the TEAL for MDR framework internally and enables cross-industry practice sharing through the open-source {teal} package. We demonstrate how early adopters modernise MDR through an open-source package while providing a flexible, cost-effective alternative to proprietary platforms.

sessions.title: Efficient and Reproducible Literature Processing for HTA Evidence Synthesis
sessions.abstract: Systematic literature reviews (SLRs) are essential for health technology assessments (HTAs) and require comprehensive evidence synthesis. AI-based retrieval systems are increasingly used to maximize coverage and reduce the risk of missing relevant studies. However, they often generate large literature sets with many false positives, requiring substantial manual post-processing.We present a script-based workflow for efficiently reducing large literature sets while maintaining completeness. First, structured information, such as PICO elements, is extracted using prompt-based methods to enable rule-based filtering of clearly irrelevant records. Second, lightweight text-processing algorithms, including Levenshtein distance–based similarity measures, are used to group related records by key identifiers. This reduces the literature set to a manageable size without excluding relevant studies.Our approach bridges the gap between experimental AI-based systems and practical, production-ready SLR workflows. It enables reproducible and transparent review processes while substantially reducing manual effort, thereby supporting comprehensive and unbiased evidence synthesis for HTAs.

sessions.title: Accelerating Regulatory Responses Through a Harmonized Clinical Data Warehouse
sessions.abstract: Building an integrated database capable of addressing safety questions, supporting regulatory readiness, and enabling effective medical communication is a complex task. These challenges increase when the database must incorporate both interventional and non-interventional studies, support pooled and study-level analyses, and allow smooth inclusion of future studies with heterogeneous designs. Achieving this requires significant flexibility in both programming strategies and data structures.This presentation shares the solutions we implemented, and the challenges we faced, while following a CDISC-like framework designed to support critical safety and efficacy analyses. We describe the strategy adopted to harmonize and pool SDTM data content while ensuring traceability. We also detail the methodology used to generate ADaMs datasets that summarize multiple data groupings, different period durations, and study selections criteria.This session will highlight the strategic decisions and key lessons learned in creating a flexible data warehouse designed for multi-purpose analyses.

sessions.abstract: Take a break in the Exhibition Hall to enjoy refreshments, expand your professional network, and explore exhibitor solutions. Play to Win!
