sessions.title: Open-Source AI Pit of Success: Governance Within the ACE (AI Statistical Environment)
sessions.abstract: This presentation explores the transition from Statistical Computing Environments (SCE) to the ACE (AI Statistical Environment) where AI availability and governance is integrated for users. We demonstrate how organizations implement a "AI Pit of Success" for open-source users via Posit Integrations, ensuring AI is open-source aware and ready. Attendees will learn how these tools integrate within an ACE infrastructure, providing users with the Posit Assistant for AI enablement. The session highlights the role of the "Clinical AI Fabric" in providing a secure, VPC-internal orchestration layer with Amazon Bedrock (or similar) in the ACE. Finally, we showcase how this governed ACE approach enables human-in-the-loop reviews and agentic workflows, providing a foundation for AI code-first of clinical reporting.

sessions.title: Beyond the Script: Why a Growth Mindset Is the Best Programming Tool
sessions.abstract: The role of programmers is evolving, as pharma businesses look to adapt their ways of working and leverage the power of technology to deliver submissions in the most efficient possible manner.This paper examines how the role is changing and looks at ways in which programmers will need to adapt in response. We will look at the impact of technological evolution, such as the introduction of new programming languages and AI tools to the programming pipeline.In the short term, these evolutions provide challenges for programmers, both from a technical perspective, in terms of the time taken to learn how to use the new tools and the mistakes which will come with any learning process and are a necessary part of professional growth, and from a mental perspective, with the uncertainty around the impact on programming roles in the future. To overcome these challenges, it is vital for programmers to adopt a growth mindset, seeing it as a development opportunity, where the long term gains will outweigh the short term pains, with newfound efficiencies allowing programmers to place more focus on higher value activities such as uncovering insights into the data and the story it tells.

sessions.title: Give Your AI Coding Assistant a Live R Session: From Iterative Exploration to Reproducible ADaM Analysis
sessions.stream: Machine Learning, AI & Large Language Models
sessions.abstract: Modern coding assistants discard session state between interactions. Every follow-up re-reads data, re-fits models, and re-spends tokens reconstructing context already computed. For biostatistics, where the work is inherently iterative: fit, inspect, adjust, refit - this statelessness turns a natural workflow into an expensive loop of redundant setup.We explored a different paradigm: through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), the AI connects to a sandboxed R REPL, executes code, inspects actual data and errors, and iterates in a persistent session alongside the programmer. Domain guardrails enforce CDISC conventions and admiral-style patterns. Once complete, the session is synthesized into a standalone, reproducible analysis script.Since variables and intermediate results live in the R session rather than the prompt, context window is focused on the current analytical question instead of bloated with previously generated output, reducing token consumption and improving response quality.We present the architecture and demonstrate it live, doing exploratory analysis of ADaM data using conversational prompts. All tooling is open-source and available today.

sessions.title: SDTMIG v4.0: Are You Ready For It?
sessions.abstract: The imminent release of the CDISC SDTMIG v4.0 / SDTM v3.0 represents a pivotal moment for SDTM standards. As a major version update, it introduces significant changes that sponsors should begin preparing for now. Key updates include support for Multiple Subject Instances (MSI), the transition from SUPPQUAL to Non-Standard Variables (NSVs), and metadata restructuring aligned with SDTM Model v3.0. The –BLFL variable has been removed and Sections 1–4 have been reorganized for improved clarity and usability. New domains such as Event Adjudication (EA), along with five additional body system domains, further expand representational capabilities. Updates to domains such as Protocol Deviations (DV) and the addition of the Laboratory Results Conventional (LC) domain facilitate alignment with regulatory expectations. Also notable, splitting the Disease Response (RS) domain into RS and a new Clinical Classifications (CC) domain. This paper explores what’s new in SDTMIG v4.0 and provides practical guidance to help sponsors navigate this era of transition.

sessions.title: Delegation: The Art of Letting Go Without Losing Control in High-Stakes Teams
sessions.abstract: Delegation is a leadership necessity, yet many managers hesitate to let go for fear of losing control, especially in complex, high‑stakes environments. This session explores the transition from task‑assigner to leader‑developer and what truly enables teams to take ownership without compromising quality or accountability. Drawing on principles from Turn the Ship Around and real‑world experience leading biometrics teams, the talk introduces a practical framework of three layers of delegation: task, accountability, and ownership. And we will explore why most leaders unintentionally stop at the first.Attendees will gain practical strategies to expand ownership while maintaining clarity and quality; setting decision boundaries, preventing reverse‑delegation, and creating conditions where independent thinking can thrive. Common delegation traps are discussed alongside simple, applicable methods to build trust, capability, and confidence within teams.Ultimately, participants will leave with a clear leadership framework that reframes delegation from merely handing off tasks to a deliberate and sustainable tool for developing stronger, more accountable teams.

sessions.title: Cutting the Queue: How to Reduce Programming Runtimes via Parallel Processing
sessions.abstract: As clinical trials increase in size and scope, datasets are becoming larger and more complex, resulting in longer program runtimes to generate them. A full run-through of a large study’s datasets may represent several hours of runtime, but we can complete the run in a fraction of the time by splitting processing into several smaller runs.The first step to consider is how many parallel threads to use - more threads means a shorter run, but too many threads will lead to diminishing returns and potential server issues! When running multiple threads it’s particularly important to consider dependencies between different programs, both in the same thread and between different threads. We can use intelligent blocks to keep different threads in sync and avoid race conditions.We want to split programs between threads to divide runtime as equally as possible. However, this isn’t as simple as giving each thread the same number of programs - an ADLB program for example may take 50 times as long as the simplest ADaM program. We can use proxies (e.g. program length, log length or dataset size) or recorded times from prior runs to estimate how long each program is likely to take to run.

sessions.title: How to Migrate Without Migrating
sessions.abstract: Data migration is often the biggest risk in system implementations, with significant impact on cost and timelines. When Novo Nordisk faced migrating 130TB of data from a legacy on prem Statistical Computing Environment (SCE) to a cloud based Databricks SCE, we sought an alternative to disk-based or long-running batch migrations—while keeping all legacy data accessible.Our solution was to migrate without migrating. By extending the existing on prem backup into Azure using standard backup functionality, we enabled direct extraction of data to Azure Blob Storage, which then seamlessly integrated with Databricks catalogs. This provided a full copy of the legacy SCE data in the new environment.Users can work directly with legacy formats (e.g., SAS7BDAT) or convert data to Delta tables using a validated SAS tool - only transforming data when it is needed. This approach dramatically reduces migration time, risk, and complexity while ensuring users have access to all legacy data.

sessions.title: Redact, Protect, Disclose: A Practical Workshop on Clinical Document Anonymisation Under EU CTR
sessions.abstract:
With EU CTR No 536/2014 now fully in force and the legacy Directive framework officially retired, sponsors and CROs face a deceptively complex operational challenge: correctly anonymising clinical documents for CTIS publication in a way that satisfies EMA guidance, protects commercially confidential information, and avoids over-redaction to the point of rendering disclosures meaningless.
Extensive redaction has been a persistent problem, with published documents often so heavily redacted that they are of little value to stakeholders and patients. Conversely, under-redaction exposes sponsors to data protection risk.
In this Hands-on Workshop, participants will work through realistic document scenarios — including protocol excerpts, CSRs, and patient narratives — making and defending anonymisation decisions against current EMA guidance. Small groups will compare approaches, surface divergent interpretations, and develop practical decision frameworks that they can take back to their own organisations.
Facilitated by TrialAssure, whose ANONYMIZE platform is deployed across European pharma and CRO programmes, this session offers practitioner-level depth on one of the most consequential — and under-discussed — compliance obligations in the post-CTR landscape.

sessions.title: The Missing Foundation of Inspection-Ready Statistical Computing Environments
sessions.abstract: A Statistical Computing Environment (SCE) can be seen as a layered architecture, with infrastructure as its foundation: servers, storage, and networking. Compliance gaps in this foundation propagate upward, making every control built on top more difficult to implement, validate, and defend during regulatory inspections. When for example the storage lacks versioning and access logs, an audit trail for dataset changes must be constructed via procedural workarounds, which increases implementation scope and reduces traceability.Despite this, the infrastructure layer is frequently treated as technical background during SCE design, selected before business and regulatory requirements are fully translated into system designs. We believe this sequencing is a root cause of validation debt that surfaces late and costs disproportionately to fix.Drawing on real-world SCE implementations, we present IT and CSV leaders with a systematic approach to connect GxP requirements directly to infrastructure design decisions, illustrated with concrete examples of compliance gaps.

sessions.title: Emotional Intelligence for Technical Minds: Navigating Change, Conflict & Reinvention
sessions.abstract: Statistical programmers work in complex delivery environments where regulatory timelines, audit readiness, cross‑functional collaboration and organisational change are routine. Teams must also adapt to evolving tools and shifting standards that increase cognitive load. Yet the capabilities that most influence performance under these conditions, emotional regulation, conflict navigation and adaptive thinking, are rarely developed within technical career pathways. Drawing on over twenty years of leadership in statistical programming and extensive coaching training, this session introduces a practical emotional intelligence framework tailored to analytical professionals. Using a simple “Pitstop” metaphor, participants will explore four core skills: recognising emotional warning lights, understanding what’s happening under the hood, regulating the internal engine and navigating change with a clear roadmap. The session includes practical demonstrations of each tool, enabling attendees to apply the techniques immediately within real‑world delivery contexts. The outcome is improved cognitive clarity, more effective communication and stronger decision‑making during periods of uncertainty.

sessions.title: Coding Assistants or Autopilots? What We Learned Rolling Out AI in Data Sciences
sessions.stream: Machine Learning, AI & Large Language Models
sessions.abstract: Are corporations truly prepared for AI-assisted programming or is it just a pipe dream? Drawing on experiences from workshops focused on implementing coding assistants, this presentation will reflect on the challenges of steering a behemoth-sized organisation to use such tools effectively, discuss common safety issues faced by users, and highlight key user pain points regarding coding assistants gathered during these sessions.The presentation will aim to answer three key questions: Are out-of-the-box tools such as GitHub Copilot suitable solutions for statistical programming and analysis? What are the security and technological prerequisites that must be resolved before implementation? Are users in the driving seat, or are they producing solutions that neither they nor their stakeholders understand?Finally, I’ll circle back to clarify what it actually takes to use these tools as a statistical programmer, and disentangle the reality from corporate jargon and buzzwords.

sessions.title: Walking the BC Journey: from Assessment Selection to Submission
sessions.abstract: This presentation explores the end-to-end lifecycle of Biomedical Concepts (BCs), detailing practical examples in driving data standardization from initial study design through to regulatory submission. The journey starts with the setting up of an instantiated BC repository designed to maximize operational efficiency and reusability. This is the basis for study-specific BC instantiations selected as study assessments and stored in the Unified Study Definitions Model (USDM) format, demonstrating how BCs serve as a single source of truth. Attendees will gain insight into how these instantiated BCs directly inform and automate downstream processes, including the configuration of Electronic Data Capture (EDC) elements, the creation of data transfer agreements, the stream-lined creation of SDTM submission datasets, and the generation of Define.xml. Finally, based on actual use cases, the strengths and limitations of the current CDISC BC library will be discussed. Ultimately, this presentation shows how BCs can be leveraged to ensure data traceability, reduce manual effort, and accelerate clinical trial timelines.

sessions.title: Breaking the Boom-and-Bust Cycle: How Management Can Create a Culture of Maintainable Productivity
sessions.abstract: With fluctuating workloads and endless urgent deliverables, burnout often feels unavoidable in high pressure work environments. However prolonged excessive stress should not have to be an accepted side effect of a successful statistical programming career. If left unaddressed, employees can risk repeatedly extending energy levels beyond their natural maximum capacity, leading to longer recovery time and subsequently feeling more pressure during future busy periods, thus creating the “boom-and-bust” cycle. While this has a huge personal impact on mental health, the reduced productivity and quality can result in significant financial losses when the cycle is embedded into the company culture. This presentation explores management techniques that prioritise stable work-life balance to encourage consistent levels of productivity across a team. This demonstrates how reframing productivity produces higher quality outputs for long term goals. These insights provide a transferable framework for leaders across knowledge‑based, high‑pressure industries seeking sustainable performance without compromising employee well‑being.

sessions.title: Automating Submission-Ready RTF TLF Generation from ADaM: A Sponsor-Owned Macro Framework
sessions.abstract: This presentation introduces a sponsor-owned macro framework developed by an in-house statistics team to automate submission-ready RTF TLF generation from ADaM datasets. The framework combines parameter-driven macro calls, standardized analysis modules, and reusable TLF templates to perform statistical analyses and produce consistent RTF outputs. It enables the sponsor to standardize statistical analysis logic, generate full TLF outputs independently in-house, and ensure consistent reporting standards across studies. The presentation will describe the workflow from ADaM input to final RTF output, including macro design approach, output standardization, validation considerations, and practical lessons learned during implementation. This work demonstrates how sponsor-owned automation can strengthen statistical programming ownership, support independent reproduction and verification of analysis results, and build internal capability to efficiently manage clinical reporting workloads.

sessions.title: Extracting Clinical Signals from Free-Text Patient Diaries: When Patient Expression and Emotions Are Reported as Events
sessions.abstract: Free-text entries in patient diaries often highlight the gap between structured clinical data expectations and the way patients naturally describe their experiences. Rather than providing discrete, medically framed inputs, patients frequently embed relevant clinical information within broader, expressive narratives. In this presentation, we examine a real-world diary entry from a clinical trial in which a participant combines detailed personal observations, emotional expression, and humor with clinically relevant information. The entry also demonstrates how patients may consciously adapt their responses based on their interpretation of how systems will react. Using this example as a representative case, we illustrate how critical clinical signals can be intertwined with non-structured, context-rich text. We discuss key data handling risks, including misclassification of non-clinical expressions as adverse events, loss of relevant clinical detail, and generation of unnecessary queries.This work demonstrates that effective data handling strategies must account for both the structure required by clinical systems and the richness of real-world patient expression.

sessions.title: The SCE is Dead! Long Live the SCE!
sessions.abstract: The monolithic Statistical Computing Environment -- self-contained, SAS-only, validated once and touched reluctantly -- is dead. Killed not by any single technology, but by the compounding demands of a world it was never designed for.The new paradigm looks nothing like its predecessor. Infrastructure as code. CI/CD pipelines that treat clinical environments with the same rigour as software releases. A shared, governed data layer accessible simultaneously by analytics workbenches, submission tools, medical writing platforms, AI models, and operational systems -- GxP and non-GxP alike. Multi-language compute as a baseline expectation, not a concession. Cloud/AI-first, open instead of closed, shared instead of siloed, SAS/R/Python/and more - the exception is now the rule. The question is no longer "which SCE should we buy?" It is: what architecture, what infrastructure, and what accelerators -- for audit, lineage, and workflow -- make this new model compliant, reproducible, and real?This presentation makes the case that the SCE is an architecture now, not an application. And examines practical applications for this brave new world.

sessions.title: Developing Tomorrow’s Talent: Why Placement Programs Matter More Than Ever. Practical Lessons from Industry
sessions.abstract: Breaking into data science and statistical programming has never felt more daunting. AI-driven disruption, rapidly evolving skill demands, and a persistent experience gap leave many students and early-career professionals uncertain about their path forward.This presentation explores how placement students deliver clear value while developing technical, professional, and problem-solving skills. Drawing on our own experience at UCB, it highlights how these programs build confidence beyond the classroom and connect with PHUSE Academia initiatives that promote career pathways and engage students with the real-world practice.Through honest reflection on what works, we show how collaboration between academia, industry, and professional communities can build sustainable talent pipelines and inspire the next generation to pursue careers in data science. Whether you are a student, a mentor, or shaping your organisation’s talent strategy, this session offers practical insight into growing careers that last.

sessions.title: From Hype to Help: Everyday AI Wins
sessions.stream: Machine Learning, AI & Large Language Models
sessions.abstract: AI is everywhere, especially LinkedIn, but for many the hardest question is still: “What can I actually use it for on Monday morning?” This presentation answers that by cutting through the hype and focusing on practical, low-risk quick wins that anyone can try today. From drafting and refining emails, creating marketing or training images, understanding unfamiliar code, generating starter code, and debugging errors, AI can help turn vague ideas into clearer plans and everyday tasks into something a little less painful.The session then moves from “cool trick” to “repeatable skill” with the often-overlooked art of prompt engineering: setting context, defining roles, giving examples, asking for structured output, iterating effectively, checking assumptions, and, most importantly, knowing when not to trust the answer. It will also cover practical considerations around token use, so you do not keep running out halfway through a task or quietly rack up an eye-watering bill.No data science PhD, secret model access, or robot overlord allegiance required. Just practical examples, realistic limitations, and takeaways you can use in your day-to-day job.

sessions.title: Harmonising Oncology Response Criteria: An SDTM Mapping Framework Across RECIST, RANO, Lugano, and IMWG
sessions.abstract: Oncology clinical trials use diverse response evaluation criteria, including RECIST 1.1, RANO, Lugano Classification, and IMWG 2016, each tailored to specific disease areas. Although CDISC SDTM provides a standardized framework for regulatory submissions, differences in assessment methodology, lesion characterization, and response definitions create challenges for consistent and traceable SDTM mappings.This paper compares SDTM mapping approaches across RECIST-, RANO-, Lugano-, and IMWG-based studies in solid tumors, neuro-oncology, lymphoma, and multiple myeloma. Key inconsistencies include lesion representation, response terminology, and variability in collecting versus deriving response endpoints.Findings show that standard SDTM domains adequately support RECIST studies, whereas RANO and Lugano often require sponsor-defined extensions or enhanced metadata strategies. The paper proposes a flexible, metadata-driven SDTM mapping framework that standardizes core structures while accommodating disease-specific differences, improving submission consistency, reviewer interpretability, and cross-study interoperability.

sessions.title: Secure Transactions in Leadership: Creating a Workplace Where People Choose to Stay
sessions.abstract: Employee retention is often framed as a problem of incentives, engagement, or culture, yet many departures are driven by a quieter force: emotional unsustainability at work. This talk argues that two well-established psychological frameworks, attachment theory and transactional analysis, offer a powerful, practical lens for understanding why people stay or leave organisations, particularly in remote and hybrid environments.Attachment theory explains how predictability, consistency, and leader availability shape employees’ sense of safety, while transactional analysis illuminates how everyday interactions either preserve adult dignity or trigger patterns of control, compliance, anxiety, and withdrawal. Together, these frameworks shift attention from individual “resilience” to the relationship between manager and employee.This session shows how clear expectations, explicit communication, calm emotional regulation, and reliable repair after missteps reduce cognitive and emotional load on staff. It also demonstrates how Adult-to-Adult leadership, rather than parental control or emotional rescuing, supports autonomy, trust, and long-term commitment.

sessions.title: Up and Down Branches: A GitHub-Centric, GenAI-Ready Validation Framework for SAS-to-R Transition
sessions.abstract: As the Clinical Assay Statistics team at GSK, we have long established trust with our Clinical Laboratories through validated SAS macros, crucial for generating documentation for regulatory authorities. We have now transitioned to R, maintaining the same level of confidence.This presentation unveils our GitHub-centric approach to validating R functions as a package. Experience the journey through repository branches: descend into new branches where specifications and acceptance criteria are captured via GitHub Issues. Ascend as pull requests document automated code review and validation, leveraging CI/CD pipelines via GitHub Actions.Importantly, this framework also enables GenAI assisted drafting and automation of the steps described above, offering a scalable path to improve productivity and standardisation in regulated environments.This approach replaces the previously fragmented, multi-document process with an integrated, streamlined and trusted workflow. Attendees will gain insights into how this enhances efficiency and reliability in function validation, with clear visibility of their position in the repository branches at any given step.

sessions.title: Cross-Platform Synchronisation in a New Statistical Computing Environment: Early Data Engineering Lessons from First User Onboarding to First Study Delivery
sessions.abstract: Implementing a new Statistical Computing Environment (SCE) in a regulated clinical setting requires more than platform deployment; it requires delivery-ready data workflows. This presentation describes Novo Nordisk’s early experience from first user to first delivery in its new SCE from an end-user and clinical data scientist perspective. The case study focuses on data handling and engineering challenges encountered during adoption, including differing data format constraints across source systems and databases, preserving consistency across platforms, and infrastructure readiness across interconnected components. To mitigate delivery risk, cross-platform synchronization was established to maintain continuity, provide a robust backup path, and enable successful study delivery despite late-emerging issues. We discuss practical lessons on stepwise implementation, showing how phased adoption, early testing, realistic expectation setting, and timely support can enable reliable delivery in a maturing environment. The presentation highlights how coordinated collaboration across technical, business, management, and automation teams strengthens resilient, delivery-ready workflows.

sessions.title: Beyond Code: Evidence Generation in an AI Era
sessions.abstract:
Artificial intelligence is rapidly transforming clinical and statistical programming, but its greatest impact may not be faster code generation—it may be the reinvention of how evidence is created, interpreted and delivered. Drawing on insights from the Programming Heads Council (PHC), this keynote explores how AI is shifting value from routine programming activities towards data integration, scientific interpretation and strategic decision support. It examines the foundations required for scaled AI adoption, the evolving competencies of the future workforce, and emerging operating models that may redefine biometrics. The future belongs not to those who produce more code, but to those who generate better evidence.
Representing the collective perspective of global industry leaders, the Programming Heads Council brings together senior experts across pharmaceutical and clinical research organisations to shape the future of clinical programming. Their work reflects a shared commitment to advancing innovation, establishing best practice, and ensuring that technological progress translates into meaningful improvements in evidence generation and patient outcomes.
In this keynote, PHC representatives will share practical insights into how organisations can move beyond experimentation with AI to achieve sustainable, enterprise-level adoption. The session will explore the cultural, operational and technical transformations required to embed AI effectively, including new ways of working, evolving skill sets, and the importance of strong data foundations.
Audiences will gain a clearer understanding of the changing role of clinical programmers, the opportunities to elevate impact beyond code, and the strategies needed to build resilient, future-ready biometrics organisations. The keynote sets the stage for a broader discussion on how the industry can embrace AI responsibly while maintaining scientific rigour and trust in the evidence it delivers.
Explore the newly released Artificial Intelligence Adoption in Statistical Programming white paper and the Programming Vision on AI manifesto, which address the inflection point our industry is in and provide the foundation for this keynote discussion.
Brought to you by the Programming Heads Council!

sessions.title: TrialHub: Connecting Clinical Trial Documents into a Cross-Study Knowledge Graph
sessions.abstract: Clinical trial knowledge is often fragmented across disconnected repositories containing Protocols, SAPs, shells, specifications and code. Questions such as “Which studies used waterfall plots?”, “What endpoints were used for this indication?” frequently rely on manual searching or institutional memory despite the information already existing within the organisation.TrialHub is a Python-based platform that transforms the study portfolio into a searchable knowledge graph spanning all clinical trial documentation. Content is extracted into structured chunks with rich JSON metadata and vector embeddings, enabling semantic search and lineage-aware retrieval across studies.LLMs operate as an intelligence layer over indexed metadata, interpreting natural-language questions and returning linked evidence directly to the source. Cross-study similarity scoring additionally identifies reused versus study-specific content patterns across protocols and SAPs.The result is a metadata-connected, searchable portfolio that supports knowledge reuse, traceability, and AI-assisted clinical document workflows like draft SAP authoring.

sessions.title: Metadata-Driven SDTM, ADaM, and TFL Automation with Integrated Generative AI Workflows
sessions.abstract: This software demonstration presents a metadata-driven framework supporting SDTM, ADaM, and TFL automation through integrated modules including Data Mapper, SAP Builder, TFL Designer, AI Code Gen, TFL Viewer, and CSR Builder. The workflow demonstrates how study metadata can be reused across data standardization, analysis planning, output generation, review, and reporting activities.The session will focus on the integration of Generative AI (GenAI) within the AI Code Gen module to support analysis code generation using metadata, standardized templates, and reusable programming patterns. Integration with GitHub enables repository-based development, version control, traceability, and collaborative code management within the automation workflow.The demonstration will present an example end-to-end workflow illustrating how metadata-driven processes combined with controlled AI-assisted development can support consistency, reproducibility, and efficiency across clinical data and reporting activities.

sessions.title: Programming Workflows: Connecting Languages
sessions.abstract:
CT01: Introducing the "Multilayer Bridging Rule" to Mastering GitHub/GitLab Workflows in Blended Environments
In the evolving era of clinical biostatistics and statistical programming, mastering collaborative tools like GitHub/GitLab is essential for effective project execution. This session will provide targeted strategies for clinical programmers, focusing on navigating GitHub's branching complexities and optimizing workflows to minimize conflicts. Attendees will learn practical tips and tricks to master version control workflows, leverage diverse programming languages, and enhance cross-functional collaboration. By adopting the multilayer bridging rule, participants will boost their adaptability in modern collaborative environments, leading to improved efficiency and successful project outcomes. Join me to master branching strategies, minimize conflicts, and excel in collaborative clinical programming.
CT02: Navigating Package Updates at Scale: Using Diffify to Govern Open-Source R and Python Dependencies in Pharma
The rapid growth of open-source R and Python ecosystems has transformed clinical data science, yet it introduces a persistent governance challenge: how do teams safely manage package updates across validated Statistical Computing Environments (SCEs) without stifling productivity or introducing undetected risk? This paper presents two connected tools for addressing this challenge. Diffify (diffify.com) provides instant, structured comparisons between any two versions of an R package on CRAN or a Python package on PyPI, surfacing changes to functions, arguments, dependencies, and namespace. These are the signals that matter when assessing update impact in a regulated environment. Building on this, we introduce a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server built around Diffify, which brings these package comparison capabilities directly into the coding assistant workflow. Rather than context-switching to a browser, data scientists can query Diffify data from within their IDE, enabling faster, more informed decisions about package updates without leaving their development environment. Attendees will leave with a replicable framework for incorporating both tools into their open-source
CT03: Connecting VS Code to any SAS Environment
Microsoft's VS Code is a multi-lingual text editor used by programmers across every language. SAS has an official extension that allows you to connect with any SAS environment and submit code and get results right in the editor. We'll look at the coding editor, SAS Notebooks, and get a brief overview of how to get set up.

sessions.title: Dataset-JSON Uncovered: Standard, FDA Pilot, Hackathons and Tooling
sessions.abstract: Dataset-JSON is a new CDISC standard for exchanging tabular clinical datasets using JSON and is positioned as a modern successor to the long-established and increasingly outdated XPT format. It has already been piloted with the FDA as an alternative transport format for regulatory submissions, generating strong interest as well as concrete feedback from both regulators and industry. This presentation introduces the Dataset-JSON standard and showcases its journey from theory to practice. It highlights the path from initial drafting, through refinement in a community hackathon, to early solution development even before finalization of the standard, ensuring alignment with real-world industry needs. The talk will also provide an overview of the emerging tooling ecosystem and discuss how organizations can start exploring Dataset-JSON today.

sessions.title: Workforce 2030: Rewriting the Future of Statistical Programming in the AI Era
sessions.abstract: Statistical Programming is at a pivotal moment. Artificial intelligence, automation, modern data platforms and increasingly complex trial designs are transforming how clinical development work is delivered and where value is created. As routine activities become more automated, the function has an opportunity to evolve from execution-focused delivery to a strategic driver of insight, innovation, and business impact.This presentation introduces a practical Workforce 2030 framework built on three priorities: future-ready roles, adaptive organization design, and next-generation operating models. It explores how leaders can redesign career pathways, build skills in AI and advanced analytics, and shift from traditional capacity-based structures to agile, capability-led teams that improve speed, quality, and scalability.Attendees will gain actionable strategies to reskill existing talent, attract emerging capabilities, and preserve regulatory excellence while embracing change. The future of Statistical Programming will not be defined by technology alone, but by the organizations bold enough to reinvent their talent, teams, and ways of working.

sessions.title: Automated SDTM Transfer Review for ADaM and TFL Readiness
sessions.abstract: Clinical programming teams often receive several SDTM transfers before final analysis. Existing validation and issue-tracking reports help with conformance review, but teams still need a clear view of transfer-to-transfer changes and possible ADaM/TFL impact. We describe a SAS-based workflow for SDTM transfer review and analysis-readiness assessment. The workflow compares previous and current packages, detects added or removed datasets and variables, reviews controlled terms and units, flags value and date issues, and extracts Trial Summary information such as cut-off dates and dictionary versions. Findings are organized with status, severity, suggested ADaM/TFL impact and reviewer actions. The workflow complements existing validation processes by adding a practical programming check before work continues: what changed in the transfer, what looks inconsistent, and where should the team review first?

sessions.title: Improving Clinical Trial Efficiency with EDC - EHR Integration
sessions.abstract: Manual transfer of data into Electronic Data Capture (EDC) systems has become a less sustainable method due to the large volume of data and growing complexity of clinical trials. Integrating EDC with Electronic Health Records (EHR) using HL7 standards such as FHIR and ODM helps improving efficiency in data transfer and data quality. This integration reduces manual data entry efforts and minimizes errors by automatically transferring data into the EDC system. It also enables the efficient use of historical and real-world data, which is especially valuable in rare disease and oncology studies. Access to comprehensive EHR data including demographics, medical history, and medications supports faster participant identification, improves recruitment rates, shortens recruitment timelines, and lowers costs. A recent proof of concept demonstrated successful data transfer from a FHIR compliant database to an EDC system. This presentation discusses the benefits, limitations, and challenges of HER - EDC integration.

sessions.title: What Happens When Someone Speaks Up? Building Psychological Safety in Virtual Teams
sessions.abstract:
In a world where collaboration increasingly happens through screens, chat windows, and virtual meetings, how do we create environments where people feel safe to speak up, challenge ideas, ask questions, and learn from mistakes?
Psychological safety is strongly linked to team effectiveness, innovation, and learning, yet many organisations struggle to foster it in remote and hybrid settings, where participation can be uneven and social cues are more difficult to interpret.
This interactive 90-minute workshop introduces the four dimensions of psychological safety: Inclusion Safety, Learner Safety, Contributor Safety, and Challenger Safety. Through discussion and practical exercises, participants will conduct a psychological safety audit, identify strengths and barriers, and explore what psychological safety looks like in everyday virtual collaboration.
By the end of the session, participants will understand how psychological safety influences performance and engagement, use practical tools to assess it within their teams, and apply actionable strategies to create cultures where people feel safe to contribute, learn, and challenge constructively, even when working remotely.

sessions.title: In the Pipeline: Using Git to Manage a Validated Statistical Computing Environment
sessions.abstract: Validation of statistical computing environments is a requirement to meet regulatory standards. When modifications are made within these environments, it is essential to implement robust change management processes and conduct revalidation to ensure ongoing compliance. Mass adoption of cloud computing has created new opportunities to improve the build and management of validated statistical computing environments (VSCEs). It also enables support for studies that rely on software which require updates over time.Cloud-native VSCEs can be deployed using the YAML language and Git source control, with deployment scripts securely stored, offering complete transparency, version control, and auditability. This approach extends beyond validated analytical software, encompassing hardware and security configurations as well.The result is a VSCE with a transparent change history, rapid disaster recovery and the ability to redeploy archived versions of environments, to support legacy study requirements, many years after submission.This paper focuses on the approach taken, and the business benefits achieved through Infrastructure as Code automation in a highly regulated workspace.

sessions.title: Beyond Autocomplete: Accelerating SAS-Language Development with the Integrated AI Copilot in Siemens Rapidminer Workbench
sessions.abstract: In the world of clinical programming, the pressure to deliver accurate results under tight timelines is ever-increasing. This demonstration explores the impact of integrating an AI-driven Copilot directly into the Siemens Workbench & SLC environment. Unlike generic AI tools, an integrated Copilot functions as a context-aware pair programmer, specifically tuned for SAS-language syntax.Attendees will see a live demonstration of how this integration moves beyond simple autocomplete to provide intelligent code generation, real-time debugging, and automated documentation. We will showcase how the Copilot leverages the underlying SLC engine to optimise code efficiency and security while maintaining the governance required in a validated environment.By bridging the gap between natural language intent and functional code, this integration empowers developers to focus on high-level logic rather than repetitive syntax. This session provides a practical look at how the fusion of AI and specialised IDEs is redefining the "power of one"—enabling a single programmer to achieve higer levels of productivity, accuracy, and code quality in their daily development tasks.

sessions.title: Evolution of the MDR: Transitioning from Static Libraries to Intelligent Knowledge Hubs
sessions.abstract: Traditional metadata repositories are evolving beyond static standards libraries into intelligent, connected knowledge platforms that support study design, automation, and submission readiness. This presentation explores how modern MDR ecosystems can leverage AI, semantic search, and historical study intelligence to improve metadata reuse and consistency across clinical programs. The session demonstrates how organizations can reduce duplication, accelerate study startup timelines, and improve standards governance by transforming metadata into an operational asset rather than a passive repository. Real-world examples will highlight integration opportunities across protocol authoring, EDC study build, SDTM mapping, and Define.xml generation. Attendees will also learn how intelligent metadata recommendations can support decision-making for standards teams, programmers, and data managers. The presentation will discuss practical implementation challenges, governance considerations, and the future role of MDRs in enabling scalable automation strategies. The objective is to show how metadata intelligence can become a foundational capability for AI-enabled clinical development operations.

sessions.title: Beyond the Baseline: Helping People Discover Their Inner Outlier of Innovation
sessions.abstract: Innovation in life‑sciences data work is often viewed as a technical challenge, yet its true catalyst is people. This session explores how leaders can help individuals move “beyond the baseline” of routine delivery and uncover their unique creative strengths — their inner outliers. By fostering psychological safety, encouraging curiosity, and creating space for experimentation, leaders can transform teams from task‑driven groups into innovation engines. Drawing on examples from data science, statistical programming, and cross‑functional clinical teams, the session highlights practical leadership behaviors that elevate human potential: reframing failure as learning, amplifying diverse perspectives, and guiding teams through ambiguity with clarity and trust. Attendees will gain strategies for nurturing environments where ideas flow freely, emerging technologies are embraced with confidence, and people feel empowered to challenge assumptions. When leaders champion the human side of innovation, teams discover new ways to think, create, and deliver impact that truly stands out.

sessions.title: From Hard Coded to Automated: Unlocking TLF Efficiency with a Central Properties File
sessions.abstract: Titles, populations, and footnotes are some of the core components of tables, listings, and figures (TLFs), yet they are often programmed manually and repeated across programs. This practice makes them error prone and difficult to maintain. This presentation will demonstrate how using a separate centralized TLF properties file can provide a solution by transforming these recurring elements into structured, programmatically accessible data. Centralization of these properties improves consistency across outputs, reduces human error and increases robustness to potential study updates. Practical examples will be shown on how this approach integrates seamlessly into standard TLF generation workflows, along with tips and tricks for flexible reuse, validation, and version control. Finally, limitations and potential extensions are discussed, such as tailoring this file to become sponsor-specific. Overall, this approach enables more efficient and reliable TLF production strengthening end-to-end automation in modern clinical environments.

sessions.title: Real-World Data Is Changing Statistical Programming. Is Your SCE Ready?
sessions.abstract: Real-world evidence has moved from supplementary data source to core regulatory strategy. The infrastructure challenge is underestimated. Most SCEs are built around a fundamental assumption that trial data has a protocol. Observational data, claims, and electronic health records do not. That structural difference breaks metadata models, complicates provenance tracking, and creates audit readiness problems that only surface when a submission is under scrutiny.The instinctive response is separate infrastructure for RWE. The cost is predictable: duplicated compliance overhead, inconsistent standards across teams, and a governance gap at the boundary between clinical and real-world data that no policy document closes.This presentation examines what a unified governance model actually requires: how metadata frameworks must be extended to accommodate protocol-free data, where provenance and traceability requirements diverge, and which scope decisions organizations consistently get wrong. Attendees leave with a concrete framework for assessing SCE readiness for RWE before a live program forces the question.

sessions.title: Hierarchical Data Models as a Robust Core Standard Enabling Traceability, Reproducibility, and Reuse of the Analysis Results Data Layer
sessions.abstract: Clinical trial protocols and statistical analysis plans are inherently hierarchical, describing high level objectives before branching into analyses and detailed rules. In practice, analysis results are typically stored in tabular data formats relying on columns to encode hierarchy with limited structural flexibility. In contrast, hierarchical S3 objects (tree-like structures) are designed to directly mirror the structure of the specification documents, enabling nested organization of results, metadata, code, intermediate outputs, model objects, and graphics by analysis concept with few structural constraints. Such hierarchical structures support end to end traceability and reproducibility aligned with CDISC 360i concepts, with S7 objects providing a natural evolution toward ARS ready results. Fit-for-purpose packages and applications can reduce technical complexities of working with these objects providing intuitive user-friendly access to results fully aligned with analysis concepts. Thus, hierarchical results layers can serve as a robust single source of truth for output displays, results datasets, applications, dashboards, and AI ready data ingestion.

sessions.title: SAS Data Maker: AI-generated Synthetic Data for Real-World Impact
sessions.abstract: SAS Data Maker gives your organization instant, compliant access to high‑quality synthetic data, empowering teams to innovate without ever exposing sensitive information. It reinforces strong governance and embeds privacy‑by‑design into every workflow, accelerating your overall data strategy.By generating realistic synthetic datasets that preserve essential statistical properties while eliminating identifiable details, SAS Data Maker directly addresses challenges around data privacy and limited access.We highlight new capabilities such as multi‑table support and advanced generation techniques, along with an intuitive interface and built‑in evaluation metrics that help teams experiment faster, validate workflows, and develop models responsibly.

sessions.title: AI as a Pair Tutor for Clinical Trial Programming: Prompt Patterns and Practical Guardrails for Faster Learning
sessions.abstract: AI assistants are increasingly used by programmers, but their most reliable value in regulated environments is as a training tool that accelerates understanding rather than generating “ready-to-run” code. This presentation describes practical workflows for using AI as a pair tutor in clinical-trial programming, including prompting for step-by-step explanations of existing code, requesting alternative implementations, and interrogating assumptions, edge cases, and performance implications. We focus on transferable techniques across SAS, R, Python, and SQL, and show how to turn AI interactions into learning artefacts such as annotated code, checklists, and unit-test ideas. Safe usage is addressed through practical guardrails to avoid sharing confidential or patient data, proprietary company information, or study-specific intellectual property with AI tools, with a reminder that AI output should be understood and reviewed before use. Attendees will leave with concrete prompt patterns and a personal learning checklist to help assess whether they've genuinely understood what the AI has explained, such as: could you explain this to a colleague, or adapt it if the requirements changed

sessions.title: Beyond the PDF: Bringing CDISC Standards to Life
sessions.abstract: CDISC standards and Controlled Terminology underpin clinical data governance but are still consumed primarily through large static documents. Finding implementation guidance, tracing terminology usage, or comparing SDTM and ADaM IG versions often relies on manual review and institutional knowledge. Standards-Browser is a Python web application providing a workflow-oriented interface over CDISC standards metadata spanning SDTM, ADaM, Controlled Terminology, and extracted IG section text. Interactive browsing, filtering, linked terminology views, and version-aware navigation replace hundreds of pages of manual searching. An indexed standards layer combined with extracted IG text enables fast natural-language querying without the runtime constraints usually encountered with large PDF documents. An LLM operates over the structured metadata and indexed guidance to provide cited answers, implementation examples, and conversational navigation while preserving traceability back to the source documentation. The result is a searchable, connected standards workflow supporting governance, implementation, onboarding, and cross-version migration activities.

sessions.title: From Shadow AI to Shared Capability: How Team Leads Enable Responsible Innovation in Regulated Programming
sessions.abstract: Statistical programming teams must meet strict regulatory expectations for traceability and reproducibility, which makes them more cautious about using AI in submission related work.Hallucination risk and unclear accountability can drive blanket avoidance or “shadow” adoption. This paper presents a leadership operating model for responsible innovation in statistical programming, using AI as the case. Innovative culture is defined in behavioural terms and translated into mechanisms: governed AI sandboxes for mock exercises with explicit exit criteria (validation evidence, documentation, peer review) before production influence; leader sponsored experiments and proof-of-concept; and structured review of AI generated plans and assumptions, not only code. A promote to standard pathway converts prototypes into shared team primitives (reusable prompts, patterns, checklists, tests) and uses failure narratives to accelerate learning without blame. Finally, metrics for successful adoption are proposed: learning velocity, time from experiment to reusable asset, adoption breadth, knowledge distribution index, and sustained improvements in quality, consistency, and efficiency.

sessions.title: Agentic QC for R and Python in Positron
sessions.abstract: This presentation discusses "Agentic QC," a shift where AI agents act as validation partners within the Positron IDE. We explore how to enhance the manual challenge of double programming by orchestrating Agents that support deriving, SDTM and ADaM datasets and TFL outputs as the primary programmer works. The session demonstrates how this ACE (AI Statistical Environment) capability utilizes Claude Code and the Posit Assistant to cross-reference code against company standards and Pharmaverse best practices. Attendees will learn how to support GxP-level rigor through an "automated check" that identifies challenges before formal validation begins. Finally, we showcase how Agentic QC supports data integrity while aiding the time-to-submission for late-stage clinical reporting.

sessions.title: Strengthening Regulatory Benefit-Risk Decision-Making With Fit-for-Purpose RWE When RCT Evidence Is Limited
sessions.abstract: Acute, life-threatening conditions may render randomized controlled trials (RCTs) impractical or ethically challenging, leading to evidence gaps in regulatory decision-making. In this case study, it is demonstrated how real-world evidence (RWE) was integrated in an European Medicines Agency (EMA) indication update of a haemostatic treatment for severe postpartum haemorrhage when uterotonics are insufficient to achieve haemostasis. The strategy included defining a clear regulatory role for RWE within the totality of evidence, identifying and assessing fit-for-purpose real-world data sources in line with ENCePP principles, and specifying an estimand for comparative RWE analyses. A previously conducted RCT was re-analysed using an outcome definition aligned across all data sources. RWE also contributed to real-world safety characterisation and informed the benefit–risk assessment supporting the final positive EMA outcome.

sessions.title: Prompting with Purpose: Agentic Coding Beyond Copy and Paste in Regulated Clinical Trials
sessions.abstract: Gen AI is becoming a practical tool in clinical and statistical programming, with agentic coding shifting work beyond copy and paste reuse toward interactive, review driven, and standards aware development. As teams face growing pressure to deliver high quality outputs within tight timelines, agentic coding, supported by tools such as GitHub Copilot, can accelerate routine programming while maintaining quality, traceability, and CDISC compliance. Using GitHub Copilot within SAS and R workflows, this paper presents practical examples of agentic coding applied to CDISC compliant SDTM and ADaM datasets. Use cases include metadata driven variable derivations, checks against study specifications, and refactoring legacy code to improve readability and traceability. The paper also outlines prompt engineering techniques that improve output relevance and consistency, and shows how agentic coding complements programmer workflows through inline suggestions, pattern reuse, and code explainability. It focuses practical ideas for using agentic coding in daily programming to improve efficiency while maintaining compliance in regulated environments.

sessions.title: A Practical Hybrid Framework for Define.xml Development Across SDTM and ADaM Using Large Language Models and Pinnacle 21
sessions.abstract: This presentation builds on prior work emphasizing the importance of understanding the ‘Roles of Each Sheet and Column’ in Define.xml Excel specifications for quality and regulatory compliance (https://www.lexjansen.com/phuse/2025/SA/PAP_SA08.pdf.). It proposes a hybrid framework combining Pinnacle 21 Community, large language models (LLMs), and human review to support efficient Define-XML v2.1 development for SDTM and ADaM. The workflow generates Excel specifications from completed datasets, then uses LLMs to augment sections such as variable descriptions and derivations based on structured inputs including implementation guides, SAPs, shells, and detailed column-level guidance. This improves consistency and accuracy of metadata generation. Critical elements requiring interpretability and regulatory judgment remain human-reviewed. Applied to a clinical study, the approach reduced manual effort for descriptive metadata while maintaining validation quality, demonstrating that a Human–LLM–tool hybrid can enhance efficiency while preserving regulatory readiness.

sessions.title: Specification‑to‑TLF in R:  An AI‑Assisted, Standards‑Driven Reporting Workflow in R
sessions.abstract: Generating submission-ready tables, listings, and figures remains a repetitive stage of clinical reporting. We present work in progress on an AI-assisted, automation-driven workflow in R and the pharmaverse that shortens the path from source documents to first-draft TLFs while keeping the statistical programmer in control.The workflow uses AI where interpretation is needed and deterministic automation where validation, traceability, and reproducibility matter most. A large language model extracts information from unstructured clinical documents, such as the SAP and protocol, to create reviewed, machine-readable output specifications. These specifications are then used with the CDISC Analysis Results Standard and related tooling to automate validated standard tables and figures, and as input to AI-assisted programming tools that draft R programs for additional outputs.The approach combines AI-supported interpretation and coding, open standards for structure, and reproducible automation for execution. Programmers remain accountable by reviewing specifications, approving generated code, and resolving cases where automation cannot yet be trusted.

sessions.title: RESIDE – A transparent, non-disclosive tool for summarising and synthesising data from Trusted Research Environments
sessions.abstract: Trusted research environments (TREs) around the world securely hold vast quantities of health-related data, from clinical trials to electronic health records. However, when publicly accessible metadata are limited, it becomes difficult to know what data is available and how they are structured. Without this information, data exploration and planning analysis prior to gaining access to the data is challenging. Here we present RESIDE, an R package that provides a transparent, non-disclosive, end-to-end solution for extracting metadata from a TRE and generating synthetic datasets that emulate the structure of the real data. The package also allows users to incorporate assumptions about correlations between variables. We demonstrate the RESIDE Package using multiple types of data such as clinical trial datasets and electronic health records.

sessions.title: What Is an AI Agent, and How Can It Be Built and Tailored for Pharma Use Cases?
sessions.stream: Machine Learning, AI & Large Language Models
sessions.abstract: Agents, the building blocks of agentic AI, represent the next evolution in AI systems. They extend the capabilities of an AI model-typically a large language model-to reason, solve tasks autonomously, interact with their environment, and improve their performance over time. For many non-specialists, the term remains abstract despite its growing presence. AI platform providers now offer configurable, though somewhat limited, agents within everyday chatbot tools, while IT departments are building more sophisticated custom AI systems.In this beginner-friendly session, we will introduce the core concepts of AI agents and use an exploratory data analysis (EDA) agent as an intuitive live demonstration to show how more advanced agentic systems can be designed and tailored to specific use cases. We will demonstrate how agents can integrate data access, cleaning, exploration, visualization, report generation, code generation, and machine learning within a single interactive workflow. The EDA example serves as a concrete illustration rather than the main focus; the broader objective is to show how the same agentic design pattern can be adapted to a wide range of pharmaceutical workflows.

sessions.title: A Causal inference Primer
sessions.abstract: Causal questions are increasingly important in clinical research, particularly as real‑world evidence informs regulatory and market access decisions. This session is an introduction for statisticians and programmers new to causal inference. We explain how causal questions differ from association analyses, and why causal conclusions depend on extra assumptions that must be stated clearly. We then walk through a workflow: define the exact causal question, think through study design, make assumptions explicit (e.g., with causal diagrams), handle confounding, and adjust for confounding and assess robustness using a short example. We also place common approaches (target trial emulation, propensity scores, weighting) into this workflow. Finally, we briefly contrast two ways causal analyses are commonly implemented today (OHDSI population‑level estimation and TMLE‑style estimation). The aim is to give attendees a practical introduction to causal thinking.

sessions.title: Data Democratisation in Clinical Research: Innovation or Organised Chaos?
sessions.abstract: Data democratisation is often presented as an inevitable step toward faster and smarter decision-making. But in highly regulated clinical environments, broader access to data can create anxiety among statisticians and data managers: Will users misinterpret results? Will governance disappear? Will specialist expertise be undervalued?This session challenges the false choice between rigid data silos and uncontrolled self-service analytics. Drawing from practical implementation experience, it demonstrates how organisations can democratise data responsibly while strengthening — not weakening — the role of data experts.The talk will cover how leadership can foster innovation without compromising scientific quality, compliance or trust. It will also share some best practices derived from collaborative projects with clients -practical challenges and how to bridge them. Attendees will leave with a framework for creating a culture where broader data access empowers the organisation while statisticians and data managers remain central to quality assurance, interpretation, and strategic decision-making.

sessions.title: Code That Writes Code That Writes Code?! Creating ADaMs in R with {admiralroche}
sessions.abstract: Writing template code is just as much an art as it is a skill, requiring balancing solid starting points with flexibility for custom adaptations. For developers, maintaining templates while ensuring consistency and eliminating repetitive tasks is a constant struggle.Over the past years, Roche's fast transition to R for ADaM programming challenged the {admiralroche} team to rethink our process, requiring constant evolution to provide fit for purpose templates. In this talk, we walk you through our journey of levelling up our templates, starting by exploring how and why we initially set up the {admiralroche} package extension and why we then centralised template maintenance by deconstructing templates into modular blocks (code that writes code). Finally, we unveil our latest frontier: dynamic ADaM template generation. By passing ADaM specifications to our package, we automatically create and assemble the right blocks into a customized template script (code that writes code that writes code!).We will discuss our challenges and learnings, sharing metrics on reduced maintenance and time saved. Join us to see why, in the quest for the ultimate ADaM template, automation trumps AI.

sessions.title: Harmonising EQ‑5D‑5L Survey Data in OMOP CDM v5.4: A LOINC‑Free, Practical Approach
sessions.abstract: Patient Reported Outcomes (PROs) are increasingly used in Real World Evidence (RWE) and Health Technology Assessment (HTA) activities. However, reuse is often restricted by data heterogeneity and insufficient standardization in clinical vocabularies. While the EQ-5D-5L is one of the commonly used PROs, its integration into the OMOP Common Data Model (CDM) is challenging in the absence of established LOINC codes. The primary objective was to outline an effective and harmonized method for accommodating EQ-5D-5L data in OMOP CDM v5.4, which is compatible with future standardization. Each assessment was handled as an individual survey record. Both individual assessment results and derived outcomes were consistently recorded. The proposed method was implemented on synthetic survey data, resulting in valid and compatible data in OMOP format, which fulfilled standard data quality criteria. A migrate‑to‑standard, LOINC‑free approach enables integration of EQ‑5D‑5L data into OMOP CDM v5.4 while preserving flexibility for future standardization and best practices.

sessions.title: Token-Efficient Clinical Programming Through Hybrid Agentic AI and Rule-Based Systems
sessions.abstract:
Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming clinical development, helping sponsors address growing pressures to deliver studies faster, improve efficiency, and reduce costs while maintaining regulatory quality. While hundreds of AI use cases have emerged across the drug development lifecycle, only a subset is delivering measurable business value and return on investment.
This interactive workshop will examine the current state of AI in clinical development, highlighting high-impact applications across biometrics and R&D, including synthetic data generation, AI-assisted data management, and agentic statistical programming. We will also explore the emerging challenge of AI inference economics, including why token efficiency is becoming an increasingly important consideration as organisations scale AI adoption.

sessions.title: Explainable AI in Clinical Development: Bridging Innovation, Trust, and Regulatory Expectations
sessions.abstract: AI is rapidly becoming embedded across clinical data review, risk monitoring, metadata management, and programming workflows. However, adoption in regulated environments depends heavily on transparency and explainability. This session examines practical approaches for implementing explainable AI within clinical ecosystems while maintaining auditability, reproducibility, and trust. Using real-world examples, we will explore how organizations are designing human-in-the-loop frameworks, deterministic outputs, controlled execution environments, and governance models aligned with evolving FDA and global regulatory expectations.

sessions.title: Kick-Starting Your DDF / USDM Journey: Lessons Learned from a Real-World PoC
sessions.abstract: The Digital Data Flow (DDF) initiative and the release of USDM v4.0, aligned with the ICH M11 guideline, provide a clear framework for digitizing clinical protocols. However, many organizations still face challenges in translating this vision into practical implementation.In this presentation, we share lessons learned from a real-world proof of concept (PoC) conducted in collaboration with data4knowledge, where a USDM-aligned Schedule of Activities (SoA) was developed based on an argenx protocol template.The PoC validated USDM applicability in practice, generated multiple stakeholder-specific participant journey views from a single source (site, participant, argenx) and established a protocol-agnostic methodology. This session provides actionable insights for teams looking to kick-start their DDF/USDM journey and accelerate adoption toward a fully digital study setup. The same USDM can be leveraged also for creation of SAP, CSR,...
