sessions.title: One Study, Two Worlds: Rethinking the Exploratory–Regulatory Boundary with a Unified Analytics Platform
sessions.abstract: One study. Two worlds. For years, statistical programming teams have known this scenario: locally installed R for fast exploratory work and a separate validated system when a study needs to submit. Two toolchains, two data locations, duplicated effort - and when an exploratory study pivots to a submission-ready deliverable, the team faces not an upgrade but a restart.This presentation describes how Boehringer Ingelheim Animal Health eliminates that workflow tax. A single unified environment serves both exploratory and GxP-regulated work - same platform, same packages, same code - with a validation layer operating underneath regardless of study type. The environment does not change when a study's regulatory status does.Human pharma has been moving in this direction for years. For Animal Health, this is a first. We share the design decisions, the implementation reality, and the transferable principles for any organisation still running parallel toolchains today.

sessions.title: Still Viewing Your Data Through a Keyhole?
sessions.abstract: We all know the situation: SAS datasets, JSON, XPT, XML and the simple question: what’s actually inside? Too often we only see our data through a keyhole.Working with clinical and structured data usually means dealing with different formats, different tools and a lot of switching back and forth, even for simple exploration tasks. Looking at data should not feel harder than understanding it.The Cumba Data Browser provides a single environment for exploring large datasets across formats including Dataset-JSON, SAS, Parquet and Excel. Users can directly navigate, search, filter and inspect their data without preparing subsets first or jumping between tools.Integrated statistics and visualizations help to quickly identify distributions, trends and outliers during the exploration process itself. The goal is simple: less technical friction and a more complete view of the data.

sessions.title: Back to the Future of CDISC Open Rules Authoring: Humans, AI, or Both?
sessions.stream: Machine Learning, AI & Large Language Models
sessions.abstract: Authoring data validation rules is inherently challenging, requiring understanding of data standards, regulatory expectations, and precise logical formulation. While the CDISC Open Rules method provides an exciting, standardized way to express validation logic in a transparent and reusable manner, writing high quality rules at scale remains time intensive and expert driven.Building on an earlier GPT based proof of concept, we evolved toward an agentic AI architecture for rule authoring. Instead of a single model, specialized AI agents refine rule intent, generate executable code, create validation test data, and review all outputs. This modular approach improves transparency, traceability, and controllability, key requirements in regulated clinical research, while supporting structured human in the loop oversight.To evaluate impact, we conducted an AI versus human experiment, comparing experienced rule authors with an AI assisted workflow for development time and rule quality. The results offer practical insights into how AI can augment expert rule authors and support scalable adoption of CDISC Open Rules.

sessions.title: AI-Driven Automated Validation of Intercurrent Event Using Raw or SDTM Data
sessions.abstract: This paper introduces an automated framework for programming and validating intercurrent events (ICE) directly from raw clinical trial data or SDTM domains, enabling Biostatisticians and validation programmers to independently verify whether Statistical Programming (SP) teams have correctly derived or imputed ICE-related datasets.The workflow standardizes identification of treatment discontinuation, rescue medication use, missed visits, and other protocol-defined intercurrent events using metadata-driven algorithms. By tracing derivations from SAP to analysis-ready datasets, the framework improves transparency, reproducibility, and quality oversight in estimand implementation. Automated comparison outputs allow Biostatisticians to rapidly detect discrepancies between independently generated ICE flags and programmer-created datasets, reducing manual review effort and minimizing risk of analysis inconsistencies. The approach also supports audit readiness by providing clear lineage and traceability across derivation steps.

sessions.title: From Kitchen to Table: Serving Insights With Internal Data Caterers and a Scalable FSP Engine
sessions.abstract: In the age of AI, organizations must fundamentally rethink the strategic role of Statistical Programming and their strategic use of Functional Service Provider (FSP) partnerships. This paper presents Bayer’s Data Caterer model, tracing the journey from building the “kitchen” to running it at scale. While FSPs have traditionally been used as capacity buffers, AI is reshaping workflows and challenging assumptions about in‑house tasks. Using a product centric operating model and introducing operational lead analyst akin to a sous-chef, Bayer separates strategic ownership from standardized execution. Internal teams shift their focus from “cooking” to owning the menu: defining strategic intent, shaping insights, and enabling decisions for product teams, while external partners evolve into scalable execution engines supported by Centers of Excellence. We share key lessons learned on combining process excellence and discuss how this model prepares organizations to absorb AI disruption while elevating internal capabilities in a rapidly changing landscape.

sessions.title: Automating ATOXGR Derivation: A SAS Macro Approach to Translating CTCAE Criteria into Executable Logic
sessions.abstract: Manual implementation of CTCAE-based toxicity grading for laboratory data (ADLB ATOXGR derivation) is typically performed using study-specific SAS code, where programmers interpret CTCAE criteria from source documents and translate them into hard-coded rules. This process is time-consuming, error-prone, and must be repeated whenever CTCAE versions are updated.This paper presents an automated SAS macro-based solution that removes the need for manual interpretation by converting CTCAE criteria from structured source files into machine-readable logic. The macro reads CTCAE definitions, transforms them into a standardized intermediate representation, and dynamically generates executable SAS code for ATOXGR derivation in ADLB datasets.By decoupling derivation logic from hard-coded implementations, the solution adapts across CTCAE versions with consistent structure, enabling scalable and reusable workflows. This approach reduces programming effort, improves consistency, and enhances traceability of toxicity grading aligned with regulatory source definitions.

sessions.title: Keeping ADaM Stable When the Registry Is Not: Programming Lessons from Long Term European RWE
sessions.abstract: Long term European real world evidence (RWE) studies increasingly rely on registry data mapped to the Observational Medical Outcomes Partnership common data model (OMOP CDM). While OMOP provides a structured mapping framework, partial implementations and evolving registry sources often result in frequent changes to data structures, mappings, identifiers, and source definitions. These characteristics create substantial challenges when deriving stable, ADaM structured datasets from OMOP based data sources.This presentation is based on two registry studies with up to 15 years of follow up, where vendor provided, partially OMOP mapped data changed during the study lifecycle. Programming approaches had to absorb upstream instability while ensuring stable and consistent ADaM datasets suitable for planned analyses and integration with other ADaM datasets. Addressing these challenges required well defined programming strategies and close collaboration across programming and statistical teams.The session focuses on practical, programming led solutions and presents a reusable framework for maintaining stable ADaM structured analysis datasets in the presence of unstable registry data.

sessions.title: Afternoon Break
sessions.abstract: Take a break in the Exhibition Hall to enjoy refreshments, expand your professional network, and explore exhibitor solutions. Play to Win! While you're in the Exhibition Hall, use the PHUSE Events App to check in at exhibitor booths, earn points and achievements, and climb the live leaderboard. Keep taking part in activities throughout the event to earn even more points!

sessions.title: AI: The New ‘X’ in GxP: A Practitioner’s Roadmap
sessions.abstract: As AI transitions from a pilot technology to a core component of the clinical data science pipeline, the Statistical Programmer is becoming the primary auditor of algorithmic integrity.Building on the principles of “Good AI Practice” (GAIP), established by the FDA and EMA, this presentation moves beyond ethical theory into practical application. We will examine the 2026 regulatory reality, explore how to answer the question: "Can I defend the integrity of the process that generated my TLFs?” and imagine what regulatory submissions will involve in the coming years. We will talk about documentation, human control and risk-management and finish off by looking at ensuring compliance without reinventing the wheel.

sessions.title: CDISC Open Rules: Progress, Performance, and Foundations for the Future
sessions.abstract: CDISC Open Rules is redefining how data conformance validation is performed across the industry. Significant progress has been achieved on both the rules and the CDISC Open Rules Engine (CORE), with major refactoring efforts focused on improving performance, scalability and long-term sustainability. This presentation will provide a comprehensive update on the current state CORE: from the rule authoring process and completion status to the engine and the technical enhancements implemented so far. The roadmap ahead will outline the plans for expanding rule coverage, governance, and innovations that will enable broad adoption through open-source collaboration. Attendees will leave with a clear view of where CORE stands today, a practical understanding of how to integrate open-source CORE validation into existing submission pipelines, and concrete ways to contribute their expertise to shape the future of CDISC Open Rules as the open-source reference implementation for conformance rules.

speakers.name: Els Janssens
speakers.job_title: Data Management System and Process Manager

sessions.title: From Study Lead to Molecule Lead: Navigating Growth, Complexity, and Identity in Statistical Programming
sessions.abstract: Career progression in statistical programming often follows a technical trajectory, but moving from study-level responsibility to molecule-level leadership introduces a significant shift in scope, mindset, and sustainability. This presentation shares a real-world perspective on stepping into a dual role as both study lead and Analytical Data Science (ADS) molecule lead within a global pharmaceutical environment.Overseeing multiple studies requires new approaches to prioritisation, delegation, stakeholder management, and self-leadership, while balancing strategic oversight with continued hands-on delivery.This presentation shares personal experience and learnings about redefining professional identity, building trust across study teams, and developing sustainable ways of working in increasingly complex structures. It also reflects on challenges such as shifting expectations, letting go of control, and managing competing demands—and invites participants to share their own tips and strategies.

sessions.title: AI-nonymous: Training AI models without exposing the study
sessions.stream: Machine Learning, AI & Large Language Models
sessions.abstract: When training AI models, we want to provide data that we encounter day-to-day. But, of course, clinical data has strict confidentiality and regulatory restrictions.. This paper will show how we can anonymise a study while maintaining as much useful information as possible. We'll demonstrate which variables need to be redacted, and provide practical approaches so that we can maintain the integrity of the data. For example, we want to hide the subject IDs, while still being able to relate a given subject's AE data to their lab data. We'd also like to be able to remove the anonymisation afterwards in order to compare datasets produced with our original ones to validate the process , without compromising the anonymity of the final data. In addition to datasets, we need to anonymise study documents, such as the CRF, TLF shells, the dataset specs and the SAP - we'll go through how identifying information can creep into these and how to remove it while maintaining usability. And perhaps most importantly of all, we need to comply with GDPR and reassure sponsors in the robustness of this process, and we'll be touching on our experience of these conversations.

sessions.title: Re-Randomisation Tests in Clinical Trials: A Simulation Case Study and Practical Guidance
sessions.abstract: A re-randomisation test in a clinical trial serves as a tool for evaluating whether the trial has detected a true treatment difference, or if the results are simply a random fluke from a Type 1 error. They can be performed for any randomised trial, but regulatory authorities such as the EMA explicitly request them for adaptive designs like dynamic allocation. However, awareness of these tests is generally low, and they can involve multiple operational challenges.In this case study, we describe the technical details of the test, demonstrate how to perform it in SAS and R for a simulated clinical trial using dynamic allocation, and explain how to interpret the results under different scenarios. Additionally, we provide practical guidance on the test and highlight potential logistical difficulties, for example, how to determine if the test is appropriate, and how to prepare for the test while remaining blinded.

sessions.title: Aim for Sufficient, Not Perfect: A Risk-Based Prioritisation Framework in Clinical Trial Deliveries for the Statistical Programmer
sessions.abstract: In Novo Nordisk we are facing an increased workload, due to increases in complexity and number of trials, while not expecting an increase in work force. Though AI and automation might partly help us, we believe that the lowest-hanging fruit in optimising the use of our time, is to do less. To help prioritising our effort to the trials and tasks where it has the highest impact, we have introduced a framework encouraging our statistical programmers to do less on trials and tasks where the extra work has the lowest value. This consists of a 3-step tiering model for trials and six degrees of freedom for tasks. For each tier-level, we have set caps on e.g. number of TFLs or level of review. Similarly, we introduce points-of-no-return for corrections, and generally encourage a higher degree of documenting errors of low importance, rather than correcting them. In this talk we will present the outline of this model, as well as our initial experiences with implementing such a change.

sessions.title: Beyond Code: Collaboration Challenges in Pharma Open Source
sessions.abstract: Open-source adoption in the pharmaceutical industry continues to grow, yet sustainable contributions and long-term collaboration remain significant challenges. Compared to other industries, contribution models in pharma are often limited by complexity, compliance expectations, fragmented ownership, and uncertainty around governance and maintenance responsibilities.This presentation explores key challenges surrounding open-source collaboration in clinical research using OpenStudyBuilder as a practical example. It outlines the considerations, experiences, and developments that led to the creation of a collaborative alliance model designed to strengthen industry alignment, co-development, and long-term sustainability. The session highlights how the alliance evolved, its current state, and its future direction in advancing OpenStudyBuilder toward enabling a truly connected digital data flow for the pharmaceutical industry.

sessions.title: SDTM in the Pipeline: Automated SDTM from Data Drop to Review-Ready with Scheduled Orchestration
sessions.abstract: SDTM delivery typically involves multiple manual steps—retrieval, comparison, conversion, validation, reconciliation, and summarisation—where inefficiencies and errors may arise during handoffs. This presentation explains our scheduled, end-to-end Azure DevOps parent pipeline that automates SDTM delivery from data receipt to review-ready outputs. Python components handle data retrieval and verification over SFTP, while SAS processes (SASPy/IOM) and cross-delivery comparisons operate at RAW and SDTM levels. The pipeline automates XPT generation, executes Pinnacle 21 CLI validation, reconciles findings across deliveries, and updates team trackers. Integrated governance includes real-time Microsoft Teams notifications, reviewer approval gates, and retention of audit-ready logs and reports. Attendees will see how our innovative, layered, non-disruptive approach enhances efficiency, consistency, and auditability while allowing teams to maintain familiar workflows.

sessions.title: The Future Regulatory Ecosystem: AI, Digital Evidence, and Intelligent Submissions in the Next Decade
sessions.abstract:
The pharmaceutical industry stands at a regulatory inflexion point. As health authorities worldwide reshape their expectations for clinical data submissions, sponsors face an urgent imperative: evolve the submission ecosystem now or face mounting defensibility risks in the future.
This panel brings together experts to explore the key themes shaping the future of regulatory submissions and agency partnerships:
• The growing role of AI in submission dossier preparation, review, quality control, and regulatory assessment.
• Increasing automation, incorporating global standards and end-to-end digitalisation of regulatory processes across the product lifecycle.
• The expansion of real-world data, digital health technologies, and novel evidence sources within regulatory decision-making frameworks.
The panel will discuss emerging regulatory initiatives, opportunities for greater efficiency and transparency, and potential challenges relating to validation, trust, explainability, data integrity, and compliance. It will also explore how health authorities may leverage AI-enabled review environments, structured data submissions, and integrated evidence ecosystems, as well as what sponsors should do today to prepare for the future.

speakers.name: Helene Royo
speakers.job_title: Director and Team Lead, Data Science Acceleration @ Roche

sessions.title: From Deliverable Validation to Standards Lifecycle Validation Using CDISC CORE
sessions.abstract: Clinical validation activities are traditionally focused on final SDTM package and Define.xml files. However, many inconsistencies originate much earlier through collection definitions, controlled terminology usage, and SDTM implementation decisions.This presentation explores how CDISC CORE can be used earlier in the standards lifecycle to validate data collection definitions, SDTM libraries, and controlled terminology metadata before deliverables are generated.The discussion focuses on the operational value of validated upstream definitions and how they improve the reliability of processes such as SDTM conversion, Define.xml generation, annotated CRF creation, and standards automation workflows.By applying executable validation rules earlier in the lifecycle, organizations can strengthen consistency across standards assets and reduce the propagation of implementation inconsistencies.

sessions.title: Cracking the Code: Mastering ATS (Applicant Tracking Systems) to Land Your Dream Job
sessions.abstract: In today’s competitive job market, ATS (Applicant Tracking Systems) are the gatekeepers of the “Pharma Club” (Industry). They’re just scanning for the "right" keywords and throwing everything else into the "rejected" pile. Understanding how ATS works can significantly enhance a candidate’s chances of landing an interview. However, there is no need to worry! This presentation is here to help you crack the code. We’ll show you how to make your resume ATS-friendly by including keyword optimization and formatting guidelines. You will dodge formatting disasters and avoid common mistakes that will make an ATS “skip” your profile. By the end, you’ll know exactly how to write a resume that gets noticed by both ATS and the human recruiters. Following “key principles” you will improve your “PERSONAL CODE” readability in an ATS-driven recruitment process, ensuring YOUR application reaches decision-makers.

sessions.title: AI-Assisted Safety Trend Analysis for Late-stage Oncology Studies
sessions.stream: Machine Learning, AI & Large Language Models
sessions.abstract: Reconciling safety trends between interim and final analyses is often a scramble, and the legacy approach relies on copy paste and manual review. This paper presents an AI assisted workflow for a late stage Phase III oncology study that ingests two safety reports with different data cutoffs; unifies them into a single comparative report, and highlights what has changed, like: overall AE rates, CTCAE grade shifts, Grade ≥3 and drug related events, dose interruptions/reductions, deaths, serious AEs, and discontinuations. Using SAS generated outputs combined with lightweight generative review, the method computes clear deltas, ranks the largest movers, and flags areas for deeper programmer investigation. Robust guardrails ensure every AI “headline” is verified against source data and tables, with traceable annotations. The outcome is faster, reproducible insight with fewer surprises and more time for meaningful discussion. We also share practical prompts that transform safety tables into concise storyboards, accelerating sponsor and governance review.

sessions.title: Beyond Manual QC: AI Assisted Detection of Human Error in Large Scale TLF Review
sessions.abstract: In large clinical studies, the number of TLF outputs can reach hundreds, with total page counts extending to thousands, often under tight timelines for programming and review. Even with rigorous validation processes, human error remains unavoidable, particularly when identifying inconsistencies across large volumes of outputs.This paper introduces a scalable framework for automated TLF output review, scanning outputs at the page level to identify inconsistencies such as population mismatches, cross table discrepancies, and structural deviations that may be missed during manual QC. The framework is implemented in Python and uses generative AI models adapted to clinical studies to perform contextual and layout aware assessments, alongside deterministic comparison methods to validate population counts against source data.This approach enables earlier detection of high risk issues, reduces manual effort, and improves the consistency and efficiency of large scale clinical reporting review.

sessions.title: Modernising Clinical Data Workflows Through Platform Innovation
sessions.abstract: This presentation shares argenx's, use-case-driven evaluation of SAS Viya and Posit R as a next-generation advanced analytics platform spanning Clinical Data Acquisition, Quantitative Sciences and beyond. Use cases stress-tested in 2025: Cloud auto-scaling and in-memory computing, R connectivity, multi-language programming (SAS, R, Python), VS-Code and Co-Pilot integration, Custom App(s), Self-Service Analytics Dashboards (RWD), SAS Clinical Acceleration (as replacement for SAS LSAF in 2027), AI/ML model governance, in-database scoring (Databricks) for Clinical Biomarker data, and metadata cataloguing. Overall, this work provides a practitioner-level blueprint for adopting cloud-native analytics in regulated environments—enabling faster insights, regulatory confidence, and scalable growth through a federated, cross-functional operating modelWe are aiming to go-live for Test/Prod GxP SAS Viya environments by Sep, as such we will also share our learnings on the early implementation and Posit R deployment (hosted by SAS and managed by OCS with support of Open Analytics).

speakers.name: Stijn Rogiers
speakers.job_title: Head of Data Integration and Standards (Data Acquisition)

sessions.title: Cross Industry Evaluation of Open Source R Packages for Clinical Trial Quality Management
sessions.abstract: The IMPALA consortium and PHUSE Open RBQM workstream lead industry collaborations to advance open-source statistical tools for clinical trial quality management. Recently, IMPALA members evaluated the {ctas} R package by detecting standardized anomalies injected into fifteen studies across three companies. These anomalies targeted site-level features—including average, standard deviation, range, unique value ratio, auto-correlation, and local outlier factor—within patient time series. By merging confusion matrices into a shared performance metric, we confirmed {ctas} effectively detects outliers and established collaborative recommendations for its default parameters.This shared evaluation approach proved more interpretable than our previous assessment of the {simaerep} package, which used inconsistent company-specific strategies. To support industry adoption, we integrated these tools into the PHUSE {gsm} framework by developing {gsm.simaerep} and {gsm.ctas} extensions. These efforts ensure high-quality, open-source monitoring solutions are both adaptable and accessible for modern clinical trial oversight.

sessions.title: Scaling Clinical Data Review with R Shiny: Real-Time, High-Performance, Flexible, Cost-Efficient
sessions.abstract: Commercial platforms have long been the default for large-scale clinical data review across ongoing trials, but they are costly, rigid, and slow to meet evolving needs. At Regeneron, we developed an R package enabling efficient implementation of study-level R Shiny apps to replace commercial tools entirely. The apps deliver comprehensive coverage – Demographics, AEs, CMs, Disposition, Exposure, Labs, Vital Signs and many more – via a modern UI with interactive filtering and clickable visualizations that drill from aggregated analysis to patient-level data. The app ingests near real-time data streams, so reviewers always work from the latest data, accelerating decisions. We prioritize performance by moving away from popular but performance-heavy libraries, achieving sub-second response times, much faster than prior commercial solutions. The framework balances standardization and customization, ensuring consistent deployment across all Regeneron trials while remaining adaptable to study-specific needs. This work demonstrates what open-source tooling can achieve in clinical data review – delivering flexibility, real-time insights, cost savings, and superior performance at scale.

sessions.title: SDRG Automation Made Possible!!!
sessions.abstract: Creating and updating SDRG in connection with submission to various authorities often involve long and tedious manual processes that can benefit from a makeover.Based on Phuse SDRG template, Novo Nordisk has incorporated a solution that front-loads the creation of submission ready SDRG, including study-specific details and conformance validation reports, into an automated flow that also encompasses the generation of SDTM and define-XML in various versions. With this addition, we close the loop of submission deliverables related to study data.In this presentation, we will share the considerations (balancing complexity, efficiency, agility and user friendliness), design and technical implementation of our metadata/data-driven solution that leverages the power of multiple programming languages and machine-readable formats.

sessions.title: Navigating Career Pathways in the Clinical Industry
sessions.abstract: Career progression for programmers and statisticians is not limited to linear, role specific advancement. Professionals increasingly seek upward movement and will try to achieve this by either rising within their departments or making lateral transitions across functional areas. This presentation explores logical and achievable career pathways within clinical programming and statistics, focusing on the skills and experiences required for progression and mobility. We examine differences between the following pathways and the skills and experiences required for each. Firstly, the Vertical Advancement from individual contributor roles to technical leadership or management, highlighting the growing importance of communication, business understanding, and stakeholder engagement alongside technical expertise. Secondly, the Cross Departmental moves, identifying transferable skills and realistic transition points between functions such as programming, statistics, data science, and operational roles.

sessions.title: AI Programmer: Autonomous Generation of CDISC-Compliant ADaM Datasets via Multi-LLM Cascade Architecture
sessions.stream: Machine Learning, AI & Large Language Models
sessions.abstract: The creation of CDISC-compliant ADaM datasets remains a major bottleneck in clinical trial reporting. AI Programmer introduces a fully autonomous pipeline that converts clinical specifications into validated R code with no human intervention until final review. The system uses a six phase multi-LLM cascade: Gemini’s long context window processes complete study documents for relevance filtering and dependency extraction, while Claude generates the final R implementations. A dependency graph framework determines variable derivation order and selects domain appropriate comparison keys (ADSL, BDS, OCCDS) to enable accurate row level validation. Compliance is enforced through a penalty weighted match rate that evaluates both value accuracy and dataset completeness, applying penalties for missing or extra rows against gold standard outputs. In deployment across four production studies, the architecture demonstrated zero shot generalization to unseen ADaM domains, achieving over 50% first pass accuracy. Key safety domains such as ADAE achieved 70–77% success, supporting the feasibility of end-to-end automated regulatory grade dataset generation.

sessions.title: Longitudinal Funnel Plots for Determining KRI Thresholds - The {gsm.timez} R package
sessions.abstract: Observing site-level key performance indicators is an integral part of risk-based quality monitoring in clinical trials, often represented as simple ratios. A typical example is adverse event rate over time, with monitoring thresholds defined using normal approximations. The funnel plot method dynamically adjusts these thresholds based on denominator counts, allowing for wider margins for smaller sites. However, the likelihood of clinical events largely depends on the study protocol and the schedule of assessments. To address this, we extended the funnel plot method to control for the time each site has spent on the study, implemented in the R package {gsm.timez}. We apply the funnel plot method to growing time windows of cumulative event counts for each site, creating study-month specific thresholds. This approach highlights whether flagged risk at a site is emerging, persisting or resolving. These temporal risk dynamics are displayed on a heatmap, enabling cross-site comparisons. The {gsm.timez} package builds on the Good Statistical Monitoring {gsm} framework and has been open-sourced by the IMPALA Consortium, a cross-industry organization developing tools for quality analytics.

sessions.title: UCB’s Transition to Open-Source: A Managed Identity Shift, not a Technology Migration
sessions.abstract: UCB’s transition to open-source was framed not as a tools change but as a managed shift in professional identity and perceptions of legitimacy.For programmers, whose authority is tied to SAS, a credible transition must go beyond retraining people, to reshaping what counts as competent work.The programme was built around four pillars: making the industry shift to open-source visible and undeniable; building technical capability; reframing professional identity around open-source; and embedding the practices so they persist without programme support.They were delivered through four workstreams: Communications, Training, Operational Use Cases, and Webhub, with project management holding coherence across them.The initiative was continuously evolving, regularly engaging both internal and external programmers to encourage shared ownership and embed the cultural change.The presentation explains the principles behind this framework and how they enabled a self-sustaining ecosystem; what worked, what resisted, and the successes that shaped sustainable adoption.It is offered as a case study in treating open-source transitions as an identity problem first, and a technical one second.

sessions.title: A Case Study in Adoption and Adaptation of Open-Source Statistical Software for Industry: MetaInsight
sessions.abstract: Open-source statistical software provides powerful tools without the cost of building and maintaining bespoke solutions in-house or the licencing costs of commercial software. However, software developed by academics may not meet the requirements for use in a regulated environment, such as validation and reproducibility. We present these barriers within a case study of the successful adaptation and adoption of a point and click network meta-analysis (NMA) tool developed in R by statisticians and software engineers at the Universities of Leicester and Glasgow. Whilst the analyses conducted in the app were statistically robust, they were not reproducible and it was difficult to install and run the app on secure corporate networks. In collaboration with the Global Biostatistics and Data Science team at Boehringer Ingelheim we have worked to make the app more suitable to deploy and use. We have made analyses reproducible outside of the application, converted the app to a CRAN package and added the ability to save analyses and access the data. Teams at Boehringer Ingelheim can now conduct NMAs via a simple to use interface, whilst keeping data secure and being confident of the results.

sessions.title: Death by a Thousand Spreadsheets: Making the Connection for Streamlined CDISC 360i Workflows
sessions.abstract: SDTM workflows remain fragmented across spreadsheet specifications, define.xml generation, Reviewer’s Guides, and annotated CRFs, with the same metadata repeatedly recreated across disconnected artefacts. This duplication creates maintenance burden, metadata drift, and inconsistencies throughout the submission package.This work presents a JSON-native SDTM mapping architecture in which standards, Controlled Terminology, sponsor metadata, and protocol-derived metadata are connected dynamically through APIs rather than maintained in spreadsheets. A single machine-readable metadata layer acts as the canonical source for downstream outputs.From the same metadata structure, SDTM transformation logic can be generated in SAS, R, and Python, while define.xml, Reviewer’s Guide content, and aCRFs are rendered automatically rather than independently authored. Conformance validation using CDISC CORE is integrated directly into the workflow.The result is a reproducible, traceable, metadata-connected workflow demonstrating a practical implementation of the CDISC 360i vision using existing standards and open-source tooling.

sessions.title: AE Individual Swimmer Plots for Integrated Safety Visualization in Clinical Trials
sessions.abstract: Swimmer plots are well established in oncology for displaying treatment duration and response over time. This approach can also be applied to safety data, yielding AE individual swimmer plots that provide insight into adverse events across safety domains.These plots are generated in SAS 9.4 using adverse events from ADaM ADAE dataset.Presenting timing, duration, severity, and potential relationship of adverse events to treatment in a single display offers a comprehensive individual-level view and enhances understanding of participant heterogeneity.AE individual swimmer plots can be extended to incorporate treatment exposure and additional safety data, creating a more complete participant safety profile. This enables visualization of adverse event evolution over time and supports identification of temporal patterns, relationships, and potential safety signals.Overall, AE individual swimmer plots are a powerful visualization tool that improves interpretation of adverse event data and strengthens participant-level safety assessment in clinical trials.

sessions.title: Accelerating Safety Aggregate Reporting Using Generative AI for Cross‑System Information Consolidation
sessions.abstract: Preparation of Safety Aggregate Reports requires early-stage consolidation of critical information dispersed across multiple structured and unstructured sources, making project initiation time‑consuming and resource‑intensive. We propose a Generative AI–enabled document assembly framework that automatically compiles prerequisite project content into a standardized document before analytical work begins. The solution applies large language models and rule‑based extraction to harmonize information from prior submissions, quality control artifacts, clinical trial metadata repositories, tracking tools, document management systems, workflow logs, and statistical programming results. Key outputs include study lists with all the protocol information, design summaries of ongoing studies, safety aggregate report type and submission context, and pre‑populated communication templates. By replacing manual cross‑system searches with a single automated consolidation document creation tool, the approach aims to reduce time to first draft, improve quality and consistency, mitigate risks of potential delays, simplify documentation completion, and increase overall team capacity.

sessions.title: An R Package for End‑to‑End Quality Control of ADaM Datasets and Aggregate Report Deliverables
sessions.abstract: Statistical programming in clinical research supports the preparation of analysis datasets and regulatory reports derived from source data, across individual or aggregated studies. As the pharmaceutical industry evolves towards the adoption of open-source programming languages, Quality Control (QC) must adapt to remain robust and efficient. This work presents a standards-aware R package of QC functions supporting two-step validation and independent use across reporting requirements. ADaM datasets are rebuilt from SDTM data and compared with the corresponding analysis datasets, while reports are recreated to validate the final tables. In this way, both the data and the outputs are confirmed within a unified framework. In addition, a preliminary QC function compiles and validates key study metadata from internal databases, ensuring consistency and completeness prior to downstream validation activities.With minimal user input, the package delivers immediate QC results and detailed comparisons for detected discrepancies. This approach is broadly applicable across the pharmaceutical industry to a wide range of reporting workflows.

sessions.title: Beyond Swimmer Plots: Discovering Hidden Patient Journey Patterns Through Visual Fingerprints and Clustering
sessions.abstract: Traditional swimmer plots depict individual patient journeys but often fail to reveal deeper patterns within them. This presentation introduces a novel approach that transforms longitudinal clinical data into compact “patient fingerprints,” encoding key events such as dosing changes, adverse events, and responses along a unified time axis. These visual signatures enable rapid comparison across patients while preserving temporal complexity. Building on this representation, we apply unsupervised clustering techniques to identify recurring journey archetypes, such as early responders with transient toxicity or patients with delayed response following dose modification. The approach integrates SDTM and ADaM datasets into a reproducible pipeline, supporting scalable generation of both individual-level and cohort-level insights. By combining intuitive visualization with data-driven grouping, this method moves beyond descriptive plots toward pattern discovery. It offers a practical framework for enhancing clinical interpretation, supporting cross-functional discussions, and uncovering signals that may be obscured in traditional analyses.

sessions.title: Boost Your Comparison!
sessions.abstract: The goal of the %compare-ds macro is a clear and improved dataset comparison in one call. Developed to support IDDI statistical programming activities, the macro builds upon PROC COMPARE by adding several automated enhancements. The two datasets are automatically sorted by the “ID” (key) variables, and the differences are printed into more complete and clear tables. Moreover, there are many parameters in addition to the classic PROC COMPARE options. There is the possibility to standardize character variables to match even though there are some differences in casing, blank spaces, special characters… and it is then applied identically on both sides to get a more reliable result. You can also add “data options” linked to the input datasets from macro parameters. Another improvement is the creation of two datasets by input: one containing the duplicate records and one containing the records present in the input dataset but not its counterpart.

sessions.title: Building It Right the First Time: A Practical Playbook for First-Time QC Programming
sessions.abstract: Efficiency in statistical programming requires proactive error prevention. This poster introduces a comprehensive "First-Time QC Playbook" designed to build quality into every step of SDTM, ADaM, and TLF development.Traditional QC approaches often rely on finding errors after the fact, causing rework and delays. Our playbook shifts this approach by using metadata-driven checks and smart automation at key development stages. By using standardized checkpoints and automated verification, programmers can fix potential issues before formal QC begins.The methodology demonstrates how preventive quality measures reduce back-and-forth cycles, speed up delivery, and strengthen deliverable quality. Key components include pre-QC self-check lists, metadata consistency checks, and automated cross-domain relationship verification.This practical framework provides actionable strategies that teams can immediately adopt to shift from reactive to proactive quality. We include usage scenarios, before/after workflows, checklists, and automation templates teams can tailor to accelerate first-time QC.

sessions.title: Building Next-Generation Talent: AstraZeneca’s Oncology Programming Graduate Program
sessions.abstract: AstraZeneca’s Programming Graduate Program was designed to strengthen in-house talent by giving early-career programmers structured exposure across the drug development pathway, through a targeted curriculum where rotations are integral. Over two years, graduates complete rotations (6-8 months each) across Oncology Early and Late, Global Medical Affairs, Payers, or Statistics, contributing to key reporting events and building a bigger‑picture view of the medicine lifecycle before joining permanent teams. In this poster, we outline the Early Career Team model with a dedicated cohort line manager who aligns expectations, coordinates development, and strengthens belonging. We also showcase graduate contributions to study milestones via these rotations and to non‑project AI, open‑source and other initiatives, demonstrating measurable impact early in their careers. Graduate feedback highlights clear progression pathways, real‑world accountability, and room to innovate. These outcomes build AstraZeneca’s internal capability, support the AI30 goal, and advance the 2030 Ambition.

sessions.title: Building a Unicorn Farm: Rethinking Skills‑Based Career Pathways Across Standards, Data Science, and Automation
sessions.abstract: Career progression in clinical programming is often shaped by linear pathways, influenced early by education that channels individuals into defined specialisms. While these foundations are valuable, they can limit how skills evolve and are recognised over time. As careers develop, people build broader capabilities through experience, curiosity, and exploration, often combining deep technical expertise with cross‑disciplinary strengths. However, these blended skillsets do not always have clear or valued progression routes, with advancement still closely tied to seniority and people management.Within Veramed’s Technical Solutions Group (TSG), we developed Unicorn Farm, a skills‑based approach that embraces these differences, identifying high‑impact skill combinations and enabling structured, non‑linear career pathways. Using skills matrices and evolution maps, we introduced advanced technical roles aligned with management seniority, emphasising expertise, influence, and mentorship.Attendees will gain practical insights into building flexible career pathways, recognising technical leadership, and creating space for people to grow beyond the paths they were originally set on.

sessions.title: Closing the Gap from Bedside to Reporting: Lessons Learned Using BDC as EDC
sessions.abstract: Bedside Data Capture (BDC) has long been regarded as the “holy grail” of clinical trial data collection, promising the elimination of paper-based processes, improved data quality, and significantly faster timelines from source to reporting. As BDC has become a reality at many clinical trial sites across the industry, the next logical step is to evaluate the use of the BDC database as the source Electronic Data Capture (EDC) system.This poster describes the implementation of BDC as EDC within a Phase I CRO statistical programming department and outlines the benefits achieved, including enhanced data quality and reduced reporting and programming timelines. It also examines the challenges encountered, such as implementing change management within and across departments, and the inherent limitations that necessitate innovative approaches from programmers.

sessions.title: Define.xml 2.1: Common Implementation Mistakes and How to Avoid Them
sessions.abstract: Background: Define.xml 2.1 plays a key role in providing clear and traceable SDTM and ADaM metadata for regulatory submissions. Despite this, teams often encounter recurring issues that affect validation outcomes and slow down review. Typical problems include mixing Define.xml 2.0 and 2.1 elements, incomplete or inconsistent codelists, unclear variable origins or derivations, missing or improperly linked supporting documents, and XML structural errors that trigger P21 validation failures. Together, these issues reduce metadata readability and increase rework during submission.Objectives: This poster shares practical lessons learned from multiple Define.xml 2.1 implementations and identifies the most common and impactful errors.Methods: We propose a prevention-focused approach that combines targeted P21 checks with an internal automated checklist covering metadata consistency, controlled terminology, XML structure, and document linking.Conclusions: Practical examples and clear recommendations help improve accuracy, consistency, and overall regulatory readiness.Keywords: Define.XML, Pinnacle 21, CDISC, SDTM, ADaM, metadata

sessions.title: Dynamic Report Generation with R Markdown and Proc Stream
sessions.abstract: R Markdown is a system that blends plain text with executable code—commonly R, SAS, and Python—to produce fully reproducible documents, dashboards, and even R Shiny applications. An R Markdown (.Rmd) file can be rendered into formats such as PDF, DOCX, or HTML, with HTML outputs offering interactive features. By unifying narrative, computation, and visualisation, it enables you to write, analyse, and present results within a single, streamlined workflow. However, creating .Rmd files directly in a text editor has its limitations. Although R Markdown supports dynamic text, it offers limited programming logic and text substitution outside of code chunks. This is precisely where the SAS macro language shines. When paired with Proc Stream, it allows all text to be parsed programmatically first, making the generation of .Rmd files far more flexible and dynamic. The presentation introduces this innovative concept and then illustrates it through a practical application.

sessions.title: Hero-in-the-Loop: A Super Squad Approach to SDTM Creation & Validation
sessions.abstract:
Behind every high-quality, CDISC-compliant SDTM dataset lies a team of data-driven heroes: Data Managers, Standards Managers, Clinical Programmers, and Biostatisticians, each bringing their own unique skillsets and expertise to the fight for clean, conformant data.Our heroes may hail from different domains, but they share a common trait: a working knowledge of CDISC standards. Already familiar with the tools of the trade, this foundational knowledge becomes their secret weapon: breaking down long-standing silos and enabling smarter, more collaborative workflows than ever before.
In a world of evolving standards, AI-assisted processes, and ever-increasing expectations, the path to submission success isn’t always linear. Understanding the strengths of each role opens up opportunities to rethink traditional processes.This poster will present our SDTM Squad, outlining the signature skills and superpowers each role brings to the clinical trial data lifecycle, supercharged by emerging contributions of AI. By highlighting the strengths of this dynamic team, we’ll demonstrate that with the right strategy and collaboration, regulatory compliance can be both faster and more heroic.

sessions.title: Key Takeaways From the PHUSE RWD Guidelines for Programming and Analysis Processes White Paper
sessions.abstract: This poster summarises key insights from the PHUSE white paper RWD Guidelines for Programming and Analysis Processes, which provides practical guidance for statistical programmers and cross functional teams involved in real world evidence (RWE) studies intended for regulatory submission. The paper highlights the growing importance of real world data (RWD) in complementing randomised controlled trials through broader patient representation, long term safety evaluation, and evidence generation in complex clinical settings. The poster focuses on major themes including study planning, feasibility assessments, protocol and SAP development, fit for purpose data evaluation, vendor engagement, and governance through the proposed RWD Study Council and RACI framework. It also emphasises the role of statistical programmers in ensuring data quality, standardisation, reproducibility, and regulatory readiness throughout the study lifecycle. Additional topics include confounding, bias mitigation, data provenance, ethics, and privacy considerations under frameworks such as GDPR and HIPAA. Overall, the guidance supports more transparent, reliable, and submission ready RWE studies.

sessions.title: Local AI's Dirty Secret: Your Workstation's Carbon Bill
sessions.abstract: When we discuss the environmental impact of AI we focus on massive data centres and the resources they consume, but what about the workstation running on your desk eight hours per day? This presentation reveals the hidden three-year cost of local AI computing through comparative analysis of consumer hardware options, from laptops and mini computers to dedicated GPU systems. The findings are stark: the most powerful option produces emissions equivalent to international flights or thousands of miles of driving, while costing more annually than many expect to pay upfront. Yet testing shows most users' actual workflows run perfectly on hardware they already own. This talk presents a decision framework for choosing AI computing power based on genuine need rather than perceived requirements, potentially saving attendees thousands in costs and significant carbon emissions.

sessions.title: Multidimensional Stacked Plots for Clinical Data Visualization and Real-Time Analytics
sessions.abstract: As clinical trial data becomes increasingly complex, there is a growing need for visualization methods that present multiple analytical dimensions within a clear and interpretable framework. This poster demonstrates the use of multidimensional stacked plots, including heat maps and stacked bar plots, for enhanced clinical data exploration and monitoring.The approach integrates with CDISC SDTM and ADaM standards to support scalable, metadata-driven, and reproducible visualization workflows. These visualizations enable simultaneous representation of treatment groups, adverse event severity, response categories, longitudinal trends, and subject populations.The poster also highlights integration with real-time dashboarding environments, enabling dynamic updates and interactive clinical review during study conduct. By combining standardized clinical datasets with interactive visual analytics, the solution supports faster signal detection, improved risk assessment, and more efficient decision-making across clinical development teams.

sessions.title: Operationalising the DC Domain in SDTM IG 4.0
sessions.abstract: The increasing use of subject re screening and re enrolment in clinical trials has highlighted limitations in how subject level data are represented in SDTM, particularly within the DM domain. When subjects participate more than once, DM alone cannot capture multiple enrolments or maintain clear traceability of demographic data, increasing review effort and the risk of misinterpretation.SDTM IG 4.0 introduces the Demographics for Multiple Participations (DC) domain to address these gaps by representing each enrolment as collected. This poster presents IQVIA’s practical experience implementing the DC domain across a range of study designs. It outlines patterns, key metadata considerations, and examples of DM–DC alignment that support transparent review and downstream ADaM creation. The poster also summarizes cross industry feedback, challenges encountered during adoption, and pragmatic solutions proven effective in practice. Attendees will leave with a clear understanding of when and how to use DC and how to transition standards as organizations move toward SDTM IG 4.0.

sessions.title: PHUSE Working Groups Highlights
sessions.abstract: The PHUSE Working Groups aim to create a collaborative and transparent environment where academia, regulators, industry, technology providers, and other stakeholders can address computational science needs crucial for health product development and regulatory review. This collaborative effort ultimately ensures the delivery of safe and effective medical products to patients. The nine PHUSE Working Groups have made significant contributions, publishing both new deliverables and launching new projects. These efforts have been showcased at both in-person and virtual events. Each project and event aligns with the PHUSE mission to Share, Contribute, and Advance, providing valuable resources for the community. The Working Groups consist of volunteers from diverse sectors, including academia, pharmaceuticals, biologics, devices, contract research organizations, core laboratories, technology vendors, SDOs, and regulatory agencies. Participation is open to all interested individuals. For more information, contact workinggroups@phuse.global.

sessions.title: Parallel Submission-Ready CDx Data: Standardisation that Speeds Precision Trials and Review
sessions.abstract: Companion diagnostics (CDx) guide who can join a study and who can safely receive a targeted therapy. Regulators encourage co-development of the drug and the CDx, and coordinated review models (such as FDA–CMS Parallel Review) show how aligning evidence can speed access decisions. In real programs, parallel submission of the therapy and CDx increases pressure on clinical teams to deliver CDx data that are clean, traceable, and ready early—while assays, vendors, and cut-offs may still evolve.This poster shares a practical approach to CDx data standardisation that supports faster, more consistent submissions. We structure CDx data around the specimen, test method/platform, assay version, result validity, and final interpretation, and align these elements to CDISC concepts and FDA data conformance expectations. Standard derivations produce subject-level “CDx eligible” flags and concordance summaries with local testing, with automated checks for invalid runs and repeat testing. The result is less reconciliation, smoother joint drug–diagnostic review, and clearer patient selection evidence.

sessions.title: Poster Session – Sponsored by Entimo
sessions.abstract: Attendees can explore posters, exchange viewpoints, and uncover strategies in an interactive setting. Sponsored by: Entimo

sessions.title: Push, Test, Deploy: CI/CD for Multi-Environment Clinical Data Workflows
sessions.abstract: Building and maintaining automated clinical data flow requires consistent quality across frequent changes, multiple contributors, and heterogeneous execution environments. In Novo Nordisk, we adopt a Git based CI/CD approach to develop and implement a standards driven framework, with automated deployment to both Databricks and SAS Viya environments. Our CI/CD pipeline integrates automated testing as a core component of the release process, linking version controlled code directly to test execution and deployment. This supports traceability, reproducibility, and consistent validation outcomes across platforms used in downstream clinical workflows. To address the challenge of scaling test coverage, we introduce an AI assisted approach for test creation, where program requirements and examples are used to generate reusable, rule based test cases aligned with predefined testing standards. Human review and standardised templates are used to ensure test transparency and regulatory suitability.

sessions.title: QCTLCOMPARE: No More Chaos for QC Tracking
sessions.abstract: Maintaining a clear and up‑to‑date overview of QC progress for clinical reporting deliverables is challenging in environments with frequent data updates and parallel programming. QC of outputs often requires reruns after new data transfers, manual review of comparison results, and separate maintenance of tracking systems. For large studies with hundreds of outputs, these activities are time‑consuming, error‑prone, and reduce transparency of overall study status.This poster introduces QCTLCOMPARE, a SAS® macro developed to standardize and automate QC comparisons for clinical trial tables and listings. The macro compares production RTF outputs with QC datasets by converting outputs into SAS datasets and applying structured checks using PROC COMPARE. Results are presented in an HTML comparison report and simultaneously recorded in a central programming tracker immediately after each QC rerun. This enables real‑time visibility of QC status across outputs without additional manual tracking. Practical examples illustrate reduced effort, improved efficiency, and enhanced traceability.

sessions.title: R You Creating ADRG?
sessions.abstract: Preparing ADRG (ADaM Reviewer’s Guide) documents is often manual and time-consuming. This presentation demonstrates how to use R, in particular Quarto, to automate part of the process to create ADRG.docx file. To do so we are reading ADaM datasets and metadata and using this info to print the information into the ADRG text. Using parameterized Quarto templates into the workflow helps in reproducibility, reduce programmer handwork, improve consistency, and accelerate review cycles. Practical examples and code snippets show implementation steps and limitations. The final document will not be submission ready, but it will be closer than a standard template, thus reducing programmer time in manual work.

sessions.title: Reducing ADaM and SDTM Specification Rework with a Metadata-Driven Generation Framework
sessions.abstract: Manual creation and maintenance of ADaM and SDTM specifications can require substantial effort and introduce discrepancies when dataset structures change during development. To reduce this manual workload, we implemented a metadata-driven programming framework that automatically generates standardized ADaM and SDTM specifications from centrally maintained source metadata. The framework extracts variable attributes, derivation logic, controlled terminology, and dataset-level details, then transforms them into specification output through programmatic processing. This approach reduces repeated editing, improves consistency between specifications and derived datasets, and supports faster updates when metadata change. By minimizing manual intervention, the framework also helps strengthen traceability and maintain alignment with ADaM sand SDTM standards throughout the development cycle. The poster describes the programming approach, metadata structure, and operational benefits of the solution, with emphasis on reducing manual work and improving efficiency in ADaM and SDTM specification production.

sessions.title: Rethinking Bias in Real-World Evidence: A Structured Framework for Health Equity Analytics
sessions.abstract: Real-world data (RWD) offers valuable opportunities for monitoring population health and assessing health inequalities. However, its validity is often undermined by systematic biases inherent in the collection, analysis, and interpretation of the data. This approach outlines a concise methodological framework to explain how biases related to selection, measurement, and time related, as well as confounding factors arise in RWD and distort estimates of health inequalities. Common mitigation approaches include propensity score based methods for confounding, inverse probability weighting for selection bias, validation and sensitivity analyses for measurement error, and time dependent modeling alongside target trial emulation for time related bias. It should be noted that these biases can distort the estimation of inequality indices, with the comparison before and after bias correction serving as a key tool for reliable quantification. The proposed framework offers a structured basis for a more transparent and reproducible analysis of RWD in health equity research.

sessions.title: Set, Flag, Filter: A Practical Framework for Implementing Estimand Strategies in Clinical Trial Data
sessions.abstract: Estimand strategies are increasingly used in clinical trials, especially since the ICH E9 (R1) addendum introduced an estimand framework for study design. As the complexity of both trials and study designs rises, the approaches to estimand strategies often become more intricate as well. It is therefore essential to establish a robust method for capturing intercurrent events and incorporating them into analysis datasets, whilst ensuring that estimand strategies are applied transparently.This paper describes how an occurrence-structured ADICE (Intercurrent Events Analysis Dataset) dataset can be used to track intercurrent events, along with record-based flags that integrate with other analysis datasets. By using these flags, programmers can simply filter data according to the estimand strategy needed for each analysis. Practical examples included in this poster equip readers with methods they can apply in their own clinical trials, while providing a framework adaptable to more complicated analysis requirements.

sessions.title: The Adventures of a Validated Statistical Computing Environment: A Journey From Startup to Scale up
sessions.abstract: Validated statistical computing environments are essential to pharmaceutical and life sciences organisations, but their design and implementation must reflect the scale, maturity, and regulatory needs of the business. A solution that is appropriate for a startup may not meet the operational, security, and compliance requirements of a larger organisation.This poster explores how the needs of a small pharmaceutical company evolve as it grows, and how those changes affect the design and governance of a validated statistical computing environment. It outlines the common requirements that apply across all stages, including system security, regulatory compliance, and user consistency, while highlighting the additional demands that emerge as organisations scale.The poster also considers how careful architectural planning can support growth from a small initial implementation to a larger enterprise environment without disrupting established ways of working. The aim is to provide a practical framework for designing systems that are scalable, compliant, and sustainable across the business lifecycle.

sessions.title: The Mouse Behind the Keyboard
sessions.abstract: Animal testing in clinical research is a reality we can't ignore. Despite incredible advances in medicine, nothing can quite replicate the intricate, whole-organ systems of living creatures like humans. Because of this, pharmaceutical companies are legally bound by strict international and UK regulations to ensure patient safety. But what if we looked at it from the mouse's perspective? In this paper, we’ll dive into the breakthroughs that were only possible thanks to these animals. We’ll also explore how the industry is working to safeguard their wellbeing, using the guiding principles of the 3Rs—replace, reduce, and refine—paving the way for more ethical, innovative research.

sessions.title: Turning Up the Heat: A Comparative Analysis of Heat Map Generation in R and SAS
sessions.abstract: Heatmaps are a graphical representation of data using colour coding to describe relative intensity of observed values in a matrix. In recent years, the use of heat maps within the healthcare and the pharmaceutical industry have increased due to their ability to visualise large and often complex data in an easier manner. As organisations look at adopting open-source alternatives such as R over traditional languages like SAS, an important question surfaces: what are the comparative benefits and limitations of each language for this specific application? This paper aims to compare both software’s to generate a heatmap using identical datasets whilst examining native options and inherent imitations. We will explore similarities and differences between both approaches to evaluate the effectiveness of the software to create the same type of output and provide a recommendation to users to select the best suited language for their specific requirement.

sessions.title: Unearth the Unexpected: D·I·Gging Beyond Standard TLFs with Open Source Applications
sessions.abstract: Have you ever wondered if there's more to your data? Have there been questions from clinicians resulting in dozens of tables, listings and figures (TLF) – just to find out there's nothing to see? Bayer's Data Insight Generation (D·I·G) project addresses this challenge through a portfolio of interactive and open-source R Shiny applications that support exploratory analysis of safety, efficacy, subgroup, benefit-risk, and time-to-event data. Built to answer specific scientific questions, each app enables interactive, visual exploration that goes far beyond standard clinical trial analyses. In practice, these tools facilitate communication and discussions within the study team while reducing post-hoc TLF production and accelerating insight generation. As a result, the D·I·G portfolio makes high-quality interactive data exploration accessible to any team working with clinical trial data.

sessions.title: Unexpected Retrospective CBER Requests: Lessons Learned Across Three Years of Vaccine Submissions
sessions.abstract: At PHUSE EU 2023, we shared initial experiences with CBER review expectations for vaccine submissions, including unexpected requests for retrospective modifications to SDTM and ADaM deliverables extending beyond existing FDA guidance and common industry implementation practices.Since then, industry initiatives presented at CDISC EU 2025 have aimed to improve alignment on CBER expectations and facilitate cross-sponsor exchange of regulatory feedback and additional data requests. Despite these collaborative efforts, subsequent regulatory interactions demonstrated that the scale and operational impact of retrospective requests had been significantly underestimated.This poster summarizes observations gathered over three additional years of interaction with CBER. We describe the volume, nature, and timing of retrospective requests affecting SDTM structures, ADaM derivations, and downstream TFLs. In several cases, requests were received after datasets and Clinical Study Reports (CSRs) had been finalized, resulting in substantial rework, re-validation activities, and regeneration of outputs late in the review cycle.Examples of requests extending beyond current CDISC standards!

sessions.title: Unleashing SpecToADaM: Automating the Journey from Clinical Specifications to ADaM datasets
sessions.abstract: Manual translation of clinical specifications into SAS programs for ADAM datasets is time-consuming and error-prone, creating bottlenecks in clinical trials programming. SpecToADAM is a hybrid AI-assisted system that automates Excel specification translation into ready-to-review SAS or R code. Breakthrough transparency features address the critical "black box" problem in AI-assisted programming. The system provides complete variable traceability, revealing derivation methods (direct mapping, RAG-matched, or AI-generated) with similarity scores and source documentation. An integrated conversational interface enables programmers to query, understand, and refine generated code through natural dialogue, with automatic version tracking maintaining full audit trails. Testing across safety and efficacy ADAM datasets demonstrates high accuracy with code generation taking 5-15 minutes. This poster includes the system architecture, method distribution analysis, accuracy comparisons, and code refinement workflows illustrating how transparency features enable programmers to rapidly validate and refine code, transforming AI into an explainable, auditable tool for regulated clinical programming.

sessions.title: Unlocking Insights with Flexible Temporal Perspectives
sessions.abstract:
Preclinical, clinical, and real-world data represent time in different ways, ranging from scheduled timepoints and visit windows to study days and actual event dates. To support interpretation across the research phases, it is important to explore data from multiple temporal perspectives.
A connected graph database enables temporal analysis across these perspectives by preserving relationships between events, findings, and observations over time. Within clinical studies, both visits and study days are essential when evaluating data. A graph database makes it possible to investigate associations both within visit windows and on actual event dates, for example between adverse events and abnormal laboratory measurements occurring on the same day.
This poster will illustrate how different temporal perspectives can influence interpretation of data across drug development phases and how graph-based integration can support more contextual exploration of complex study data throughout the drug development lifecycle.

sessions.title: When Claude Met ADaM: A Particular Set of Skills for Agent-Assisted Programming
sessions.abstract:
AI coding agents promise faster, more consistent clinical programming, but ADaM development requires more than syntactically correct code. It requires interpretation of specifications, source data, implementation guidance, package behaviour and QC findings.
We share lessons from a framework using Claude Code to support ADaM programming with the pharmaverse admiral ecosystem. The framework builds on principles of context, control and quality. Context is managed through curated knowledge packs: structured summaries of source data, mapping specifications, selected ADaM implementation guidance, package behaviour and post-run diagnostics. Control is maintained by having the agent generate draft mapping scripts and initial QC checks for human review, positioning it as a collaborative assistant rather than an autonomous generator. We show how Claude Code's skills and agents, packaged as a plugin, encode this framework as reusable tooling. Quality is strengthened through independent QC and executable post-run checks, with outputs from agent-drafted scripts benchmarked against independent double programming on lupus ADaM datasets.
The work highlights common implementation challenges, emphasising the need for iterative refinement to evolve the agent's skills and toolsets. It demonstrates how managed context and targeted checks turn a general-purpose coding agent into dependable clinical-programming support.

sessions.title: Registration & Welcome Refreshments – Exhibition Hall Open
Off Grid, On Call: AI at the Edge of Medicine
sessions.abstract:
AI and improved connectivity are making increasingly autonomous care possible at the edge of the Earth and beyond. Dr Beth Healey has spent her career working in extreme environments: on the ice, as station doctor through an Antarctic overwinter at Concordia, a European Space Agency analogue for spaceflight; underwater, as expedition doctor for National Geographic Pristine Seas; and at a distance, as an emergency physician at Geneva’s 144 dispatch centre.
Satellite connectivity now brings telemedicine and AI-supported diagnostics to places that once had only a radio. In deep space, communication delays mean medical decision support must work without help from Earth. Closer to home, emergency services are testing new technologies, such as estimating vital signs from a smartphone camera, to support triage decisions.
Yet tools that perform well in the lab can struggle in the field. Drawing on frontline experience and her own research, Beth will explore the challenges of testing and implementing AI-enabled solutions in clinical practice: where AI genuinely helps, where it fails quietly, and what this means for anyone building or trusting AI with real-world data.
