sessions.title: Data First: Connecting the Digital Protocol to Analysis-Ready Data
sessions.abstract:
At previous PHUSE Connects, d4k have demonstrated the CDISC Unified Study Definitions Model (USDM) eProtocol standard, Biomedical Concepts (BCs), and the implementation of end-to-end study data automation through a series of technical demonstrator systems. This has made the USDM vision tangible and real for the industry.
Building on these earlier workshops, this session extends that work to address what the industry is still missing: a clear, data-focused vision for the future.
This interactive workshop will provide participants with hands-on experience of:
• Selecting a protocol from ClinicalTrials.gov for use during the session (with a pre-selected back-up protocol available)
• Loading the selected protocol into USDM
• Adjusting the study protocol and design, including the schedule of assessments, where required
• Driving data capture artefacts from the digital study design
• Loading and linking subject-level data to the digital design
• Generating SDTM datasets
• Producing artefacts such as annotated CRFs and define.xml
• Exploring analysis concepts used in:
• the automated generation of ADaM datasets
• an electronic Statistical Analysis Plan (SAP).
The workshop will focus on what is practically achievable today, demonstrating how USDM, BCs, SDTM, and ADaM can be brought together in a seamless, integrated manner. It will highlight the potential to move away from siloed, process-focused ways of working towards a data-centric model built on fully integrated standards.

sessions.title: Integrating unstructured exploratory biomarker data using CDISC SDTM standards
sessions.abstract: Exploratory biomarker (EB) data are increasingly collected alongside clinical trial data to support hypothesis generation on disease mechanisms and treatment response, but are typically not intended for regulatory submission. In practice, EB data arrive from multiple vendors in varied, non-standard formats, creating significant barriers to efficient and reproducible analysis.To address this, we applied CDISC principles and adapted SDTM to create a fit-for-purpose, catch-all Biomarker (BM) Findings domain tailored to exploratory use. This approach standardizes EB data while prioritizing usability for scientists and statisticians, and enables straightforward integration with existing submission-ready SDTM and ADaM datasets to support cross-domain analyses. Although designed for exploratory use, the BM structure also facilitates conversion into submission-ready domains should the need arise.This presentation outlines the design decisions, implementation strategy, and lessons learned when adopting CDISC standards for high-volume, multi-vendor exploratory biomarker data.

sessions.title: Healthcare Begins With Self-Care: Neuroscience-Based Tips to Improve Wellbeing and Increase Performance
sessions.abstract: Our days as statistical programmers are built on tasks that demand deep focus and sustained attention to detail. Yet staying sharp from morning to late afternoon is harder than it sounds — and the reason is not a lack of motivation or discipline. The human brain was not designed for the volume of decisions modern knowledge work demands. Research into cognitive fatigue shows that each decision we make — however small — incrementally reduces the quality of the ones that follow. By the time that 3pm review task arrives, our capacity for careful, concentrated work is already compromised. This session presents a set of practical habits and adjustments that help programmers protect their focus across the full working day. From structuring your schedule around your chronotype, to managing your environment, to knowing when to simply step away — these are small changes with a measurable impact on both output quality and wellbeing.

sessions.title: Nangula: Revolutionising clinical protocol disclosure using LLMs
sessions.stream: Machine Learning, AI & Large Language Models
sessions.abstract: Clinical trial protocol (CTP) define study objectives and must be disclosed to regulators before the start of a clinical trial. CTP disclosure process relies on manual extraction of information, which is labour-intensive, time-consuming, and error-prone. We developed Nangula, an LLM-based system to automate CTP information extraction for regulatory disclosure.Nangula uses a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) workflow combining keyword and semantic search, zero-shot prompting, and LLMs (GPT-4.1 and Claude 4.5 Haiku) to extract structured data. Built as a Streamlit application and orchestrated with DSPy, it identifies relevant sections via regex-based page detection, followed by semantic retrieval and LLM inference. Outputs are standardised using deterministic business rules and presented in an editable interface for human review. Final outputs include XML for ClinicalTrials.gov and Excel for EU CTIS submissions.GPT-4.1 accurately extracted 21 of 22 required fields, while Claude 4.5 Haiku performed strongly on inclusion and exclusion criteria. This RAG-based approach effectively automates CTP disclosure while preserving expert oversight through human-in-the-loop validation.

sessions.title: Practical Troubleshooting of PROC MIXED for Irregularly Spaced Longitudinal Data
sessions.abstract: Irregularly spaced longitudinal data can trigger convergence and covariance-structure warnings in PROC MIXED, delaying delivery of reliable results and requested outputs. This presentation uses a real-world clinical trial example to provide a practical, implementation-focused framework for troubleshooting common issues such as infinite likelihood, non-positive definite Hessian, and missing comparison output. Starting from an initial model specification, the session shows how standard covariance structures such as UN, UN(1), and AR(1) were evaluated and why they proved unsuitable. The final solution used SP(POW), which better reflects correlation across unequally spaced observations. A key lesson is that the spacing variable must represent actual elapsed time rather than ordinal visit labels; otherwise, correlation may be misrepresented. Emphasis is placed on reproducible diagnostic steps, clear decision rules, and practical SAS coding approaches that help statistical programmers move efficiently from warning messages to stable, review-ready mixed-model analyses.

sessions.title: The Escalation Problem in Biometric Teams: When Issues Reach the Wrong Level at the Wrong Time
sessions.abstract: Escalation of issues plays a critical role in how biometric teams manage risk, maintain quality, and support timely decision-making. In practice, however, escalation problems often emerge when issues reach the wrong level at the wrong time. Common signals of escalation imbalance include excessive leadership involvement in day-to-day operational decisions, delayed visibility of critical risks, repeated rework, unclear ownership, and communication bottlenecks.This paper explores the underlying causes of both over- and under-escalation across biometric organizations. Through practical scenarios and case studies, it examines how organizational hierarchy, ownership uncertainty, communication patterns, and visibility gaps influence escalation behavior, including differences between remote and onsite environments.Using practical frameworks and real-world examples, this paper provides actionable approaches for identifying escalation imbalance, improving escalation judgment, strengthening ownership and communication pathways, and helping teams resolve issues more effectively before they develop into larger operational or delivery risks.

sessions.title: Challenges and Lessons Learned from a Double Transition Journey: From Legacy to Modern Analytics Environment and from SAS to R
sessions.abstract: We describe our journey on a double transition, from a legacy environment to a modern analytics platform and from SAS to R. We addressed the challenges of translating business requirements across platforms and programming languages to ensure continuity and smooth transition. We maintained frequent and structured communication with the standards team supporting the new platform, which proved highly effective. We conducted extensive testing and proactively raised tickets for every encountered issue, actively influencing the platform design to better meet our needs. In parallel, we prepared our team through training and Q&A sessions, ensuring readiness for the new environment. We also contributed as co-authors, updating the programming master handbook, incorporating our experience and insights. Additionally, we adapted our quality control processes to align with the requirements and capabilities of the new platform and software. As the pharmaceutical industry continues shifting to open-source solutions such as R, this experience offers valuable insights.

speakers.name: Vasileios Tillis
speakers.job_title: Senior Associate, Senior Statistical Data Scientist

sessions.title: Metadata Collector: Automated Metadata Generation From Mock Shells
sessions.abstract: Statistical programmers and biostatisticians share responsibility for producing high-quality Tables, Listings, and Figures (TLFs), yet they use the same information in different formats: mock shells for design and metadata for implementation. This duplication increases the risk of inconsistency and rework.Metadata Collector bridges this gap by automatically creating and updating TLF metadata directly from mock shells in multiple output formats. The tool preserves design intent while enabling immediate use in metadata-driven programming workflows. In addition, machine learning supports automated generation of metadata variables, such as program names; a model trained on data from more than 100 clinical studies currently achieves up to 80% accuracy.By improving alignment between medical writing and statistical programming, Metadata Collector enhances consistency, reduces manual effort, and promotes unification and standardization of reporting practices across clinical studies.

sessions.title: Submitting PRO Data in Oncology Trials: From FDA Guidance to Practical Implementation
sessions.abstract: As PRO data becomes increasingly important in oncology trials, the FDA’s 2023 guidance clarifies the agency’s expectations for how missing data should be represented in submissions. Many of these expectations go beyond what is typically captured today, creating practical challenges and raising questions for study teams. This paper outlines what implementing the guidance looks like in day to day work, from data collection to final outputs. We discuss the feasibility of capturing reasons why questionnaires were not completed and the representation of those missing assessments in SDTM. We also focus on introducing phantom records in ADaM required to support FDA recommended outputs, including adding records after intercurrent events when questionnaire completion is no longer expected. In addition, we highlight several inconsistencies and areas where the guidance is not fully explicit and propose practical solutions to help teams navigate these situations and apply the guidance consistently while remaining aligned with FDA requirements.

sessions.title: Therapeutic Area Knowledge: Strengthening Collaboration Beyond the Data
sessions.abstract: The role of data scientists continues to evolve alongside growing expectations for efficiency, innovation, and cross-functional collaboration. While technical excellence remains essential, generating analyses is only part of the value technical professionals can bring to Clinical Development and Medical Affairs organizations. Drawing from experience as a data scientist supporting Global Medical Affairs in Rare Disease, this presentation explores how Therapeutic Area (TA) knowledge can strengthen collaboration between data scientists, Medical & Science teams, Medical Writing, and Medical Affairs functions. Understanding the therapeutic context behind the data helps technical professionals contribute more effectively to scientific discussions, evidence generation, and clinical storytelling. Using practical examples from Rare Disease and Medical Affairs collaborations, the session will discuss ways to build and apply TA expertise in day-to-day work, including understanding clinically meaningful endpoints, learning stakeholder language, interpreting data in clinical context, and identifying opportunities where analyses can create additional value for stakeholders.

sessions.title: Automating ADaM Specifications using Agentic AI
sessions.stream: Machine Learning, AI & Large Language Models
sessions.abstract: ADaM specifications form the foundation of clinical trial analysis, defining variable derivations, traceability, and downstream dataset generation. However, creating these specifications remains a time-intensive and error-prone process. While large language models (LLMs) offer automation potential, they lack access to critical study context such as the Statistical Analysis Plan (SAP), protocol, and SDTM metadata.This paper presents an agentic AI approach that augments LLMs with structured context retrieval. Using vector search, agents dynamically extract relevant SAP and protocol information, while function-calling interfaces retrieve SDTM metadata and ADaM Implementation Guide templates. This enables accurate generation of variables, computation methods, and predecessor relationships.In pilot evaluations, the system successfully generated approximately 80% of ADaM variable specifications with high consistency and traceability. This approach demonstrates how agentic AI can transform specification development into a scalable, metadata-driven process aligned with regulatory expectations.

speakers.name: Ashwin Kumar
speakers.job_title: AI/ML Engineering Lead – Clinical Trial Automation

sessions.title: Navigating the Noise: StatOps’ Fix for Discoverable Statistical Knowledge
sessions.abstract: GSK’s “StatOps” initiative started with a seemingly simple question: how do we accelerate modelling? To do this we needed to make it easier to find and reuse statistical code. And to help statisticians quickly apply new statistical methods. Step 1 was clear—all code goes into GitHub. The harder part was day to day use: how do we track and adapt to major changes in study design, help people find the right starting point, and make sure the code is understandable and adaptable. And what if there is no prior example? How do we help statisticians navigate a large, but disjointed set or supporting documentation for new statistical methods?Over the past year, we’ve worked with Statisticians and Tech colleagues to improve how we write, store and search statistical knowledge. We brought scattered vignettes and guidance into one place, built AI enabled search across Statistical Analysis Plans, and ran GitHub training tailored to Statisticians. We will share full overview of the project: the ideas that really made a difference, and those that did not.

speakers.name: Andy Nicholls
speakers.job_title: Head of Data Science Software and Innovation

sessions.title: ARTEMIS II – A Masterclass in Communication and Soft Skills for High‑Thriving Teams
sessions.abstract: At first glance, this title seems unrelated to People Leadership and Management in clinical research. Yet every day, we lead diverse, multidisciplinary teams under pressure, supported by cutting‑edge technology to deliver high‑quality data in fast‑paced environments. Despite proven expertise and innovation, teams still struggle with misalignment, delays and disengaged stakeholders. This presentation, will share key leadership lessons from NASA’s ARTEMIS II mission and demonstrate how these insights can be applied to successfully lead teams managing clinical trials. We will show how communication, trust, diversity and a sense of belonging are essential drivers of team performance. Beyond innovation and technology, these human elements enable alignment and accountability. Communicating well and clear is about ensuring teams and stakeholders feel heard, represented and motivated to move forward together. Lessons learned from ARTEMIS II offers a powerful lens on how strong people leadership and effective communication can transform capable teams into truly high‑performing ones.

sessions.title: Enter the Metaverse: Clinical Standards Built for AI
sessions.abstract: Clinical data standards underpin regulatory submissions and evidence generation, yet current standards and tooling were designed for manual, document‑centric workflows. As AI becomes increasingly embedded in clinical development, these limitations create inefficiencies, slow adoption, and hinder the safe and scalable use of AI across the data lifecycle. Addressing this gap requires rethinking how standards are defined, represented, and consumed by machines. Metaverse is an open‑source initiative that re‑imagines clinical data standards as AI‑ready, machine‑executable assets. By applying modern knowledge representation and software engineering, Metaverse turns data standards into the building-blocks for automation and traceability across clinical data processes. This presentation introduces the Metaverse initiative, its vision and design principles, and how it complements existing standards ecosystems. Attendees will learn how Metaverse supports AI‑enabled workflows, explore use cases, and understand how to engage with and contribute to this open‑source community.

speakers.name: Stuart Malcolm
speakers.job_title: Head of Standards, Efficiency and Automation

sessions.title: From Command Line to Shiny: Integrating CDISC CORE with R for Interactive Conformance Data Validation
sessions.abstract: CDISC CORE provides an open-source engine for executing conformance rules against CDISC standards, but in many teams its routine use remains tied to command-line workflows. This can limit adoption by reviewers, study teams, and programmers who need rapid validation feedback without terminal commands. This paper presents a production R Shiny application that brings CORE into an interactive browser-based workflow. Using processx, the application runs CORE as a managed subprocess while enabling users to launch validations, monitor progress, and review structured results from the Shiny interface. The implementation addresses practical needs in regulated clinical programming environments, including reliable CLI argument handling across CORE versions, real-time progress reporting, controlled concurrent execution on shared Windows RDP infrastructure, and an auditable run history capturing operator, engine version, datasets, controlled terminology package, and outcome. As CORE rules evolve, the application supports its use as a complementary validation process alongside established tools such as Pinnacle 21, strengthening data quality while preserving traceability and operational control.

sessions.title: When the Specification Is the Code: Zero-Drift Define-XML from Python Pipeline
sessions.abstract: In the traditional workflow, a specification author writes derivation rules in Excel, a programmer implements them in SAS or R, and a third person manually transcribes algorithms into Define-XML. Discrepancies between these artifacts are discovered, if at all, during QC weeks later. Fleet, a new open-source Python CDISC toolkit built on Polars namespace extensions, eliminates this class of defect by making the specification executable. A single define.yaml file, validated against a JSON Schema at edit time, drives both the derivation pipeline (via .from_spec()) and regulatory Define-XML 2.1 generation (via fleet define-xml). The --enrich-methods flag reads each verb's docstring and embeds it as an element, turning inline code documentation into algorithm descriptions with no manual step. Generated codelist classes provide typed, IDE-discoverable controlled terminology with full NCI concept ID traceability. This presentation demonstrates zero-drift delivery using CDISC Pilot 01: every method definition in the Define-XML traces directly to the code that produced the data.

sessions.title: Getting to Yes: Why Good Ideas Fail—and What Data Scientists Can Learn from Sales
sessions.abstract: When someone asks you a question - should your reaction be to give them an answer, or ask them "why do you ask"? Most ideas in clinical data science don’t fail because they’re wrong—they fail because they never get adopted. Whether it’s open source, AI, or process change, the hardest part isn’t the solution. It’s getting to “yes.”Technical experts are trained to be right. Organizations, however, make decisions based on risk, trust, cost, and competing priorities. The result? Strong ideas stall, die quietly, or never make it past initial skepticism.Sales professionals face this reality every day. They expect rejection, treat it as feedback, and adapt their message until it lands. What if data scientists did the same?This session challenges conventional thinking about influence and decision-making. It introduces a practical approach to reframing rejection, aligning with stakeholder incentives, and building momentum through small, credible wins.Lots of good ideas sit on the shelf or die on the vine. Why? Because impact doesn’t come from having the best idea—it comes from getting to yes.

sessions.title: Human-Centred AI Adoption in HTA Statistical Programming: Mitigating Knowledge Atrophy in AI-Augmented HTA Statistical Programming Workflows
sessions.stream: Machine Learning, AI & Large Language Models
sessions.abstract: AI can offer many benefits in terms of efficiency and insight, but one major adoption risk is increased abstraction between scientific programmers and analytical outputs. Such abstraction risks loss of accumulated domain knowledge and degradation of core skills. In turn, this may jeopardise regulatory credibility and reduce trust in submitted evidence. This paper distinguishes between transparent, explainable, and auditable methods that largely extend familiar statistical pipelines – so-called white-box AI – and more complex models whose internal mechanics are difficult to interpret – black-box AI. A concise taxonomy of these systems is proposed, ranging from rules-based and deterministic to entirely opaque models. The purpose of this taxonomy is to categorise the relative human-centredness of AI tools and to guide adoption decisions in scientific programming organisations. Lastly, next steps are presented, focusing primarily on a pilot project centred on intelligent quality checks, to capture initial evidence of knowledge atrophy and inform further adoption decisions.

sessions.title: Early Signals, Better Decisions: Action Limits as an Early Warning Mechanism
sessions.abstract: Brought to you by the Phuse Working group on QTL Threshold setting methodologies:Acceptable ranges are a component of modern centralized risk‑based monitoring. However, their practical application in ongoing clinical trials can be challenging, particularly when signals emerge late, and opportunities for mitigation are limited. This presentation explores the added value of action limits as an early-warning mechanism to complement monitoring conducted via Quality Tolerance Limits (QTLs). We illustrate how statistically defined action parameters and limits can detect emerging risks earlier in trial conduct, enabling timely, proactive intervention. By acting before QTL thresholds are approached or breached, this strategy helps preserve the statistical integrity of primary analyses, supports adequate power, and promotes sustained adherence to acceptable quality throughout the trial lifecycle.

sessions.title: Transition From a Culture of Compliance to One of Psychological Ownership
sessions.abstract: In the high-stakes environment of clinical data science, rigid adherence to SOPs often fosters a "compliance-first" mindset where employees focus on avoiding errors, trying to be safe and defensive rather than driving outcomes. While compliance ensures safety, it can stifle the innovation and accountability necessary for complex problem-solving. This presentation explores the shift toward "psychological ownership” - an environment where team members feel a deep personal responsibility for their work.We will discuss practical, proven strategies for managers to foster this mindset, including granting "how" autonomy while maintaining clear "what" goals, practicing radical transparency regarding company performance, and establishing psychological safety. By involving employees in early decision-making and shifting leadership from giving answers to asking guiding questions, organizations can move beyond mere task completion. Attendees will leave with actionable tactics to empower their teams, enhance individual accountability, and ultimately improve the quality and efficiency of clinical deliverables.

sessions.title: Establishing a Qualified R Package for PK/PD Analysis After SAS Migration
sessions.abstract: Previously, we demonstrated a GenAI‑assisted approach for migrating legacy SAS code to R as an initial step toward broader open‑source adoption. Since then, this effort has matured into a fully R‑native package for PK/PD analysis: pkadsbuildr. The package provides standardized templates for data transformation pipelines—such as NONMEM data sets—and includes over 40 domain‑specific functions covering imputation, baseline derivation, date‑time handling, and consistency checks. Beyond business logic, a full software development lifecycle has been established, including version control, unit testing, structured documentation and specifications as the basis for internal R package qualification. pkadsbuildr is now scheduled for release and use in regulated study data analysis at Boehringer Ingelheim. In parallel, supporting AI assets have evolved into a lightweight harness that assists statistical programmers in adapting package templates to study‑specific requirements. Attendees will be introduced to the package, its qualification process, and how programmers are supported in daily work.

sessions.title: ADaM Programs as Build Artifacts: The Open-Source Mighty Framework
sessions.abstract: When ADaM programs are deterministically generated from specification they become build artifacts that are regenerable and adaptive to data availability. The mighty framework, in production use at Novo Nordisk, implements this model.This presentation demonstrates three features this framework enables. (1) Derivation-level testing validates each derivation in isolation, once, then reuses it across studies; trust derives from the parts instead of review of the assembled code. (2) Pooled specifications cover all studies in a project. Study-specific expressions resolve at generation time, producing a tailored program for each study. (3) With SDTM-aware generation, derivations whose SDTM dependencies are absent are commented out automatically. Then as data arrives, regeneration activates them without manual intervention.All three require one commitment: never edit the generated ADaM program. With this approach, the programmer's effort moves from maintaining scripts to specifying them, closer to the scientific thinking that is at the heart of clinical studies.

sessions.title: PROC COMPAREing? Why Settle for the Default? A Toolkit for Effortless Data Comparisons
sessions.abstract: Are you tired of manually comparing datasets or directories after a quick PROC COMPARE overview reveals it won’t be that easy? We all know the tedious challenges: differing observation counts, too many differences for PROC COMPARE to summarize, and the need to uncover patterns in mismatches.This session introduces ready-to-use toolkits that effortlessly summarize differences in usable table outputs and eliminate the need to write code snippets from scratch each time. The toolkits provide all observations unique to one dataset, side-by-side comparisons of differing variable values from both datasets, and automated checks of whole directories in a single run.Compare smarter, not harder.

sessions.title: A Journey to Standardised Analysis Results Datasets in Alignment with CDISC ARS
sessions.abstract: Analysis results are essential in drug development, supporting regulatory submissions and informed decision-making. However, these results - commonly presented as tables, figures, and listings in static PDF reports - are difficult to reuse and lack standardization across sponsors. The CDISC Analysis Results Standard (ARS) addresses these limitations by enabling a structured, machine-readable representation of analysis results. This presentation will show how implementing Analysis Results Datasets (ARD), aligned with the CDISC Analysis Results Standard (ARS), can change the way analysis outputs are generated and used. We will describe a practical CRO implementation focused on the generation of ARD and establishing a standardized structure with scope for future expansion to analysis result metadata. Standardized ARD supports efficient double programming, consistent review processes, and provides a harmonized format for accessing and reusing results across multiple reporting activities.We will highlight practical challenges, critical design choices, and lessons learned from our implementation journey.

sessions.title: From Knowledge Transfer to AI-Guided Learning: How Mentoring Changed Over Five Years
sessions.abstract: For the past five years, I have been mentoring junior specialists and students within the Biostatistics Certificate Program at Intego Clinical. During this time, I have seen a major shift in the way people learn programming and approach problem solving, especially after AI tools became part of everyday work and study.When I started mentoring, students relied mostly on documentation, training materials, and independent research. Today, they can generate code, explanations, and examples within seconds. This has made learning faster and more accessible, especially for beginners entering clinical programming and biostatistics.At the same time, I increasingly notice challenges related to code readability, debugging, and understanding the logic behind AI generated solutions. Many students can produce working code quickly, but struggle to explain or troubleshoot it in real project situations.In this presentation, I will share practical observations from mentoring experience and discuss how mentoring approaches are evolving in highly regulated clinical research environments where validation, critical thinking, and maintainable code remain essential.

sessions.title: How to Control the Machine Spirit Without Just Praying for Success
sessions.stream: Machine Learning, AI & Large Language Models
sessions.abstract: AI talk is everywhere right now, and most of it is either sales pitches or doomsaying. What most of us actually want is something more practical: how to force the magical black box to stop using certain styles, to write structured code without burning through our tokens, and to leave our database alone when it stumbles on an API key.This paper shows what current techniques can do about exactly that, with Claude Code as our example. We will walk through system prompts for setting the ground rules, skills for teaching the model reusable patterns, hooks for catching dangerous actions before they fire, token management for keeping the bill sane, and ways to give the AI memory of what it has learned.AI shouldn't be a gamble, and it shouldn't be a séance either. Let's try to tame the machine spirit together, with the tools we already have.

sessions.title: Developing a Simulation-Informed Decision Framework for Interpretation of Interim Survival Data in Oncology Trials
sessions.abstract: Interim overall survival (OS) analyses in oncology can be difficult to interpret when progression-free survival (PFS) is favourable but OS data highlight potential harm. Such signals may reflect immature follow-up, informative censoring, post-progression therapies, or true harm, creating uncertainty for sponsors, regulators, and trial teams. Building on the work of a multi-stakeholder consortium convened by Friends of Cancer Research and aligned with FDA guidance on OS assessment, we developed a simulation-based decision framework to aid interpretation of interim OS results, to support sponsor–CRO decision-making and governance.The approach simulates correlated PFS/OS endpoints under pre-specified “truth” scenarios. Operating characteristics are estimated across different thresholds for harm, helping quantify the probability of detecting harm should it truly exist. We also describe practical ways to summarize multi-dimensional outputs for transparent discussion (e.g., heatmaps and scenario tables). Attendees will leave with a pragmatic blueprint for planning interim OS looks under a broad range of potential truths, de-risking the impact of variable OS data when PFS is positive.

sessions.title: Leading by Coaching: Practical Stories and Tools for Statistical Programming Leaders
sessions.abstract: What’s the ROI of being in the room? Personal stories you can’t google. This session shares lived moments from a Leader-as-Coach journey. Where coaching shifted delivery, trust, and careers in statistical programming. Instead of theory, you’ll hear real missteps and the exact coaching phrases that changed outcomes, then translate them into tangible tools you can use immediately. We’ll distil the patterns behind those stories into a photo-worthy micro-script for 1:1s, a coach-first decision test for high pressure moments, and a 14-day practice challenge to build habits without adding process. Attendees leave with one commitment made in the room, one question to adopt this week, and one ritual to try: practical, repeatable behaviours that help you lead more effectively through others.

sessions.title: The Evolving Role of the Analytic Software Developer: From Legacy Stability to AI-Driven, ‘Vibe-First’ Approaches
sessions.abstract: The Clinical Analytic Software Developer role is undergoing a fundamental transformation. For over a decade, the landscape was defined by stability, with tools remaining unchanged. Today, we are moving through a rapid evolution: from manual processing to human-led open-source collaboration, and now towards an AI-integrated future.While our team has long prioritised user-centric delivery over rigid infrastructure, an open-source-first mindset has accelerated this mission. By focusing on the users over systems, we provide rapid, iterative solutions to immediate challenges. We discuss our "community-first" approach: leveraging AI to build temporary workarounds today, while contributing permanent fixes back to Pharmaverse via GitHub to improve the ecosystem for tomorrow.Finally, we address the AI-driven takeover of traditional programming. This isn't just an incremental change; it is a radical pivot toward "vibe coding", where developers no longer struggle with syntax but instead orchestrate intent. We will share how our team is leading this charge, evolving from legacy stability into a future where AI-assisted creativity and user-centricity are the primary drivers of success.

speakers.name: Andy Nicholls
speakers.job_title: Head of Data Science Software and Innovation

sessions.title: Building Applications on Top of the SAS Viya APIs
sessions.abstract: SAS Viya ships a substantial REST API surface, and statistical-programming teams increasingly build internal tools - submission trackers, study dashboards, data-quality consoles, ad-hoc scoring UIs - on top of it. The hard part is rarely the API itself; it is delivering the same application across the contexts a clinical workflow demands: a standalone intranet web app, an embedded form inside a SAS Visual Analytics report, and an installable desktop client for analysts who roam between Viya environments. This presentation walks through a build pattern that ships one React/TypeScript/Vite codebase to all three targets at once. We cover the Vite alias trick that swaps the authentication implementation at build time (cookie auth, no-auth inside VA, and Electron OAuth2 PKCE behind one interface), a Go-template-safe script transform that lets minified JS embed cleanly into SAS Job Execution HTML, CSP and CORS realities, the IPC patterns required for a trustworthy desktop shell, and the renderer-side discipline that keeps the three targets behaviourally identical. Attendees leave with a concrete blueprint they can apply to their own Viya app projects.

sessions.title: Leading the Future With SAS
sessions.abstract: The SAS system provides many useful pre-compiled functions and allows users to create their own custom functions through the SAS Function Compiler Procedure (FCMP).However, SAS lacks a function for forward-looking operations. This limitation stems from the processing architecture of the DATA step, in which observations are read one at a time into the Program Data Vector (PDV). As a result, it is impossible to process a future observation while the current observation is being read.This paper explores the possibility of using PROC FCMP to construct LEAD(), the inverse of the natively available LAGn function, using a combination of the hash object, DOSUBL, and FCMP subroutines to simulate look-ahead behaviour within Base SAS.

sessions.title: Introducing PROC R
sessions.abstract: PROC R is the newest way to integrate R and SAS code in a single program. This procedure has methods for moving data between SAS datasets and R dataframes, transferring macro variables and values between the two, running SAS functions in R, and producing R graphics in SAS output. Comparable to PROC Python in general functionality, this new procedure allows programmers to use syntax from multiple languages in one executable program.

sessions.title: Digital Schedules of Activities (SoA): Why Precision and Completeness Are Essential for Operational Implementation and Interoperability
sessions.abstract: If digital protocols are to be relied upon as the single source of study truth, they must be complete, support automatic systems configuration, be interoperable, and precise. To be operationally valuable, this should reduce or ideally replace the need for QC beyond confirming that all study requirements are precisely specified for identified use cases. Current experience suggests this is often not the case; even with AI support, the QC burden frequently increases, and issue resolution times are extended. This paper discusses the experience of digitizing protocol schedules of activities and the challenges encountered in transforming these into precise, interoperable, machine-readable forms. We demonstrate how graph methods, supported by empathetic underlying specification models and SoA management tools, can achieve and confirm high precision and completeness of study operational requirements. Conversion to interoperable standards such as FHIR or USDM then ensures information consistency across a wide range of operational use cases.

sessions.title: Beyond the Syntax: Rethinking Training and Support for SAS-to-R Transitions
sessions.abstract: As the pharmaceutical industry increasingly adopts open source software, discussions often focus on technical barriers. While essential, these overlook a deeper challenge. For many Programmers, professional identity and a sense of mastery are deeply intertwined with the software they use.This talk presents a training and support programme designed to address hidden barriers during a transition from SAS to R. Drawing on interviews with Programmers, we found that dominant concerns were not technical competence, but fear of lost expertise and professional identity. The programme reframed training objectives: rather than creating R experts, rebuild confidence in programming ability independent of language. Live training sessions were designed as a liminal space: safe environments between professional identities, where participants could experiment and make mistakes without risk. Small groups worked together, debugging code in real time, shaping sessions through discussion and peer input. Feedback shows increased confidence and willingness to apply R in day to day work.

sessions.title: A Retrieval‑Augmented, Multi‑Agent Approach for Target Trial Emulation Protocol Development
sessions.stream: Machine Learning, AI & Large Language Models
sessions.abstract: Target trial emulation (TTE) provides a rigorous causal framework for generating real‑world evidence (RWE), but its practical implementation requires the precise specification of a hypothetical randomized trial and careful alignment across clinical, epidemiologic, statistical and regulatory domains. In practice, developing TTE-aligned study protocols is labor‑intensive, highly dependent on expert collaboration and vulnerable to inconsistencies, implicit assumptions, and limited traceability between design choices, and underlying causal principles. These challenges are compounded by the need to integrate heterogeneous knowledge sources such as regulatory guidance, SOPs, epidemiologic theory and prior studies. We present a retrieval‑augmented, multi‑agent framework to support TTE protocol development. The framework combines structured study intake, a hybrid knowledge base integrating vector embeddings, a knowledge graph, and specialized agents representing key expert roles (e.g., epidemiology, regulatory alignment etc.). By explicitly linking target trial components to methodological and regulatory requirements, the system enhances transparency, consistency and reproducibility.

sessions.title: See What Win Odds Hide: Unlocking Hierarchical Composite Endpoints with Maraca Plots
sessions.abstract: Hierarchical composite endpoints (HCE) are increasingly used in clinical trials to combine outcomes of differing clinical importance into a single, patient-centered endpoint. By prioritizing more severe events, HCE ensures treatment comparisons reflect meaningful clinical hierarchies. Treatment effects are typically summarized using win statistics, such as win odds, which provide an intuitive overall measure. However, these summaries can mask how treatment effects are distributed across individual components. Stakeholders often need clearer insight into where differences arise-whether from mortality, major morbidity, or less severe outcomes. The maraca plot addresses this gap by visualizing component-level contributions alongside overall effect estimates, offering a more comprehensive and interpretable view of HCE results. In this presentation, we demonstrate practical approaches to create maraca plots using SAS and R, including reproducible workflows and visualization techniques for clinical reporting. We also discuss key challenges, particularly in SAS, such as the lack of native procedures and the need for custom programming, and compare these with more flexible solutions in R.

sessions.title: Can Your Candidate Really Program? Interviewing Clinical Programmers in the GenAI Era
sessions.abstract: Generative AI assistants are rapidly becoming part of everyday programming workflows in clinical trials. While these tools can significantly improve productivity, they also create new challenges for hiring managers attempting to assess genuine programming expertise during interviews. Traditional interview methods often fail to distinguish between candidates who understand clinical data standards, validation principles, and regulatory expectations, and those who can simply generate convincing code using AI tools. This creates increasing uncertainty around what “programming competence” actually means in the AI era. The paper explores how interview processes for statistical programmers should evolve to remain effective and relevant. It introduces a practical framework for evaluating competencies that cannot be reliably outsourced to AI,including analytical reasoning, review of AI-generated code, error detection, and understanding of clinical trial workflows. The paper also provides examples of redesigned interview exercises and hiring strategies that reflect modern programming environments while preserving expectations for quality, compliance, and reproducibility in clinical research.

sessions.title: Moving Forw-ARD: Lowering the Barrier to Clinical Reporting with NEST 2.0 and {gtsummary}
sessions.abstract: In the past decade since NEST’s inception, we have built a robust foundation for R-based clinical reporting using {rtables} and {tern}. However, we have learned that even the most sophisticated engineering is only as successful as its adoption rate and user experience. The steep learning curve of the NEST 1.0 toolkit has made us re-think the balance between "architectural power" and "programmer preference."We are proud to present NEST 2.0, a strategic shift toward the {cards}/{gtsummary} ecosystem. This evolution prioritizes an intuitive, ARD-based (Analysis Results Data) workflow designed to resonate with statistical programmers. Key components of this new architecture include:Standardization: ARDs generated by {cards}/{cardx}.Customization: bridging the gap between the general functionality of {gtsummary} and the specific requirements of TLGs with {crane}.Accessibility: a comprehensive TLG Catalog providing ready-to-use starting points that significantly lower the barrier to entry.This session explores how we are refining a decade of progress to ensure our toolkit is not just a technical achievement, but a daily favorite for the people who use it.

sessions.title: Enabling Cross-Industry Collaboration With NNSynthetic: Realistic Simulated ADaM Synthetic Data and Clinical Utility Evaluation
sessions.abstract: Privacy and governance barriers often limit sharing of clinical trial data for academic collaboration. Novo Nordisk introduces NNSynthetic to address this challenge: a framework that generates realistic simulated ADaM datasets using a pharmacodynamic Emax dose-response model. It produces plausible treatment responses and between-subject variability for endpoints such as HbA1c and body weight, enabling clinical data science training without compromising patient privacy.To assess clinical relevance, models developed externally on NNSynthetic data are transferred into a controlled internal environment and evaluated against clinical trial data using pre-specified metrics. In a proof-of-concept with Aalborg University, two student groups use NNSynthetic for prediction and imputation modelling. Results show high similarity between synthetic and real datasets, with prediction performance differing by 0.04 AUROC and acceptable differences in RMSE and bias for imputation analyses. NNSynthetic reduces barriers to academic-industry collaboration, supports clinical data science education, and protects patient confidentiality while maintaining analytical relevance.

sessions.title: Demystifying CALL EXECUTE
sessions.abstract: The CALL EXECUTE routine in SAS allows code to be generated based on values in an input dataset. When handled correctly this can remove the need for explicitly defined conditional programming in many cases, and facilitate fully dynamic code. As the industry increasingly focuses on automation and data-driven programming, CALL EXECUTE has huge potential for greater use. However many programmers are unfamiliar with it, or uncomfortable with its syntax. This introductory presentation will explain the uses and benefits of CALL EXECUTE, and show how to construct a CALL EXECUTE statement. A worked example will be used to demonstrate how to apply CALL EXECUTE in a progressively more efficient way, and how to avoid common errors and bad practices.

sessions.title: Old, Not Obsolete! A Brief Introduction to Regular Expressions – and Why They Are Still Relevant
sessions.abstract: (If you already know that + is a subset of * but not of ? and that there is nothing outside ^ and $ this might not be for you) Today you can just ask AI to “give me some code to ...” - in many cases the resulting code works as intended, but the task and/or the policy of your company might require you to understand how and why it is working.Depending on what you asked, and what you data looks like the reply might contain what appears to be a string composed of random (mostly) non-alphanumeric characters... also known as a regular expression, which - simply put - is powerful pattern matching technique that dates back to 1950/60's.While you can ask AI to only use “simple code”, you can also challenge yourself and start learning regular expression. Yes, It can get really complicated really fast, but a basic understanding will get you a long way.In this paper you will get a brief introduction to the concept, some examples and practical use-cases. Oh, by-the-way... have you ever noticed that “regular expression” option in your editor’s “search and replace box”? Yep, It is not limited to “inside programs”.

sessions.title: From RAW to Ready: A Biotech's Approach to Building Standards from the Ground Up
sessions.abstract: For a company developing SDTM and ADaM standards from scratch, where should we begin? How do we get to the end goal? This paper describes how a biotech started building its own set of data standards from the ground up. We will explore the collaboration between Biostatistics, Statistical Programming, and Data Management, and any trade-offs involved. Elements of the process include going from RAW to SDTM by working with Data Management during database development and UAT, as well as working backwards from standard TFLs to drive ADaM design. Looking beyond initial development, we also explore how we could test our standards, including criteria for determining when they were ready to be used by study teams. Through this experience, we highlight our challenges and lessons learned in building SDTM and ADaM standards that are genuinely usable — not just compliant on paper.

sessions.title: Balancing Change and Delivery in Clinical Programming: Managing Evolving Tools, Standards, and Teams in the Context of Pharmaceutical Industry Transformation
sessions.abstract: The growing application of R programming and rapid development of Artificial Intelligence are reshaping the pharmaceutical industry, leading to a continuous implementation of new development tools and methodologies. While these innovations target increased efficiency, accelerate deliverables timelines, and optimized resources utilization, they present significant challenges for programmers who are required to balance the integration of new technologies with the maintenance of ongoing deliverables and meeting deadlines. Junior programmers are particularly affected, facing dual challenges while risking insufficient development of foundational knowledge of industry standards.This paper explores the advantages and disadvantages of the evolving technological environment for programmers, examining key challenges and potential solutions, and highlighting the need for adaptation effectively to these changes while maintaining high-quality standards and avoiding being overwhelmed by the pace of transformation driven by new tools and the AI era.

sessions.title: GxP-ready Agentic AI: Trustworthy Autonomy by Design
sessions.stream: Machine Learning, AI & Large Language Models
sessions.abstract: Agentic AI offers transformational potential across drug development yet sits awkwardly against the assumptions of existing GxP frameworks which assume a model-centric approach with narrow autonomy. Current guidance has not fully kept pace with the rapid emergence of agentic systems that rely on LLM-based reasoning, human approval gates and controlled tool use to achieve specific goals. We introduce a risk‑based framework of design principles for engineering GxP‑ready agentic systems, consisting of four elements: (1) clear definition of Intended Use and Context of Use with a prioritised risk register; (2) a controlled, deterministic tooling layer using the open‑source Model Context Protocol (MCP); (3) system assurance through golden evaluation sets, performance metrics and semantic consistency methods; and (4) ongoing accountability through human oversight and auditable system interactions. This framework builds on concepts from the FDA-EMA joint guiding principles, FDA Good AI Practice, and the EMA reflection paper on AI in the medicinal product lifecycle, by interpreting them at the architecture level for agentic systems.

sessions.title: Pathologist Agreement Studies: Addressing Cross-Correlated Binary Outcomes to Ensure Accurate Estimation of Uncertainty
sessions.abstract: Biomarkers are used to identify eligible patients for treatment. Pathologist agreement studies are essential to evaluate the reliability of diagnostic methods used in clinical practice. This work addresses the analysis of agreement where pathologists and tumor cases form a complex crossed and nested data structure. Three methods are explored: a method often used in practice - Clopper-Pearson (assumes independence), and two methods proposed to handle the correlation correctly - a nonparametric cluster bootstrap (resamples clusters of cases and laboratories) and a Bayesian generalized linear mixed model ([GLMM], with crossed random effects for case, laboratory, and pathologist nested within laboratory). A simulation study evaluated the bias and confidence interval coverage of these methods. Results indicate that the Clopper-Pearson method, as expected, highly underestimates uncertainty. Both cluster bootstrap and GLMM yield satisfactory coverage close to the nominal 95% in most scenarios. This work provides important guidance and recommendations for diagnostic agreement studies, ensuring accurate estimation to support reliable clinical conclusions and decision-making.

sessions.title: Unlocking Neurodiversity: Leading Standard Processes With Non-Standard Minds
sessions.abstract: Neurodiversity is often discussed as a strength in clinical data science, yet many people leaders are unsure how to translate that into day-to-day management. Drawing on my experience as a statistical programmer with ADHD, this session explores practical ways to unlock neurodivergent strengths such as pattern recognition, problem-solving and challenging assumptions. Neurodiverse teams can enhance performance and reduce blind spots, when they are structured effectively.The session focuses on small, workable adjustments across three areas: 1) Communication: using clear, consistent, structured instructions to make it easier to start and stay on track;2) Task design and prioritisation: framing work with a shared definition of “done”, what matters most, how priorities may shift, and giving direct, timely feedback to reduce rework; 3) Team culture: creating psychological safety and manager flexibility so people can be open about how they work.It’s not about special rules or major initiatives, and it’s not one-size-fits-all. The goal is to give leaders techniques they can apply immediately to improve how teams think, work, and deliver through better basics done consistently.

sessions.title: One Import, Every Layer: How Fleet Closes the Loop from CDISC Library to Clinical Tables in Python
sessions.abstract: Clinical statistical programming today requires five or more separate tools, each with its own language and metadata format, to move from raw data to a submission package. Fleet is an open-source Python toolkit that proposes an alternative workflow with a single import fleet statement. Built on Polars, Fleet registers chainable verb-per-line APIs directly on DataFrames (df.sdtm, df.adam.adsl, df.adam.occds, etc), where all verbs accumulate lazily into one execution pass. A single define.yaml drives both derivation code and Define-XML 2.1 generation, so specification and code never diverge. Using the CDISC Pilot 01 study, this presentation walks through a complete adverse-event lifecycle: from raw CSV through SDTM AE, ADaM ADAE, CDISC validation, and an AE summary table. Benchmarked on 11.5 million rows, Fleet completes an ADAE derivation in 9 seconds versus over 5 minutes for an equivalent multi-package pipeline, 35 times faster in 32% fewer lines of code.

sessions.title: From TLF Spec to Disposition Flow: A Web‑First Workflow Powered by SAS and GenAI
sessions.abstract: Creating disposition flows often depends on manual work in generic tools, where complex tables must be reinterpreted by hand. PatFlow, a web-based system for disposition flow authoring and validation, addresses this challenge by combining data, layout, and review in a single workflow. It pairs GenAI with the judgment of Medical Writers to produce study-aligned flows earlier. PatFlow integrates a React WebApp with SAS macros that generate the disposition table, big Ns, and an autoflow from patient data. Projects can be initialized from the Disposition Table Shell in the TLF specification with GenAI analyzing table structure to derive a draft graph, aligning shell and flow from the outset. Writers retain full control through a visual editor that is tailored to clinical conventions. Once study data become available, PatFlow becomes valuable for validation: it overlays counts, exploits graph morphology to detect numerical inconsistencies, and compares the initial design with a data-derived autoflow to reveal deviations in actual patient progression. In pilot use, easier authoring, earlier fit-for-purpose designs, and clearer discrepancy detection than table-only review was reported.
